### 3.2 The Listening Window

You have heard the movement once. Now we listen again, with timestamps into the Kleiber 1974 recording.

If you want to listen again — and you should, twice if you can — this time notice the specific moments below.

* **0:00–0:05.** The four-note cell, hammered in unison by the strings and clarinets. Notice that it is not yet a melody — it is _pure rhythm with one pitch dip_. Most amateurs hear it as "the opening of Beethoven 5"; experienced listeners hear it as _unisons_ , i.e., the entire orchestra playing the same pitches together, no harmony yet. The piece is opening at _maximum starkness_. Hold that starkness in your memory; the whole rest of the symphony is going to climb out of it.

* **0:05–0:20.** The cell is now in the strings, getting tossed around between the upper and lower instruments. It is no longer all-together-unisons — Beethoven has split the orchestra into voices. _The cell is travelling._ Listen for how many distinct voices you can count it in.

* **0:21–0:43.** The first long phrase, building energy, mostly the lower strings carrying a transformed version of the cell underneath fragments of it in the upper strings. _The whole texture is the cell._ Beethoven is not contrasting yet; he is sustaining one idea.

* **0:43.** A sudden horn fanfare — a strong, declarative four notes from the French horns. This is _the transition to the second theme_. The fanfare is itself a transformation of the cell (count: it is also short-short-short-LONG, just bigger and more open).

* **0:46–1:14.** **The second theme.** The strings now sing a lyrical, much more tender melody. Notice how unlike the cell this melody is — it is long, it is breathing, it is in a major key, it is _consoling_. But also notice the _cellos underneath_. They are still playing the four-note rhythm — _quietly, persistently_. The cell never leaves. It is just whispering now while the upper strings have their lyrical moment.

* **1:15–1:55.** Development of the second theme. The cell keeps surfacing in the lower strings. The energy slowly builds.

* **1:55–2:14.** A return to the cell-as-cell, now louder, now urgent. The exposition is closing.

* **2:14.** The exposition has finished. In most live performances, the conductor takes the repeat — that is, plays the whole exposition (0:00 to 2:14) over again. Kleiber takes the repeat, which is why the recording is so long. (Karajan does _not_ take the repeat in his 1963 reading. Currentzis takes a fast repeat.) The repeat is structurally important: Beethoven wrote it. It is also where you can listen for what changed on a _second hearing_ of the exact same material.

* **4:32 (after the repeat in Kleiber).** **The development section begins.** The cell, now in fragmented form, is going through key changes — the music modulates restlessly from one tonal area to another. The cell is taken apart, reassembled, taken apart again. This is the _workshop_ I promised you. About two minutes of relentless cell-transformation, mostly minor-key, mostly urgent.

* **5:30.** The development is at maximum tension. The cell is now reduced almost to its absolute minimum — just two notes at a time, hurled back and forth between the upper and lower strings. _This is the most fragmented you will ever hear the cell._

* **5:48.** **The recapitulation begins.** The opening four notes come back at full volume, all the strings together. You are back where you started — except that you have been somewhere for two minutes, and the return _means_ something it could not have meant the first time.

* **6:00.** Just after the recapitulation begins, Beethoven inserts a moment that does not appear in the exposition: a _solo oboe cadenza_. The orchestra stops. A single oboe plays a slow, sad, almost speaking phrase. Then the orchestra resumes. This is the most personal moment of the movement — the lyrical voice of a single instrument breaking through the structural symmetry. _Listen for it._ It lasts about ten seconds and it will stop your breath if you are paying attention.

* **6:10–6:55.** The recapitulation continues, working through the same material as the exposition but now in the home key. The second theme returns, now in C major (where in the exposition it was in E♭ major).

* **6:55–7:14.** **The coda.** A short closing passage built — naturally — on the cell. Final hammered unisons. The movement ends decisively, in C minor, on the cell's rhythm one more time.

The movement is about seven minutes. The cell appears in _almost every measure_. By the time the recapitulation arrives, you have heard the cell so often that its return at full volume feels like coming home — and that _feeling-of-coming-home_ is what Beethoven wanted, exactly that.

This is what the chapter means by _workshop_. Beethoven takes a four-note idea and works it from every angle. The movement is the work.

### 3.3 What's Happening in the Music

Three concepts, all of which the listening just illustrated: _motif_ , _motivic development_ , and (in preview) _sonata form_.

#### Definition: Motif

A motif is a short musical idea — usually three to six notes — distinctive enough to be recognized when it reappears in altered form, and used by the composer as material for an extended piece.

In plain language: a motif is a recognizable musical _fingerprint_. The opening four notes of Beethoven 5 (da-da-da-DUM) are a motif. The four-note opening of _The Simpsons_ theme is a motif. The two-note shark theme in _Jaws_ is a motif. The shorter and more distinctive the fingerprint, the more it can be transformed without losing its identity.

A motif is _not_ a melody. A melody is a complete musical thought, often eight or sixteen measures long, with a beginning, a middle, and an end. A motif is a piece _smaller than a melody_ — a building block out of which melodies and longer passages can be made. The four-note cell of Beethoven 5 is a motif; the lyrical second theme is a melody (and a long one).

#### Definition: Motivic Development

Motivic development is the process by which a motif is transformed across a piece of music — repeated, inverted, fragmented, lengthened, shortened, reharmonized, reorchestrated — without losing its essential identity.

In plain language: motivic development is what you just heard Beethoven doing for seven minutes. The cell is taken and put through every possible transformation: it is moved between voices, it is made loud and soft, it is fragmented down to its absolute minimum, it is buried in the texture, it is brought back to the surface, it appears in major keys and in minor keys, and at the recapitulation it returns intact. _This is the central technique of Beethoven's symphonic writing_ , and arguably the central technique of the entire Classical and early Romantic symphony.

Motivic development is a thing Beethoven did better than anyone before him and arguably better than anyone after. It is also a thing the amateur listener can be taught to hear in about an hour, which is the time it takes to listen to this movement twice with the chapter open.

#### Definition: Sonata Form (preview)

Sonata form is the most important large-scale architectural plan in classical music from about 1770 to about 1900. The first movement of almost every symphony, concerto, sonata, and string quartet from this period is in sonata form. It has three main sections:

  1. **Exposition.** The composer "exposes" the main themes of the movement. Usually two contrasting themes — a first theme (often dramatic, urgent, in the home key) and a second theme (often lyrical, in a contrasting key). The exposition often ends with a closing passage called the _codetta_. In Beethoven 5 first movement, the exposition runs from 0:00 to 2:14, with the first theme being the cell and the second theme being the lyrical melody you heard at 0:46.

  2. **Development.** The composer takes the themes from the exposition and _develops_ them — transforms them, fragments them, moves them through different keys, builds tension. This is the workshop. In Beethoven 5 first movement, the development runs from about 4:32 to 5:48.

  3. **Recapitulation.** The composer brings back the themes from the exposition, this time both in the home key (the second theme is _transposed_ into the home key, where it was in the contrasting key in the exposition). The recapitulation gives the listener the experience of _return_. Often followed by a _coda_ — a closing passage that wraps up the movement decisively. In Beethoven 5 first movement, the recapitulation runs from 5:48 to about 6:55, with the coda from 6:55 to 7:14.

You do not need to memorize this. Sonata form is taught in full in Chapter 6 (Mozart's _Eine kleine Nachtmusik_), where the piece is short enough that the whole form can be seen clearly. In Beethoven 5, we are previewing sonata form in a movement where it is operating at much larger scale. The thing to take away: _exposition, development, recapitulation_. Three sections. Beethoven's first movement is one big A — B — A' (with A being the exposition, B being the development, A' being the recapitulation), and the contents of A are _built from the four-note cell_.

#### Common Misconception

People sometimes think the four-note opening _is_ the symphony's first theme. It is not. The opening is the _motif_. The first theme is the entire first phrase of the movement — a much longer musical statement (roughly 0:00 to 0:43) that the motif powers but does not constitute. The first theme includes the unisons, the splitting between voices, the building energy, the long phrase that climbs to the horn fanfare. The motif is the _seed_ ; the first theme is what the seed grows into.

The distinction matters because if you confuse the motif with the theme, you will think Beethoven repeats the same four notes for seven minutes. He does not. He uses the motif as material, the way a sculptor uses clay, to build longer structures — themes, phrases, sections — that are the symphony's actual content. The motif is everywhere because it is the _material_ , not because it is the _content_.

#### A note on key (and why C minor matters)

The Fifth Symphony is in C minor. C minor was, for Beethoven, the key of _struggle_. Three of his most-loved pieces are in C minor: the Fifth Symphony (1808), the Pathétique Sonata (1798), and the Coriolan Overture (1807). In all three, C minor signals — to Beethoven and to the listeners of his time — _tragic urgency_ combined with the possibility of _heroic resolution_. The Fifth Symphony as a whole is the great Beethoven C-minor narrative: starting in C minor's struggle, ending (in the fourth movement, three movements from now) in C _major_ 's triumph. This is the famous _per aspera ad astra_ arc — "through hardships to the stars" — that Beethoven made canonical. We are listening only to the first movement here, the C-minor struggle. The triumph is three movements later.

You do not need to know what C minor is in technical terms (a minor key with three flats in the key signature, etc.). You only need to know that _Beethoven heard a specific dramatic atmosphere in C minor_ , and that he uses it consciously to mean _high stakes_.

### 3.4 The Stories

#### How the symphony got premiered

The premiere of the Fifth Symphony, on 22 December 1808 in Vienna's Theater an der Wien, is one of the most extraordinary concerts in the history of music — and one of the worst-organized.

Beethoven had been frozen out of Vienna's institutional concert life for several years, partly because of his temperament (which was famously difficult), partly because of his deafness (which was now severe), and partly because the Viennese musical establishment was politicking against him. He decided to put on a concert that would single-handedly reset his career — a benefit concert in which he would conduct, perform, and present new works. He rented the Theater an der Wien for one evening.

The program was roughly four hours long. It included:

* Symphony No. 6 "Pastoral" (world premiere)
* A concert aria, _Ah! perfido_
* A movement from the _Mass in C_
* Piano Concerto No. 4 (premiere of Beethoven's solo performance of it)
* Symphony No. 5 (world premiere)
* Another movement from the Mass in C
* An improvised piano fantasy by Beethoven
* The _Choral Fantasy_ , Op. 80 — composed in haste in the previous few weeks specifically to give the concert a grand finale; this is the piece whose main theme Beethoven would later reuse in the _Ode to Joy_ of Symphony No. 9

Beethoven himself conducted everything from the keyboard (or from a podium) and performed the piano concerto. The orchestra had not been adequately rehearsed; the _Choral Fantasy_ broke down mid-performance and had to be restarted; the hall was unheated and the December temperature dropped to near freezing; the audience was small.

The Fifth Symphony — the work that within a generation would be regarded as the central work of the symphonic literature — was first heard in this circumstance. By most contemporary accounts, it landed without immediate impact. The audience was cold and exhausted by the time the symphony was played; the performance was rough; nobody walked out of the Theater an der Wien that night thinking they had just heard the most important symphony of the era.

The judgment came later. By 1810 — two years after the premiere — E. T. A. Hoffmann had reviewed the symphony and declared it one of the supreme works of music. By 1830 it was canonical. By 1900 it was the most-performed orchestral work in the standard repertoire, and the four-note opening was already on its way to becoming a cultural icon.

#### Hoffmann's 1810 review

Ernst Theodor Amadeus Hoffmann — better known today as the writer whose stories were turned into Offenbach's _Tales of Hoffmann_ and Tchaikovsky's _Nutcracker_ — was in 1810 a critic for the _Allgemeine musikalische Zeitung_. He wrote a long, ecstatic review of the published score of Beethoven's Fifth Symphony.

The review is sometimes called _the founding document of Romantic music criticism_. Before Hoffmann, music criticism had largely consisted of describing what happened (the form, the technique, the workmanship). Hoffmann instead described what it _felt like_ — and he made enormous claims for what music could _mean_. Music, he argued, was the highest of the arts because it spoke directly to the listener's spirit without the mediation of words or images. Beethoven's Fifth Symphony, he wrote, opens up "the realm of the colossal and immeasurable," and the listener experiences "the abyss of the infinite."

This is overheated by modern standards. But it set the tone for the next century of how Europeans wrote about music. Beethoven's symphonies became, for the educated listener, _quasi-spiritual experiences_. The concert hall became the secular successor to the cathedral.

The Hoffmann review is also where we find one of the first uses of the four-note opening as _the soul of the symphony_. Hoffmann is the writer who taught readers to hear those four notes as the destiny-laden Idea. The "fate knocks at the door" story (which Schindler invented later) extends the Hoffmann hearing into apocryphal quotation. The cultural icon of Beethoven 5 has its roots in this 1810 review.

#### Three readings of the same opening

Now to the work-vs-interpretation muscle. We have three named recordings; let's hold them in the same hand.

**Carlos Kleiber / Vienna Philharmonic, 1974 (Deutsche Grammophon).** The most-loved Beethoven 5 of the second half of the twentieth century. Kleiber was a fanatical, hard-to-pin-down conductor — son of the conductor Erich Kleiber, an introvert, a perfectionist, a man who would refuse to record unless every detail was right and who therefore made very few recordings. The 1974 Beethoven 5 came out of his collaboration with the Vienna Philharmonic in a session of perfectionist drilling. What you hear is _electric_ : very fast tempi (the first movement at about seven minutes; some conductors take nine), absolutely tight ensemble, every entrance perfectly placed, the four-note cell delivered with a kind of _crackling urgency_. The recording is often described as "definitive" — which is overstated but understandable. It is the reading most amateur listeners are taught to start with.

**Herbert von Karajan / Berlin Philharmonic, 1963 (Deutsche Grammophon).** Karajan recorded the Beethoven symphonies four times across his career. The 1963 cycle is the most celebrated. Where Kleiber is electric, Karajan is _lacquered_ — a polished, beautifully proportioned, brass-forward sound that the Berlin Philharmonic of the 1960s had been built around. The first movement is taken slightly slower than Kleiber's, with longer phrases and a heavier weight on each entry. The four-note cell here is less _urgent question_ and more _declarative announcement_. Some listeners find this reading too heavy; others find Kleiber too rushed. The differences are at the level of _aesthetic preference_ , not of right-and-wrong. (Worth noting: Karajan's 1963 reading does not take the exposition repeat; Kleiber's does. This alone makes the Karajan reading shorter and gives it a different shape.)

**Teodor Currentzis / MusicAeterna, 2018 (Sony Classical).** Twenty-first-century iconoclasm. Currentzis, a Greek conductor based in Russia until recent years, runs his orchestra MusicAeterna as a kind of musical commune; the players are paid only when they record, the rehearsal hours are insane, the conventional tempo and balance markings are systematically reconsidered. The 2018 Beethoven 5 is _fast_ — even faster than Kleiber — and the orchestral sound is much _drier_ , with period-inflected timpani and historically informed bowings. The four-note cell comes out almost percussive. Some listeners find this reading thrilling; others find it manneristic. It is unambiguously different from both Kleiber and Karajan, and it asks the listener to reconsider what she thought "Beethoven 5" sounded like.

These three are the work-vs-interpretation triangle the chapter wants to plant in your ear. _Beethoven 5 is not one work — it is three works in these three readings, and many more in others._ By Chapter 8 (the _Goldberg Variations_) we will be holding four readings of the same piece. By Chapter 26 (Adams's _Shaker Loops_) we will be holding readings by Adams himself, by Edo de Waart, and by the Bay Area minimalist ensembles. The triangle starts here.

#### Cross-piece links

* If the symphonic _workshop_ method — building a long movement out of a tiny cell — interested you, the natural next listen is **Beethoven's Symphony No. 7** (1813), whose first movement is also built on a relentless rhythmic motif. The "Dance Symphony," as Wagner called it.
* If you want the most extreme version of _motivic development_ in classical music, listen to **Brahms's Symphony No. 4** (1885), finale (Chapter 18 of this book). Brahms takes a single eight-note bass line and writes thirty variations on it without ever letting the listener feel he is repeating himself.
* If you are curious about the _per aspera ad astra_ arc — minor-key struggle to major-key triumph — listen to the _whole_ Fifth Symphony in one sitting. The fourth movement's arrival in C major, after the third movement's bridge passage, is one of the great structural moments in symphonic literature. (We will not focus on it in this book; this chapter is the first movement only. But you should hear the arc once.)
* The four-note cell echoes, transformed, in many later composers' work. The whole nineteenth-century C-minor symphonic tradition — Brahms's First, Bruckner's Eighth, Tchaikovsky's Fourth in F minor as a cousin — is in some sense answering Beethoven's Fifth: the _per aspera ad astra_ arc the Fifth made canonical kept asking subsequent composers what they could do with it.

#### Conversation Seeds

* _Ask the companion to compare the opening four notes in Kleiber 1974, Karajan 1963, and Currentzis 2018 — they differ in tempo by close to 30 percent and the difference is the whole interpretation._
* _Ask the companion about the legend that Beethoven said "thus fate knocks at the door" — and why every modern Beethoven scholar is now nearly certain he didn't say it, and how Anton Schindler's biographical forgeries shape the popular understanding of Beethoven to this day._
* _Ask the companion about E. T. A. Hoffmann's 1810 review of this symphony — the review that arguably invented Romantic music criticism, and what changed in how Europeans wrote about music after it._
* _Tell the companion which return of the opening motif in the development section moves you most — and ask her where she'd point you next._
* _Ask the companion to recommend three other Beethoven symphonies to listen to in order — and to say why that order._

### 3.5 Exercises

#### Concept Check

**Q1.** What is the difference between a _motif_ and a _theme_?

Hint

One is shorter. One can be built from the other.

**Answer:** A motif is a short musical idea — usually three to six notes — distinctive enough to be recognized when it reappears in altered form. A theme is a longer, more complete musical thought, often eight or sixteen measures, with a beginning, a middle, and an end. A motif can be the _material_ a theme is built from. The four-note opening of Beethoven 5 is a motif; the entire first phrase of the movement (roughly 0:00 to 0:43) is the first theme, and that theme is built from the motif.

**Q2.** What are the three main sections of sonata form?

**Answer:** Exposition (the composer states the main themes, usually two contrasting themes in different keys), development (the composer transforms the themes, fragments them, moves them through different keys), and recapitulation (the themes return, both now in the home key). Often followed by a coda — a closing passage that wraps up the movement. The first movement of Beethoven's Fifth Symphony is in sonata form; so is the first movement of _Eine kleine Nachtmusik_ (Chapter 6), where the form will be taught in full.

### Chapter Summary

The first movement of Beethoven's Fifth Symphony is, structurally, a sustained exercise in _motivic development_ — a four-note cell put through every transformation Beethoven could find, across seven minutes, in sonata form (exposition, development, recapitulation, coda). The cell is short-short-short-LONG. It appears in nearly every measure of the movement.

You met the work-vs-interpretation muscle: three named readings (Kleiber/Vienna 1974, Karajan/Berlin 1963, Currentzis/MusicAeterna 2018) that differ in tempo, articulation, and balance enough that they almost feel like three different pieces. By Chapter 8 we will be holding four readings of one work.

You learned that the "fate knocks at the door" line — the most famous quotation about the symphony — is almost certainly something Beethoven never said; it was retrofitted onto the symphony by Anton Schindler after Beethoven's death. The fate-narrative shapes how generations have heard the music; taking it away makes the _workshop_ hearing more available.

You learned about the 1808 premiere — the roughly four-hour Vienna concert in the freezing hall, the under-rehearsed orchestra, the _Choral Fantasy_ that broke down mid-performance. You learned that the symphony was _not_ received as a masterpiece on its premiere; the canonization came over decades, with E. T. A. Hoffmann's 1810 review as a founding document of Romantic music criticism.

The next chapter takes you to **Vivaldi's _Four Seasons_** , two short movements (the "Spring" first movement and the "Winter" second movement). After Beethoven's _workshop on a motif_ , Vivaldi's _programmatic depiction of weather and seasons_ is a sharp pivot — and a deeper kind of listening for a piece you almost certainly already half-know.

The composer protagonist Beethoven, met here in his first symphonic chapter, will return in **Chapter 13** (the _Eroica_ Symphony, his Classical-to-Romantic hinge) and **Chapter 14** (Symphony No. 9 and the late string quartets, his late-style summit). Three Beethoven chapters total. We have just met him.

---

## Chapter 4: Vivaldi, _The Four Seasons_ — "Spring" I and "Winter" II

Imagine a red-haired Venetian priest in 1720, walking through the courtyard of a girls' orphanage, sheet music tucked under one arm, on his way to the music room where forty teenage girls are waiting with violins. The priest does not say Mass. He has not said Mass in years; a chronic chest condition (probably asthma, possibly something worse) leaves him short of breath, and he has been quietly excused from the altar. His role at the Ospedale della Pietà is to run the music. The girls are foundlings, orphans, or children whose families could not keep them; the Pietà is one of four such institutions in Venice that takes them in and gives them a vocation. Music is the vocation here. By age sixteen, the best of these girls play violin or sing in choral works at a level that draws tourists from across Europe — princes, ambassadors, _grand-tour_ English aristocrats — into the Pietà's chapel to hear them on Sundays. The priest writes them concertos at a rate of one or two a month.

His name is Antonio Vivaldi. He is forty-two. Around 1720 he composes a set of four violin concertos, each named after a season, each prefaced with a sonnet describing what the music depicts — the spring breeze, the cuckoo, the shepherd's nap, the gathering storm, the chattering teeth of winter cold. The set will be published in 1725 in Amsterdam as _Il cimento dell'armonia e dell'inventione_ , Op. 8 — "The contest between harmony and invention" — concertos numbers one through four of the set are _Le quattro stagioni_ , _The Four Seasons_.

For nearly two centuries after his death, Vivaldi was almost forgotten. He died in poverty in Vienna in 1741, was buried in a pauper's grave, and his music sat in libraries unplayed. The twentieth century rediscovered him — slowly through the 1930s and 1940s, then all at once after the _Four Seasons_ became, in the 1960s and 1970s, one of the most-recorded pieces of classical music in history.

You almost certainly know it. You have heard "Spring" in cell-phone hold music, in airline boarding announcements, in dental-office waiting rooms, in coffee-shop playlists, in television commercials for everything from yogurt to luxury cars. The piece has been pop-cultural saturated to a degree few classical works have ever endured. _The Four Seasons_ has become the _aural wallpaper_ of the modern world.

This chapter is going to do for _The Four Seasons_ what Chapter 3 did for Beethoven 5: give you back the music underneath the wallpaper.

### 4.1 Before You Listen

#### Hook anecdote — the sonnets that came with the music

Most amateur listeners have heard "Spring" without knowing that Vivaldi wrote _poetry to go with it_. When the set was published in 1725, each concerto was prefaced with a _sonetto dimostrativo_ — an "illustrative sonnet" — describing scene by scene what the music depicted. Whether Vivaldi himself wrote the sonnets or whether he collaborated with an unnamed poet is unresolved; either way, they appear in the publication under his authority and they are clearly written to fit the music.

The sonnet for "Spring" reads, in modern English paraphrase:

> _Springtime is come. The birds salute it with festive song, and zephyrs blow through the streams, murmuring their gentle whispers. Then thunder and lightning, the heralds of spring, come on, covering the sky with a black mantle; and when they fall silent, the little birds return to their melodious enchantment._

This is what the first movement depicts — and Vivaldi marks the score precisely with the sonnet's images. The opening cheerful tune is labeled "Spring has come." A passage where three violins play overlapping fast figures is labeled "song of the birds." A passage with quietly rocking strings is labeled "murmuring streams." A sudden loud burst with rapid tremolos is labeled "thunder and lightning." Then the birds come back.

This is _programmatic music_ — music that depicts specific external things. Most classical music does not do this; most classical music is _absolute music_ , where the form is its own subject (a sonata-form first movement is _about_ its sonata form, not about anything outside it). Vivaldi's _Four Seasons_ is one of the most explicit pieces of programmatic music in the entire repertoire, and it predates Berlioz's _Symphonie Fantastique_ (Chapter 16, where program music gets its great Romantic instance) by more than a hundred years. The Baroque, it turns out, was already doing what we think of as a nineteenth-century invention.

For the "Winter" second movement, the sonnet reads:

> _To pass quiet, contented days by the fire, while outside the rain pours down and soaks everyone._

That is the scene: a person inside, by a hearth, while a cold rain falls outside. The Largo is two minutes long and you will hear the _fire_ in the warm solo violin melody and the _rain outside_ in the pizzicato (plucked) accompaniment underneath, dropping like raindrops.

#### What to notice

For the "Spring" first movement, listen for three things:

  1. **The ritornello.** The cheerful opening tune comes back several times across the movement, in different keys, between the solo passages. _Ritornello_ literally means "little return" — the recurring orchestral refrain. Count how many times you hear it. (In most readings, about four or five times.)
  2. **The birds.** About twenty seconds in, three violins start playing fast overlapping figures — high, chirping, restless. _That is the birds._ Vivaldi has the strings imitate bird-song almost literally.
  3. **The thunderstorm.** About a minute and a half in, the music suddenly turns minor-key and stormy — fast tremolos, descending scales, dramatic flashes. _That is the thunder and lightning._ It is brief, then the birds return.

For the "Winter" second movement, listen for two things:

  1. **The melody.** A warm, slow, sustained violin melody — almost a hymn. _That is the person by the fire._
  2. **The pizzicato.** The accompaniment is _plucked_ , not bowed — individual short notes, dropping at regular intervals. _That is the rain._

Two layers. Fire and rain. The whole movement is built on the relationship between them.

#### One-sentence backgrounds

**Vivaldi,_The Four Seasons_ , Op. 8 Nos. 1 and 4 (RV 269 and RV 297)**: A set of four programmatic violin concertos composed around 1720 at the Ospedale della Pietà in Venice and published in Amsterdam in 1725, each preceded by a sonnet describing what the music depicts.

**"Spring" first movement (Allegro)** : ~3 min. The arrival of spring, with birds, a stream, a thunderstorm, and birds again.

**"Winter" second movement (Largo)** : ~2 min. A quiet scene by a fireplace while rain falls outside.

### 4.2 The Listening Window

#### "Spring" first movement (Antonini / Il Giardino Armonico, 1994)

This recording is fast, sharp, and theatrical — a period-instrument reading that wants the music to feel as fresh and surprising as it must have felt in 1725, before it became aural wallpaper.

* **0:00–0:11.** The ritornello — the cheerful opening tune in E major. The whole ensemble plays it together; the soloist has not entered yet. _Memorize this tune._ You are going to hear it three or four more times.

* **0:11–0:20.** Solo violin enters and the ritornello continues to interleave with it.

* **0:23.** **The birds.** Three violins (one of them the soloist) start playing fast overlapping high figures — chirps, trills, runs. They overlap and answer each other, the way birds do in a tree. _Vivaldi has marked the score "Canto degli uccelli" — "song of the birds."_

* **0:50.** **The stream.** The texture shifts: a softer, rocking accompaniment in the strings, with the soloist playing a flowing line above. _Vivaldi has marked the score "Scorrono i fonti" — "the streams flow."_

* **1:10.** A return of the ritornello — the cheerful tune, but now in a slightly different key (the dominant). This is the _second_ ritornello.

* **1:20.** **The thunderstorm.** Suddenly the music goes minor-key. The lower strings play fast tremolos (rapidly bowed repeated notes), the upper strings play descending scale-figures like lightning flashes, the energy spikes. _Vivaldi has marked the score "Tuoni e lampi" — "thunder and lightning."_ The storm passes in about twenty seconds — fast and violent, like a real spring thunderstorm.

* **1:42.** **The birds return.** The minor-key panic clears; the high overlapping bird-figures come back. Spring has resumed.

* **2:00 onward.** The ritornello returns one more time, the solo violin develops material from the bird passage, and the movement closes with a final ritornello statement.

This back-and-forth between ritornello (orchestra together) and solo passages (with depicted scenes) is the entire architecture of the movement. The ritornello is the _frame_ ; the solo passages are the _pictures hung in the frame_. The form has a name: _ritornello form_. It is the standard Baroque concerto form, and Vivaldi was its most prolific master.

#### "Winter" second movement (Antonini / Il Giardino Armonico, 1994)

After the cold and stormy first movement of "Winter" (which we are skipping), the Largo arrives like a relief. The whole scene is interior. Indoors. Warm.

* **0:00–0:08.** The pizzicato accompaniment begins — short, plucked notes from the second violins and lower strings, falling at regular intervals. _This is the rain._ Notice how steady it is, how indifferent to whatever else is happening. Rain just falls.

* **0:08.** The solo violin enters with the melody. _This is the person by the fire._ The melody is in E♭ major (warm key), sustained (slow bow strokes, the notes long and singing). Above the rain, the warmth.

* **0:08–1:00.** The melody develops. It is long, breathing, almost like a Bach chorale. The pizzicato keeps falling underneath without varying. The fire stays warm; the rain keeps falling.

* **1:00–1:40.** The melody intensifies slightly — climbing higher, growing more expressive — without ever abandoning its hymn-like calm. The rain underneath does not change.

* **1:40–2:00.** The melody descends and resolves; the pizzicato fades. The fire glows; the rain has slowed.

The whole movement is _two textural layers held in juxtaposition_. There is no development, no transformation, no drama. The interest comes from the _contrast_ and from how perfectly the contrast is sustained for two minutes. This is one of the great calm moments in the entire Baroque repertoire — and it is in a piece most people associate with the cheerful pop-cultural "Spring" first movement.

If you took only one thing from "Winter" II, it should be this: _the music's beauty is in the relationship between the warmth on top and the steady rain below_. Once you hear it, you cannot un-hear it.

### 4.3 What's Happening in the Music

#### Definition: Programmatic Music

Programmatic music is music that depicts specific external things — scenes, stories, characters, weather, places — and gives the listener clues (titles, prefatory texts, marked passages in the score) about what to hear.

In plain language: music that is _about something_ , where the something is not the music itself. Vivaldi's _Four Seasons_ is programmatic because each concerto depicts a season's scenes, and the sonnets tell you which passage depicts which scene. Berlioz's _Symphonie Fantastique_ (Chapter 16) is programmatic because the symphony tells a story of a young artist's opium-fueled obsession with a woman. Mussorgsky's _Pictures at an Exhibition_ is programmatic because each movement depicts a painting. Most film scores are programmatic.

The opposite of programmatic music is _absolute music_ — music whose form is its own subject, with no extra-musical reference. Beethoven's Fifth Symphony first movement (Chapter 3) is absolute music: it is _about_ the development of a four-note motif through sonata form, not about anything outside the music. Most of Bach's instrumental music is absolute. Most of Brahms's symphonies are absolute.

The distinction between programmatic and absolute music was a hot debate in the nineteenth century. Wagner and Liszt were on the programmatic side (music should depict, narrate, evoke); Brahms and Hanslick were on the absolute side (music should be its own subject). The debate sometimes gets called _the War of the Romantics_. The twentieth century mostly resolved it by deciding both can produce great music, and by realizing — looking back to Vivaldi — that the distinction is older than the nineteenth century thought.

#### Definition: Ritornello Form

Ritornello form is the standard Baroque concerto form, in which an orchestral refrain (the _ritornello_) alternates with solo passages, and the ritornello returns several times across the movement, often in different keys.

In plain language: imagine a song where the chorus returns several times between different verses, and the chorus is the same melody but sometimes in a different key. The chorus is the ritornello; the verses are the solo passages. The "Spring" first movement is in clear ritornello form: ritornello (E major) — solo with birds — ritornello (related key) — solo with stream — ritornello — solo with thunder — ritornello (returning to E major to close).

Ritornello form was the Baroque period's main solution to the question _how do you organize a piece longer than a song and shorter than an opera?_ The ritornello provides recurring landmarks that orient the listener; the solo passages provide variety. Once you know the form, you can hear any Baroque concerto first movement on these terms, and they almost all reward the listening: Bach's Brandenburg Concerto No. 3 (Chapter 7), all of the Handel concerti grossi, the violin concertos of Vivaldi himself (he wrote over five hundred, of which the _Four Seasons_ are merely the four most famous).

#### Definition: Pizzicato

Pizzicato is a string-playing technique in which the player plucks the string with a finger instead of bowing it, producing a short, dry, percussive note.

In plain language: pluck instead of bow. The Italian word literally means "pinched." Pizzicato is notated in the score with the abbreviation _pizz._ ; the return to bowing is marked _arco_. Pizzicato sounds like a guitar or harp note — short, decaying quickly, no sustain. Bowed string sound is the opposite — long, sustained, capable of singing.

In the "Winter" Largo, the pizzicato in the lower strings is what makes the rain sound like rain. If you imagine bowed strings playing the same notes, it would sound more like a sigh — long, sustained, expressive. The pizzicato makes it sound like _falling_ , like _drops_. Vivaldi is using a specific technical choice (pizz. vs arco) to produce a specific depictive effect.

#### Common Misconception

People sometimes treat programmatic music as somehow _less serious_ than absolute music — as if music with a story or a depicted scene were a stunt, while music without one were "pure." This is a nineteenth-century prejudice, deeply embedded in the high-Romantic conservatory tradition, and it is wrong.

Programmatic music can be as deep as absolute music — and absolute music can be as superficial as programmatic music. The difference is not about depth; it is about _technique_ and _aesthetic strategy_. Programmatic music uses external references (titles, scenes, characters) as a way of organizing musical material; absolute music uses internal references (themes, motifs, harmonic relationships). Both produce great works; both produce shallow works. _Pictures at an Exhibition_ is great programmatic music; many absolute-music symphonies of the nineteenth century are forgettable. Beethoven 5 is great absolute music; many programmatic tone poems of the late nineteenth century are now museum pieces.

The amateur ear sometimes finds programmatic music _easier to enter_ because the scene helps the listener know what to listen for. But the depth of the music is a separate question from the accessibility of its surface.

### 4.4 The Stories

#### Vivaldi at the Ospedale della Pietà

The Ospedale della Pietà was one of four Venetian _ospedali grandi_ — large charitable institutions caring for foundlings, orphans, and children of impoverished families. The four ospedali — Pietà, Mendicanti, Incurabili, Ospedaletto — were specifically for girls; comparable boys' institutions existed but operated differently. The girls received room, board, education, and a vocation. At the Pietà, the vocation was music.

By the early eighteenth century, the _figlie del coro_ (literally "daughters of the choir") of the Pietà had become a Venetian tourist attraction. They sang and played violin at Sunday services from a high gallery, hidden behind metal grilles from the worshippers below. The grilles preserved the institutional fiction that these were anonymous orphans serving God; the music coming through the grilles was the most accomplished sacred music in Venice, and visiting nobility came specifically to hear it.

Vivaldi was hired in 1703, when he was twenty-five, as the _maestro di violino_ — the violin master. He was supposed to teach violin technique to the girls. Over the next forty years his role expanded: he wrote concertos for the orchestra to play, he became _maestro de' concerti_ (master of concerts), he sometimes left for several years to compose operas in Mantua or Rome, then returned. The Pietà would commission concertos from him by the year; some years he produced over a hundred, written specifically for the players currently at the institution.

This is important for understanding _The Four Seasons_. The concertos were not designed for famous touring soloists; they were designed for the talented seventeen-year-old in the Pietà gallery — Anna Maria of the violin, or Chiara of the cello, or whoever the current standout was — to play. The technical demands are real but not impossible; the music is theatrical in ways that work in a chapel performance where the player is hidden behind a grille and the orchestra is small. The _Four Seasons_ are _institutional music_ , written for a specific room, for specific players, on a budget. They became universal music; they did not start that way.

#### Forgotten for nearly two centuries

Vivaldi died in Vienna in July 1741, while traveling on business — he had been trying to obtain a court position from the Emperor and had run out of money. He was buried in a pauper's grave in the Hospital Cemetery near the present-day Karlsplatz (the site is now under the Vienna Technical University campus). The young Haydn, who would arrive in Vienna as a Stephansdom choirboy a few years later, may have walked past the lost grave site without ever knowing it was there.

For nearly two centuries, Vivaldi was almost completely forgotten. His operas had not been performed since his death; his church music was lost in libraries; his concertos were known mostly because Bach had transcribed about ten of them for keyboard, and the Bach transcriptions were what kept Vivaldi's name in the historical record. _The Four Seasons_ itself was largely unplayed.

The rediscovery happened in stages. In the 1920s and 1930s, Italian scholars (especially Alberto Gentili and Olga Rudge — who happened to be Ezra Pound's partner, an odd footnote in twentieth-century cultural history) located a huge cache of Vivaldi manuscripts in monastic libraries near Turin. The manuscripts were edited and slowly published. The first commercially distributed complete recording of _The Four Seasons_ is usually attributed to Louis Kaufman with Henry Swoboda and the Concert Hall Society Orchestra in 1947.

The pop-cultural explosion came after I Musici's 1959 recording (Felix Ayo as soloist), which sold extraordinarily well, and especially after Neville Marriner's Academy of St Martin in the Fields recording with Alan Loveday in 1969. From the 1970s onward, _The Four Seasons_ became the single most-recorded classical work in history — at last count, over four hundred commercial recordings — and the soundtrack of every hold-music application on earth.

The forgetting and the over-saturation are two halves of the same story. A work the seventeenth-century world ignored became the work the twentieth century used as background noise. Vivaldi himself, if you could play him a 2020s YouTube recording of "Spring" being used in a yogurt commercial, would probably be astonished — partly at the technology, partly at the choice of music. He thought he was writing chapel music for a girls' orphanage.

#### The three readings

**Il Giardino Armonico / Giovanni Antonini, with Enrico Onofri as soloist, 1994 (Teldec).** A period-instrument reading. The ensemble plays with gut strings, no shoulder pads, minimal vibrato, sharp historical articulation. Tempi are fast; dynamics are extreme; the storm in "Spring" first movement is almost violent. The aesthetic is "let's hear the music as the 1725 listener might have heard it, before two hundred years of nineteenth-century interpretive layers were added." Some listeners find it shocking; others find it revelatory. It is the recording I have chosen as primary because it is the _least pop-cultural_ of the standard options — the reading that most defamiliarizes the music.

**Janine Jansen / Candida Thompson and members of the Amsterdam Sinfonietta, 2003 (Decca).** A modern-instrument reading, but small-ensemble and crisply played. Jansen is a Dutch violinist of extraordinary tone and personality. Her reading is _intimate_ — much smaller orchestra than the standard symphonic reading, much more chamber-music feel. It sits between the period-instrument reading and the lush mid-twentieth-century symphonic reading. A natural second listen after Antonini.

**Nigel Kennedy / English Chamber Orchestra, 1989 (EMI).** The reading that single-handedly made Vivaldi pop-culturally famous in the late 1980s and early 1990s. Kennedy is a flamboyant English violinist (he insisted on the single name "Kennedy" for several years; he is often photographed in soccer jerseys with spiked hair) who plays the _Four Seasons_ with theatrical drama and idiosyncratic phrasing. His 1989 recording sold over two million copies — by far the most-purchased classical recording of the late twentieth century — and is what most listeners who grew up in the 1990s think of when they think of Vivaldi. It is a _modern, glamorous, slightly mannered_ reading. Compared to Antonini, it is much smoother; compared to Jansen, it is more theatrical.

These three readings are an exercise in _the same piece at three different aesthetic positions_ : period-historical, modern-intimate, modern-glamorous. The differences are large enough to be heard easily; the music is the same.

#### Cross-piece links

* If you loved the _Four Seasons_ , the natural next listen is **Vivaldi's _L'Estro armonico_ , Op. 3** — twelve concertos for various combinations of solo violins and strings, the publication that made Vivaldi internationally famous in 1711 and that Bach studied obsessively. The Concerto in B minor for four violins (RV 580) is the most-loved of the set, and Bach transcribed it for four harpsichords.
* For more _programmatic_ Baroque music, listen to **Heinrich Biber's _Mystery Sonatas_** (about 1676) — fifteen violin sonatas each depicting a meditation on the rosary mysteries, including remarkable scordatura (re-tuning) effects.
* For the _next great programmatic symphony_ , jump ahead to **Berlioz's _Symphonie Fantastique_** (Chapter 16). Just over a century after Vivaldi, the program-symphony idea returns with a vastly larger orchestra and a more personal subject (opium-dream obsession with a woman) rather than a generic season.
* For the _Bach side_ of the Vivaldi/Bach interaction, listen to **Bach's Concerto for Two Violins in D minor, BWV 1043** — which is essentially Bach's response to Vivaldi's two-violin concertos. Vivaldi was the model; Bach was the deepening. Chapter 7 introduces Bach.

#### Conversation Seeds

* _Ask the companion which of the three "Spring" readings (Antonini period-instrument, Jansen modern-intimate, Kennedy modern-glamorous) is most likely to defamiliarize the piece for someone who has heard it as hold music their whole life._
* _Ask the companion about the Ospedale della Pietà — what kind of institution it was, why Vivaldi spent forty years there, and what kind of girls were playing his concertos in the 1720s._
* _Tell the companion which specific moment in "Winter" Largo struck you most — the pizzicato rain alone, the entrance of the violin melody, or the way the two layers stay in perfect parallel without ever crossing — and ask her what other Baroque music sustains a similar two-layer juxtaposition._
* _Ask the companion about the 1920s rediscovery of Vivaldi — what manuscripts were found, who found them, and what role Ezra Pound's partner Olga Rudge played in the story._
* _Ask the companion to play you the first movement of a different Vivaldi concerto in ritornello form (for example, the "Summer" concerto's first movement, or the Concerto for Two Violins in B minor, RV 580) and to help you hear the ritornello form structure as a recurring pattern across Vivaldi's output, not just in "Spring."_

### 4.5 Exercises

#### Concept Check

**Q1.** What is _programmatic music_ , and what is the opposite (the term, and what it means)?

Hint

One depicts external things; the other is its own subject.

**Answer:** Programmatic music is music that depicts specific external things — scenes, stories, characters, weather — and gives the listener clues (titles, prefatory texts, marked score passages) about what to hear. The opposite is _absolute music_ , which is music whose form is its own subject, with no extra-musical reference. _The Four Seasons_ is programmatic (the sonnets describe scenes, the score is marked with depicted images). Beethoven 5 first movement (Chapter 3) is absolute (no scene, no story, just the development of a four-note motif).

**Q2.** What is _ritornello form_?

**Answer:** The standard Baroque concerto form, in which an orchestral refrain (the _ritornello_) alternates with solo passages, and the ritornello returns several times across the movement, often in different keys. The ritornello provides recurring landmarks that orient the listener; the solo passages provide variety. The "Spring" first movement is a clear instance: ritornello (E major) — solo with birds — ritornello (related key) — solo with stream — ritornello — solo with thunder — ritornello returning. The form was the Baroque period's main solution to organizing a piece longer than a song and shorter than an opera.

### Chapter Summary

The first movement of Vivaldi's "Spring" concerto and the second movement of his "Winter" concerto from _The Four Seasons_ (Op. 8, Nos. 1 and 4, composed around 1720 at the Ospedale della Pietà in Venice, published 1725 in Amsterdam) are two of the most-listened-to and most-saturated pieces of classical music in the world.

"Spring" first movement is a piece of _programmatic music_ in _ritornello form_ : an orchestral refrain alternates with solo passages depicting specific scenes from the prefatory sonnet — the song of birds, the murmuring stream, the thunderstorm, the birds returning. The form (ritornello — solo — ritornello — solo) is the Baroque concerto's standard architecture, of which Vivaldi was the most prolific master, having written over five hundred concertos for the players at the Pietà.

"Winter" second movement (Largo) is a study in _textural juxtaposition_ : a warm sustained violin melody above a steady pizzicato accompaniment, the fire and the rain held in parallel for two minutes without development. The _pizzicato_ — plucked rather than bowed strings — is the specific technical choice that produces the raindrop effect.

You met three readings: Antonini / Il Giardino Armonico 1994 (period-instrument, fast, theatrical, defamiliarizing), Jansen 2003 (modern-instrument, chamber-intimate), and Kennedy 1989 (modern-glamorous, the recording that made Vivaldi pop-culturally famous in the late twentieth century). The differences between them are large enough to be heard easily; the music is the same.

You learned that Vivaldi was almost completely forgotten for nearly two centuries after his death — buried in a Vienna pauper's grave in 1741 — and rediscovered through a 1920s manuscript find in monastic libraries near Turin. The first complete commercial recording of _The Four Seasons_ was made in 1947; the piece became pop-cultural ubiquity only in the late twentieth century. The canon, the chapter argued, is contingent — shaped by technology, marketing, and historical accident as much as by intrinsic quality. The Vivaldi rediscovery is a useful corrective to thinking of the canon as natural.

The next chapter takes you to **Dvořák's Symphony No. 9 "From the New World," second movement Largo** — another piece you almost certainly know in fragments (the famous English-horn melody has been turned into a Christmas carol, a school-song, an airline-commercial soundtrack). Habit #4 from the Six Listening Habits to Unlearn — _skipping the slow movement_ — gets explicitly resolved there. The slow movement is most often the heart; the Dvořák Largo is the proof.

Composer Protagonist Vivaldi met here in his only chapter; we will not return to him in this book. But the _Baroque pulse_ he established will recur in Chapter 7 (Bach), and the _programmatic music_ tradition he started will recur in Chapter 16 (Berlioz).

## Chapter 5: Dvořák, Symphony No. 9 "From the New World" — Movement II

A homesick man sits at a desk in Manhattan. It is the winter of 1893. He is fifty-one years old, Czech, recently arrived in America to serve as director of the National Conservatory of Music in New York at a salary that, back in Bohemia, would have made him a rich man. His wife and two of their children are with him; the other four are still at home in Prague, and he misses them every day. He has been writing letters back to Europe complaining about the New York meat ("not as good as Bohemian"), the New York winters ("cold but without snow that lasts"), and the New York pace ("everyone runs"). He has also been writing music.

The work in front of him is a symphony — his ninth — and he has been thinking, on instruction from the conservatory's American patron Jeannette Thurber, about _what an American symphony might sound like_. He has been listening to spirituals sung by his Black students. He has been reading Longfellow's _Song of Hiawatha_. He has been talking with Harry T. Burleigh, the African-American baritone studying at the conservatory, who sings spirituals at Dvořák's apartment in exchange for composition tutoring.

For the second movement of the symphony, he writes a slow melody. It is in the English horn — an instrument he uses here for almost the first time in a symphony. The melody is simple, plain, walking. It does not quote a specific spiritual; it sounds _like_ a spiritual. Decades later, after the symphony has become the most-loved work in the symphonic repertoire, William Arms Fisher (a Dvořák student) will write English lyrics to the melody and call it "Goin' Home." Generations of American children will learn the tune as a song, not knowing it came from a symphony. Generations of European listeners will learn the melody as _the_ Dvořák melody, not knowing it was thought of as American.

The English-horn melody from the second movement of Dvořák's Symphony No. 9 is among the most-loved themes in the symphonic literature. It is a slow movement that you should not skip. It is the heart of the symphony, and it is the proof of Habit #4 from Chapter 1: the slow movement is most often the heart, and skipping it is skipping the music's reason for existing.

### 5.1 Before You Listen

#### Hook anecdote — the night Dvořák first heard a spiritual

In the autumn of 1892, a few weeks after Dvořák arrived in New York, his student Harry T. Burleigh — a twenty-five-year-old baritone from Erie, Pennsylvania, who had grown up listening to his blind grandfather sing — visited the Dvořák apartment on East 17th Street. Burleigh was on a small scholarship; he could not afford composition lessons at the conservatory's stated rate; Dvořák had quietly agreed to teach him for free.

What happened in that apartment over the next several months is one of the more remarkable transfers in American music history. Dvořák, who had grown up in a Bohemian village singing folk songs and who had spent his life believing that _folk music is the soil from which great composition grows_ , asked Burleigh to sing him spirituals. Burleigh sang. Dvořák listened. He asked Burleigh to repeat each spiritual several times; he wanted to memorize them. He took down the melodies in notation. He played them back to Burleigh on the piano, sometimes harmonizing them as he played.

The spirituals he learned that winter included "Swing Low, Sweet Chariot," "Deep River," "Go Down, Moses," and "Nobody Knows the Trouble I've Seen." Dvořák was moved by them in a specific way: he heard in them what he had heard in Bohemian folk music — the _plaintive walking tune above a steady ground_ , the _pentatonic shapes_ , the _minor-key inflections that resolved into peace rather than into struggle_. He decided that _American_ classical music should draw on these melodies the way Czech classical music had drawn on Bohemian folk songs.

In May of 1893, Dvořák published a now-famous interview in the _New York Herald_ declaring that "the future of music in this country must be founded on what are called the Negro melodies. This must be the real foundation of any serious and original school of composition to be developed in the United States." The statement caused enormous controversy — both because most white American composers of 1893 were uninterested in being told they should be drawing on Black music, and because the statement implicitly devalued the Anglo-Saxon hymn-tune tradition many of them did draw on.

Dvořák was right and ahead of his time, and the rest of the twentieth century proved him right. The Symphony No. 9, completed a few weeks after this interview, was his demonstration in music of the principle he had articulated in words. The English-horn melody you are about to hear is the demonstration's emotional center.

#### What to notice

The Largo runs about twelve minutes. Listen for three things.

  1. **The opening chorale.** Before the famous melody arrives, the orchestra plays a slow, hushed chord progression — about twenty-five seconds of soft brass chords, each chord held, the keys shifting. _This is the chorale._ It is sometimes called _the gate to the melody_. After the chorale, the English horn enters.
  2. **The English-horn melody.** Beginning at about 0:30, the English horn plays the famous tune — slow, walking, plain, sad. It is in D♭ major (a warm key Dvořák chose carefully; we will get to why). The tune is about sixteen measures long and it states itself twice. After the second statement, the music modulates.
  3. **The middle section.** Around four minutes in, the music shifts into a different mood — faster, more agitated, with woodwind solos that quote other themes from elsewhere in the symphony. _This is the middle section_ of an A-B-A structure. Then the English-horn melody returns.

The whole movement is A — B — A: the chorale-and-melody, the agitated middle, the chorale-and-melody returning. Same shape as the Grieg "Praeludium" in Chapter 2. Different scale — twelve minutes versus three — and very different emotional weight, but the same architectural plan.

#### One-sentence background

**Dvořák, Symphony No. 9 in E minor "From the New World," Op. 95, B. 178** — composed in 1893 in New York City, premiered by the New York Philharmonic on 16 December 1893 at Carnegie Hall, conducted by Anton Seidl; second movement Largo, ~12 minutes.
