### 9.2 The Listening Window

#### Sinfonia (Gardiner reading, ~3 minutes)

* **0:00–1:20.** **The slow, dotted opening.** The orchestra plays in unison: a long-short-long-short rhythmic pattern (the _dotted rhythm_), grand and majestic. The harmony is in E minor (a serious key); the dynamics are forte (loud). This is the _French overture_ 's opening section, and it is consciously _ceremonial_ — like the opening of a royal procession.

* **1:20–1:35.** **Transition.** The slow opening ends on a half cadence (an inconclusive ending that points forward). The orchestra pauses briefly.

* **1:35–3:00.** **The fast fugal section.** A _fugue subject_ enters in the upper strings — a fast running figure. A second voice enters with the subject; then a third; then a fourth. The texture is _contrapuntal_ (four voices weaving). The energy is forward, urgent. This is the _French overture_ 's fast section, and it is in classic Baroque fugal style — exactly like the Bach fugues you heard in Chapter 7, only in an Italian-French-English idiom rather than a German one.

* **3:00.** A final E-minor cadence closes the Sinfonia. The next movement (an accompanied recitative for tenor — _Comfort ye, my people_) follows immediately.

The Sinfonia teaches you the _French overture_ form — slow-and-majestic followed by fast-and-fugal — which was the standard opening for Baroque operas, oratorios, and large orchestral suites. The same form is used in Bach's Orchestral Suites Nos. 1–4, in Lully's tragedy overtures, in many Handel operas. Once you can recognize the slow-dotted-plus-fast-fugal pattern, you can identify a French overture in seconds.

#### Hallelujah Chorus (Gardiner reading, ~4 minutes)

This chorus, in D major, is one of the most-recognized pieces of music in the world. Listen with the timestamps below to hear the architecture.

* **0:00–0:08.** **Opening "Hallelujah" call.** The entire chorus and orchestra burst in with the four-syllable _Hallelujah_ motif — three short notes on the same pitch (Hal-le-lu) followed by a higher held note (jah). The motif is unison, fortissimo, in D major. Memorize it.

* **0:08–0:25.** **First contrapuntal section.** The chorus splits into four voices (soprano, alto, tenor, bass) and the _Hallelujah_ motif is echoed between the voices, with brief contrapuntal weaving. Then a new text enters: _For the Lord God omnipotent reigneth_ — sung by the sopranos and altos in unison while the orchestra plays the _Hallelujah_ motif underneath. The pattern of _contrasting two textual phrases_ (the _Hallelujah_ and the _For the Lord God omnipotent reigneth_) over different musical materials is established here and will recur.

* **0:25–0:50.** **Second contrapuntal section.** _For the Lord God omnipotent reigneth_ is now treated as a _fugue subject_ — first the sopranos sing it, then the altos enter with it, then the tenors, then the basses. Meanwhile the _Hallelujah_ motif is heard intermittently in unison interjections. The texture is _dense, contrapuntal, energetic_ — Handel is showing what choral writing can do at full intensity.

* **0:50–1:20.** **Transition and key change.** The music modulates to A major (the dominant). New textual material enters: _The kingdom of this world is become the kingdom of our Lord and of His Christ; and He shall reign for ever and ever_. This text is presented in a slightly more _homophonic_ texture (chorus singing together in chords rather than weaving contrapuntally). The energy holds steady; the music remains in the forte-to-fortissimo range.

* **1:20–2:00.** **King of Kings, and Lord of Lords.** _This is the chorus's first major climax._ The text _King of Kings_ and _Lord of Lords_ is sung by tenors and basses on long sustained notes (held), while the sopranos and altos sing the text _Hallelujah_ in shorter rhythmic figures above. Each statement of _King of Kings_ climbs to a higher pitch — first the sopranos sing _King of Kings_ at one pitch, then at a higher pitch, then at a still-higher pitch — _the climbing soprano line_ the chapter asked you to listen for. The climb is the chorus's structural build.

* **2:00–2:30.** **The climax begins to resolve.** The repeated _King of Kings_ and _Lord of Lords_ statements continue, but the music now starts to drive toward the final cadence. The chorus is at full intensity; the orchestra is at full intensity; the listener can feel the end approaching.

* **2:30–3:30.** **The final fugal section.** Handel returns to fugal treatment for the closing — the chorus weaves the _Hallelujah_ motif in dense counterpoint, with overlapping entries and full four-part texture, building toward the final cadence.

* **3:30–4:00.** **The final cadence.** The chorus and orchestra arrive at a long sustained chord. The _Hallelujah_ motif is repeated, more slowly, in unison, then in counterpoint, then in unison again. The final _Hallelujah_ — long, held, in unison D major — is followed by a one-bar pause and then a final orchestral chord. The chorus is over.

The chorus is structured around three textual ideas — _Hallelujah_ , _For the Lord God omnipotent reigneth_ , _The kingdom of this world is become the kingdom of our Lord and of His Christ; and He shall reign for ever and ever_ — plus the climactic _King of Kings, and Lord of Lords_. Handel alternates between _unison statements_ (everyone together) and _contrapuntal treatments_ (the voices weaving the text), with the _King of Kings_ passage as the structural climax. The whole architecture takes four minutes; the effect is one of the great public moments in Western music.

#### The standing-up tradition

A historical note. Since at least the late eighteenth century, audiences at _Messiah_ performances have traditionally _stood_ during the Hallelujah Chorus. The tradition is sometimes attributed to King George II, who supposedly stood at the London premiere (March 1743) when the chorus began — and the audience, following royal protocol, stood with him. The story is doubtful (no contemporary source mentions it; George II may not have been at the premiere; the tradition only enters the historical record decades later), but the practice has continued for over two hundred years. In most modern _Messiah_ performances in the English-speaking world, the audience still rises at the opening _Hallelujah_ and remains standing through the end of the chorus.

This tradition is a small but interesting detail about classical music's social conventions: the audience _participates_ in the work, in a small ritualized way, at one specific moment. The standing acknowledges that something important is happening — and the something important is itself in part _the audience's collective recognition_ of the chorus's stature. The tradition is a self-reinforcing loop: the chorus is great because the audience rises; the audience rises because the chorus is great. Either way, the participation is part of the _Messiah_ 's social life.

### 9.3 What's Happening in the Music

#### Definition: Oratorio

An _oratorio_ is a large-scale musical setting of a religious or moral text for soloists, chorus, and orchestra, _performed without staging, costume, or acting_ — that is, presented as concert music rather than as theater. Oratorios are typically in multiple movements (arias, recitatives, choruses, instrumental movements) like operas, but without the dramatic apparatus of the operatic stage.

In plain language: an oratorio is _opera without the costumes and sets_. The singers sit (or stand at the edge of the stage); they sing their roles without acting them out; the audience listens as it would at a symphony concert.

The oratorio form was developed in early-seventeenth-century Italy as a way of mounting large religious works during Lent, when the opera houses were closed. The form spread to Germany (where Bach's _Passions_ are oratorios in all but name), to France, and especially to England, where Handel made the _English-language oratorio_ a major commercial genre in the 1730s and 1740s. The _Messiah_ is the most-famous instance, but Handel wrote many others — _Israel in Egypt_ , _Samson_ , _Saul_ , _Solomon_ , _Judas Maccabaeus_ , _Jephtha_. Almost all of these are still performed.

The oratorio's _un-staged_ nature was important historically. In eighteenth-century England, religious dramas were not allowed in churches (they were considered too theatrical) and not allowed in theaters as staged productions (they were considered too religious). The oratorio's compromise — religious text, concert-hall format, no staging — let the form thrive in both settings.

#### Definition: French Overture

A _French overture_ is a Baroque instrumental form for opening operas, oratorios, and large orchestral suites. It has two main sections:

  1. A **slow, majestic opening** in dotted rhythms (long-short-long-short). The character is ceremonial, like the opening of a royal procession. Ends on a half cadence (inconclusive ending that points forward).
  2. A **fast, fugal continuation** with a fugue subject in running notes. The character is energetic, contrapuntal, building. Ends on a perfect cadence (definitive ending) in the home key.

The form was crystallized by Jean-Baptiste Lully at the court of Louis XIV in the second half of the seventeenth century. It was the standard opening movement of French-style Baroque works — operas, ballets, instrumental suites — and was adopted across Europe in the early eighteenth century. Bach's Orchestral Suites in B minor and D major both begin with French overtures (though Bach calls them _Ouvertures_ and writes them at much larger scale than Lully did). Handel's _Messiah_ opens with a French overture; so do Handel's opera _Rinaldo_ , his oratorios _Israel in Egypt_ and _Saul_ , and most of his orchestral suites.

After about 1750 the French overture largely vanished from the repertoire — replaced by the Classical-period _sonata-form_ overture (which Mozart and Beethoven wrote for their operas) and later by the Romantic-period _concert overture_ (Mendelssohn's _Hebrides_ , Berlioz's _Carnaval romain_). But the French overture's _slow-then-fast_ shape remained influential. Listen for it in any opening movement that begins with a stately slow section and breaks into faster activity.

#### Definition: Recitative vs Aria

In opera and oratorio, the two main _vocal_ movement types are _recitative_ and _aria_.

A _recitative_ is a sung passage that imitates the rhythm of natural speech — fast, often unmetered, with the words clear and the melody minimal. Recitative is used for _narrative_ content (telling the story, advancing the plot, delivering information). There are two kinds: _secco_ recitative (with only harpsichord accompaniment, called "dry" because the texture is sparse) and _accompagnato_ recitative (with full orchestral accompaniment, for more dramatic moments).

An _aria_ is a sung passage in which a character expresses an emotion or reflection in a fully developed musical setting — slower, melodic, often with elaborate vocal display. Arias are used for _emotional_ content (the character pausing to feel and to articulate the feeling).

In an opera or oratorio, recitatives and arias alternate. A recitative sets up the situation; an aria responds to it. The plot moves forward through the recitatives; the emotion deepens through the arias.

In _Messiah_ , you hear this pattern throughout. _Comfort ye, my people_ (tenor recitative, accompanied) sets up the prophetic announcement; _Ev'ry valley shall be exalted_ (tenor aria) responds with elaborate vocal display. _Behold, a virgin shall conceive_ (alto recitative, secco) sets up the Nativity prophecy; _O thou that tellest good tidings to Zion_ (alto aria) responds. And so on through the work. The chorus interjects collective commentary at major structural moments.

This chapter focuses on the _opening Sinfonia_ (no voices yet) and the _Hallelujah Chorus_ (full chorus, no soloist). But the alternation of recitative-and-aria underneath the choral movements is the work's rhythmic architecture, and a listener who wants to hear the full _Messiah_ should listen for it.

#### Common Misconception

People sometimes assume the _Messiah_ is a _Christmas piece_. It is not, originally. The work was premiered in Dublin in April 1742 — that is, at Easter, not Christmas. It is structured as a _whole-life-of-Christ_ oratorio: Part I covers the prophecies and Nativity; Part II covers the Passion, Crucifixion, and Resurrection; Part III covers the promise of redemption and the final triumph. The Easter content — the Passion, the Resurrection, the _Hallelujah_ — is at the structural center of the work; the Christmas content (the _Comfort ye_ , the _Pifa_ shepherd's music, the _Glory to God_ chorus) is at the opening.

The _Christmas association_ developed in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, especially in the United States, where the _Messiah_ became a Christmas-season tradition through community chorus performances and through specific Part-I excerpts (the _Hallelujah_ chorus included, even though it actually closes Part II). This is fine — the work is large enough to support multiple seasonal traditions — but the original Easter context is worth remembering. _Messiah_ is not a Christmas piece; it is a _whole-Christian-narrative_ piece that opens with Christmas, peaks at Easter, and closes with eschatology.

The chapter focuses on the Hallelujah Chorus (Easter content, Part II closer) and the Sinfonia (the work's opening, no specific seasonal content). Both are non-Christmas. Both are pieces a year-round listener can engage with.

### 9.4 The Stories

#### Handel — the biographical sketch

Georg Friedrich Händel was born in Halle, Saxony, in 1685 — the same year as Bach (born in Eisenach, about 100 miles south of Halle) and Domenico Scarlatti (born in Naples, the third of the three great Baroque composers of 1685). The three never met; their careers ran in parallel without contact.

Handel's father was a barber-surgeon who wanted his son to become a lawyer. The boy's musical talent emerged early — he reportedly smuggled a clavichord into the attic and practiced at night when his father was asleep — and by his teens his father had relented and allowed him to study music with the Halle Cathedral organist Friedrich Wilhelm Zachow. Handel matriculated at the University of Halle (briefly) in law, then dropped out and moved to Hamburg in 1703 to join the Hamburg Opera as a violinist, then composer.

From 1706 to 1710 he toured Italy — the standard finishing school for any European composer of the early eighteenth century. He worked in Rome, Naples, Florence, and Venice; he met the Scarlattis (father Alessandro and son Domenico), Corelli, the Venetian opera composers; he composed Italian-language operas and chamber music; he learned the Italian operatic style at its source. He returned to Germany in 1710 as Kapellmeister to the Elector of Hanover.

In 1712 he visited London, was paid well for an opera commission, found the city congenial, and never went back to Hanover for more than brief visits. He settled in London for the rest of his life — fifty-seven years. (When his former Hanoverian employer, the Elector, became King George I of England in 1714 through the Hanoverian succession, Handel famously had to make amends; the _Water Music_ of 1717 is sometimes said to have been composed as a reconciliation, though the documentary support is incomplete.)

From 1712 to about 1738 Handel was London's leading composer of _Italian opera seria_ — running opera companies, hiring singers, composing one or two operas a year. His operas include _Rinaldo_ (1711, the first Italian opera composed for London), _Giulio Cesare_ (1724), _Rodelinda_ (1725), _Orlando_ (1733), _Ariodante_ (1735), _Alcina_ (1735). About forty operas total. They were enormously successful in the 1710s and 1720s; they became increasingly difficult to fill the theater for in the 1730s as English audiences turned against Italian-language opera; by the late 1730s Handel's opera companies were failing and Handel himself had been bankrupt at least once.

The shift to English-language oratorio was a _commercial-survival_ move as much as an artistic one. Oratorios were cheaper to produce (no costumes, no sets, no expensive Italian singers — English-speaking singers were cheaper and more plentiful), were religiously palatable to the Methodist-evangelical movement that was reshaping eighteenth-century English religious culture, and could be performed during Lent when the opera houses were closed. Handel's first English oratorio, _Esther_ (1732), was successful; _Saul_ (1739) was successful; _Israel in Egypt_ (1739) ran into trouble (some thought it had too much chorus and not enough aria); _Messiah_ (1741) was hugely successful. From 1741 onward, oratorios were Handel's main genre. He wrote about fifteen of them in his last eighteen years, until his eyesight began to fail around 1750.

He died in London on 14 April 1759, at age 74, having become a British subject (1727), a Doctor of Music at Oxford (1733, though he declined the honorary degree), a household name in London cultural life, and one of the wealthiest composers of his generation. He was buried in Westminster Abbey on 20 April 1759, with three thousand people in attendance.

#### What was happening in mid-eighteenth-century London

Handel's London — the city in which the _Messiah_ was composed, premiered, and made famous — was the largest city in Europe (about 600,000 people in 1740) and the commercial capital of the British empire. It was a city of:

* _Coffee-houses_ , where the male middle and upper classes conducted business, gossip, and political conversation; the coffee-house was the eighteenth-century equivalent of the social-media platform.
* _Theaters_ , including the King's Theatre in the Haymarket (where Handel's operas were performed) and Covent Garden (where his oratorios were).
* _Pleasure gardens_ — Vauxhall, Ranelagh, Marylebone — outdoor entertainment venues where orchestras played for paying customers in elaborate settings.
* _Charitable hospitals_ , including the Foundling Hospital (which became the _Messiah_ 's long-term institutional home) and the Royal Hospital for Seamen at Greenwich.
* _Religious revival_ , especially the Methodist movement of John Wesley and the broader evangelical revival of the 1730s and 1740s.

Handel sat at the intersection of these cultural currents. He wrote for the opera theaters, the oratorio theaters, the charitable hospitals (the _Foundling Hospital Anthem_ and the annual _Messiah_ benefit performances), and indirectly for the religious revival (the oratorios' scriptural texts gave him content the Methodist audiences could embrace). His career is the story of a composer whose music _moved with the market_ — adapting from Italian opera to English oratorio when the operatic market declined, adapting from aristocratic to middle-class audiences when the cultural balance shifted. Compared to Bach, who never adapted to any market and stayed in his Lutheran Kantor's job for thirty years in Leipzig, Handel is the _commercial composer_ of his generation — making a living, then a fortune, by writing what audiences would pay to hear.

This is not a critique. Handel's commercial responsiveness produced the _Messiah_ and the great oratorios. Some great art is made under commercial pressure; some great art is made under institutional protection; some is made in opposition to both. The eighteenth century happens to give us one composer of each variety: Handel (commercial London), Bach (institutional Leipzig), and one composer in between (more on him in Chapter 6 already — Mozart, the freelance experimenter in Vienna a generation later). The three trajectories are different; the music produced by each is great.

#### The Foundling Hospital and the long _Messiah_ tradition

A small but important detail: from 1749 onward, Handel conducted an annual _Messiah_ benefit concert for the Foundling Hospital, a charity for abandoned children founded by the philanthropist Thomas Coram in 1739. The Foundling Hospital was one of the first major charitable institutions of the modern English type — a hospital not for the sick but for the abandoned, taking in children left at its gate and providing them with care, education, and an apprenticeship until adulthood. Handel was a governor of the hospital from 1750 until his death; the annual _Messiah_ concerts raised substantial funds; Handel left the Hospital both a copy of his manuscript score and a small income from royal annuities in his will.

The _Messiah-as-charitable-event_ tradition is one of the work's defining social features. Almost every _Messiah_ performance since 1750 has had some charitable dimension; many of the standard performance traditions (the participatory standing for the _Hallelujah_ , the community-chorus model, the Christmas-season fundraisers) have been shaped by this association. _Messiah_ is not just a piece; it is an _institution_ , with charitable, ritual, and seasonal traditions that have evolved continuously for over 270 years.

This connects the work to a broader principle: _some classical works are not only artworks but also social rituals_. _Messiah_ is one; Beethoven 9 is another (which is why orchestras play it on New Year's Eve in Japan and at major civic ceremonies elsewhere; see Chapter 14); the Mozart Requiem is a third (often performed at major memorial events; see Chapter 12). The ritual function is part of the work's life. The artwork is real; the social ritual is also real; they are not the same thing but they are entangled.

#### The four readings

**John Eliot Gardiner / English Baroque Soloists / Monteverdi Choir, 1982 (Philips Classics).** Gardiner's reading is _period-instrument, smaller ensemble, sharply articulated_ — the historically informed reading that became the new standard from the 1980s onward. The Monteverdi Choir's diction is exemplary (every word audible); the orchestra plays with gut strings, period winds, and natural trumpets; the tempi are slightly faster than the older traditional readings. This is the recording I recommend as the primary for amateur listeners — it gives the most direct sense of what Handel's own ensembles may have sounded like.

**Trevor Pinnock / The English Concert, 1988 (DG Archiv).** Pinnock's reading is also period-instrument but with a slightly different sound — a brighter, more transparent texture than Gardiner's. The choir is smaller; the orchestra is slightly more intimate. Both Gardiner and Pinnock represent the _historically informed Messiah_ , but they differ in temperament — Gardiner is more dramatic, Pinnock more chamber-like.

**Sir Colin Davis / London Symphony Orchestra / Tenebrae Choir, 2006 (LSO Live).** A _modern-instrument_ reading on a slightly smaller scale than the older traditions. Davis brings symphonic grandeur to the work without resorting to the enormous Victorian-era choral forces (Beecham's 1959 RPO/RCS reading uses a chorus of about 200; Davis uses about 40). The result is a _middle path_ — modern instruments, period-influenced articulation, full but not bloated. For a listener who finds period-instrument readings too austere and traditional readings too inflated, Davis 2006 is the natural compromise.

**Sir Thomas Beecham / Royal Philharmonic Orchestra / Royal Choral Society, 1959 (RCA).** The _grand Victorian tradition_ in its mid-twentieth-century form. Modern instruments, large symphony orchestra (about 80 players), enormous chorus (about 200 singers), traditional cuts (some movements omitted), traditional tempi (slower than the period-instrument readings). Beecham's _Messiah_ is _the Victorian_ sound — what most twentieth-century English-speaking listeners encountered as "the Handel sound" until the 1980s. It is unfashionable today but historically important and many of its readings of individual numbers are still benchmarks.

Four readings, spanning roughly fifty years and four substantially different aesthetic positions. _Period-instrument-dramatic_ (Gardiner), _period-instrument-chamber_ (Pinnock), _modern-instrument-middle_ (Davis), _modern-instrument-Victorian-grand_ (Beecham). The work-vs-interpretation muscle continues to build. _Messiah_ probably has the largest interpretive range of any work in this book — the work has been continuously performed for 270 years, in dozens of different traditions, and the recorded literature contains roughly two hundred commercial versions.

#### Cross-piece links

* If you loved the Hallelujah Chorus, listen to the **other great choruses in the _Messiah_** — _And the glory of the Lord_ (Part I), _For unto us a child is born_ (Part I), _All we like sheep have gone astray_ (Part II), the final _Amen_ fugue (Part III). The work has at least a dozen choral movements that would, in a less-known oratorio, be the highlights.
* For more Handel oratorios, listen to **Saul (1739)** — particularly the _Dead March_ (Saul's funeral) and the David-Saul duet _In sweetest harmony they lived_. **Israel in Egypt (1739)** is more chorally weighted than the _Messiah_ (about three-quarters of the work is choruses); the plague choruses are extraordinary. **Solomon (1748)** has the famous _Arrival of the Queen of Sheba_ sinfonia. **Theodora (1750)** is Handel's most-personal late oratorio.
* For more **Handel operatic arias** , listen to **Cecilia Bartoli's Handel album** (Decca, 1999) or **Joyce DiDonato's _Drama Queens_ album** (Erato, 2012). Handel wrote some of the greatest soprano and mezzo arias in the operatic repertoire — most of which have been rediscovered only in the past forty years.
* For the **French overture form** in Bach, listen to **Bach's Orchestral Suite No. 1 in C major, BWV 1066** — the opening movement is a classic French overture in the Handel tradition. Bach and Handel both inherited the form from Lully; both deepened it.
* For **eighteenth-century English-language sacred choral writing more broadly** , listen to **William Boyce's anthems** , **Maurice Greene's anthems** , and **Henry Purcell's church music** (especially the _Funeral Music for Queen Mary_). Purcell (1659–1695) was the great English composer of the generation before Handel, and his music shaped the English choral idiom Handel adopted when he settled in London.

#### Conversation Seeds

* _Ask the companion about the twenty-four-day composition of the _Messiah_ in August–September 1741 — what is documented, what is legend, and what was Handel's working method like in that compositional fever._
* _Tell the companion which of the four readings (Gardiner 1982 period-instrument-dramatic, Pinnock 1988 period-instrument-chamber, Davis 2006 modern-middle, Beecham 1959 Victorian-grand) you preferred, and ask her what your preference reveals about how you want the _Messiah_ to sound._
* _Ask the companion about the standing-up tradition during the Hallelujah Chorus — when it started, whether the King George II story is true, and what it means that classical-music audiences participate in this one specific moment in this one specific work across two and a half centuries._
* _Ask the companion to compare the _opening of the Hallelujah Chorus_ with the _opening of Bach's B-minor Mass _Sanctus___ — two of the greatest Baroque choral entries, written in the same period, with strikingly different temperaments. What is Handel doing that Bach is not, and vice versa?*
* _Ask the companion about the Foundling Hospital and the _Messiah_ -as-charitable-event tradition. What is the relationship between a piece of music and a social institution? How has this association shaped how we encounter the work?_

### 9.5 Exercises

#### Concept Check

**Q1.** What is an _oratorio_ , and how does it differ from an opera?

Hint

Both have singers, orchestra, and dramatic narrative. The difference is in _what is on stage_.

**Answer:** An oratorio is a large-scale musical setting of a religious or moral text for soloists, chorus, and orchestra, performed _without staging, costume, or acting_ — as concert music rather than as theater. An opera has the same musical elements (soloists, chorus, orchestra, recitatives, arias) but is performed _with_ staging, costumes, acting, and theatrical settings. The form developed in seventeenth-century Italy and was made the major English-language vocal genre by Handel in the 1730s and 1740s. The oratorio's un-staged nature was historically important because eighteenth-century English convention did not allow religious dramas to be staged; the oratorio's concert-hall format provided a compromise. _Messiah_ is the most-famous example; Handel wrote about fifteen others.

**Q2.** What is a _French overture_?

**Answer:** A Baroque instrumental form for opening operas, oratorios, and large orchestral suites. It has two main sections: a slow, majestic opening in dotted rhythms (long-short-long-short), followed by a fast, fugal continuation in running notes. The form was crystallized by Jean-Baptiste Lully at the French court of Louis XIV in the late seventeenth century and was adopted across Europe in the early eighteenth. Handel's _Messiah_ opens with a French overture; so do Bach's Orchestral Suites and many other large Baroque works. After 1750 the form largely disappeared, replaced by the Classical-period sonata-form overture.

### Chapter Summary

This chapter introduced **Handel's _Messiah_** (HWV 56, composed in twenty-four days in August–September 1741, premiered in Dublin April 1742) through two short sections: the **opening Sinfonia** (a classic _French overture_ in slow-then-fast form, ~3 minutes) and the **"Hallelujah" Chorus** (the famous chorus closing Part II, ~4 minutes).

You learned **oratorio** (large-scale religious choral work performed without staging), **French overture** (Baroque opening form: slow-dotted then fast-fugal), and **recitative vs aria** (the alternation between speech-like narrative and melodic emotional response that drives all opera and oratorio).

You met **Handel** in his single chapter — born the same year as Bach (1685) in central Germany, toured Italy in his twenties, settled in London in his thirties, anglicized his name, ran Italian-opera companies in the 1710s and 1720s, shifted to English-language oratorio in the late 1730s when the operatic market declined, composed the _Messiah_ during a commercial-survival pivot, became the most-loved composer in eighteenth-century England, died wealthy and was buried in Westminster Abbey. The Handel-Bach contrast — _commercial London_ versus _institutional Leipzig_ , _theatrical_ versus _interior_ — is one of the great parallel-temperaments stories in Western music.

You met four readings of the _Messiah_ : Gardiner 1982 (period-instrument, dramatic), Pinnock 1988 (period-instrument, chamber), Davis 2006 (modern-middle), Beecham 1959 (Victorian-grand). The work-vs-interpretation muscle has now encountered its widest spread — the _Messiah_ has been continuously performed for 270 years and the recorded literature contains hundreds of versions.

You met the **Foundling Hospital tradition** and the **standing-up tradition** in the Hallelujah Chorus — two examples of how the _Messiah_ has become _not only an artwork but also a social ritual_. The work is encountered through these scaffolds as much as through the score; the mature listener can hold both modes.

The next chapter takes you to **the Classical period** — the era of Haydn, Mozart, and Beethoven, roughly 1750 to 1820, where the Baroque pulse softens, clarity replaces complexity, and the _symphony, string quartet, sonata, and concerto_ become the four pillars of the standard genres. Chapter 10 anchors on **Haydn's String Quartet Op. 76 No. 3 "Emperor"** — the string quartet as the most intimate of forms, the _conversation among four voices_ in which Haydn's wit and depth lived in full.

Composer Protagonist Bach exits the book (we will not return to him in focused chapters, though his shadow is everywhere). Composer Protagonist Handel met here in his single chapter. Composer Protagonist Mozart resumes in Chapter 11; Beethoven resumes in Chapter 13. The book is now leaving the Baroque and entering the Classical period.

## Chapter 10: Haydn, String Quartet Op. 76 No. 3 "Emperor"

Four musicians sit in a private music room in a Viennese aristocratic house in the late 1790s. Two play violins; one plays viola; one plays cello. They are seated facing one another in a square, so that each player can see every other player's bow arm and music stand. The host — a Hungarian-Austrian count whose family has commissioned the music — sits a few feet away with a small group of guests. There is no concert hall, no paying audience, no applause between movements. The four players begin a piece by Joseph Haydn, the most famous composer in Europe, whose roughly sixty-eight string quartets have made the genre what it now is.

The room is quiet enough that the slight breath of each player before a downbeat can be heard. The cello starts a phrase; the first violin answers it; the second violin and viola comment in the middle. The players are listening to one another with the absolute attention four people sharing a quiet room can bring. The host is listening with the same attention. There are _eight ears_ in the room, and they are all on the same piece of music.

This is _chamber music_ — music for a small group of instrumentalists, played in a small room, for a small audience. It is the most _intimate_ of classical music's standard genres. The string quartet, specifically — two violins, viola, cello — is sometimes called _the highest form of musical conversation_ , because the four players are equals (no soloist, no orchestral mass behind them), the texture is transparent (four voices, none of them doubled), and the music can develop ideas at the level of subtlety that only conversational intimacy supports.

Haydn wrote about sixty-eight string quartets across his career (the exact count depends on which sketches and reattributions you accept). He is sometimes called _the father of the string quartet_ , which is partly true: he did not invent the form (it had existed in Italian and Austrian chamber music since at least the 1740s), but he _defined_ it across his career — establishing the four-movement plan (fast — slow — minuet — fast), the equal partnership of the four voices, the developmental complexity that distinguishes the quartet from a divertimento, and the emotional range the genre would carry into Mozart, Beethoven, and beyond.

This chapter focuses on **String Quartet Op. 76 No. 3 in C major** — composed in 1797, published in 1799, one of six quartets in Haydn's Op. 76 set commissioned by Count Joseph Erdődy of Hungary. The nickname "Emperor" comes from the second movement, which is a set of variations on a tune Haydn had just composed for the Austrian Imperial anthem _Gott erhalte Franz den Kaiser_ — a tune that later became the German national anthem under different lyrics. The whole quartet runs about twenty-five minutes; this chapter focuses on the second movement (the _Emperor_ variations themselves, ~10 minutes) and gives shorter treatment to the other three movements.

### 10.1 Before You Listen

#### Hook anecdote — the anthem and what happened to it

In the autumn of 1796, Austria was at war with France. Napoleon had been campaigning in Italy and was threatening the Austrian heartland. The Habsburg court in Vienna wanted a _national hymn_ — a melody the people could sing to express loyalty to Emperor Franz II — and asked the most-famous composer in Austria to write one. Joseph Haydn, sixty-four years old, recently returned from his second London visit and at the height of his international reputation, accepted the commission.

He took as his model "God Save the King," the British anthem he had heard performed nightly in London concerts. He wanted something equally hummable, equally memorable, equally suited to mass singing. He worked on the tune in late 1796 and early 1797. The result was _Gott erhalte Franz den Kaiser_ — "God Preserve Franz the Emperor" — first performed on the Emperor's birthday, 12 February 1797, at the Burgtheater in Vienna. The audience sang along; the tune was a success; Haydn was reported to have wept at the reception.

A few months later, Haydn used the same tune as the theme for the second movement of a string quartet he was composing for Count Erdődy. Across four variations, he kept the tune intact in each variation, passing it from instrument to instrument (first violin in variation 1, second violin in variation 2, cello in variation 3, viola in variation 4) while the other three players elaborated counter-melodies and figurations around it. This is the _Emperor_ movement, and the technique — keeping the tune intact and elaborating around it — is unusual in variation form; most variation sets transform the theme itself, while Haydn preserves it and lets the variation happen _in the accompaniment_.

The afterlife of the tune is one of the strangest in the history of national anthems. _Gott erhalte Franz den Kaiser_ served as the Austrian Imperial anthem from 1797 to 1918, with the text updated for each successive emperor. After the dissolution of the Austrian Empire in 1918, the tune was adopted by Weimar Germany in 1922 as the German national anthem, with new lyrics ("Deutschland, Deutschland über alles") by August Heinrich Hoffmann von Fallersleben, originally written in 1841 and used unofficially before 1922. Under the Third Reich (1933–1945), the first stanza of these lyrics became associated with Nazi nationalism and is now performed only at neo-Nazi events. The third stanza, however — _Einigkeit und Recht und Freiheit_ , "Unity and justice and freedom" — has been the official German national anthem since 1952 (in West Germany) and 1990 (in reunified Germany).

So: Haydn's 1797 melody for the Austrian Imperial anthem is _also_ the melody of the contemporary German national anthem (using its third-stanza lyrics) and is _also_ the second-movement variations of his 1797 string quartet Op. 76 No. 3. The same tune across three lives. When you hear the _Emperor_ movement, you are hearing the _original use_ of a melody most twenty-first-century listeners know in its national-anthem form.

#### What to notice

For the **first movement** (~9 min): listen for the _conversation among four voices_. The opening figure is a simple ascending three-note motif; it is passed around among the four players, each one taking it, transforming it slightly, and handing it on. This _handing-around_ of motivic material is the central technique of Haydn's quartet writing — and one of the central techniques of the string quartet as a genre. The whole first movement is in sonata form (Chapter 6 ground); listen also for the _exposition's two themes_ (first theme: the ascending three-note motif and its continuation; second theme: a more lyrical melody in the dominant key) and for the _return_ of the first theme at the recapitulation.

For the **second movement, the Emperor variations** (~10 min): this is the chapter's main focus. Listen for the _anthem tune_ first as it appears in the opening Theme statement (the first violin plays it; the other three accompany). Then count the _four variations_ , noticing which instrument carries the tune in each:

* **Theme** (first violin carries the tune; other three accompany).
* **Variation 1** (second violin carries the tune; first violin plays elaborate decoration above it; viola and cello accompany).
* **Variation 2** (cello carries the tune in the bass register; other three play counter-melodies above it).
* **Variation 3** (viola carries the tune; first violin, second violin, and cello weave around it).
* **Variation 4** (first violin returns to carrying the tune, with the other three now in fuller four-part harmony).

The tune itself does not change. Across the five statements, the _accompaniment_ and _texture_ are what vary. This is the essential technique of the movement — and the reason the variations are sometimes described as _the most reverent variation set in the literature_ : Haydn refuses to alter his anthem, even decoratively. He treats the tune as sacrosanct.

For the **third movement, the Minuet** (~4 min): listen for the _triple-meter dance rhythm_ (three beats per bar, with the emphasis on the first) and for the contrasting _trio_ (the middle section of a minuet, traditionally for three players or with a thinner texture). The Minuet is in C major; the trio is in A minor.

For the **fourth movement, the finale** (~4 min): listen for _the dramatic minor-key opening_ — the movement begins in C minor, not C major, which is unusual for a closing movement and signals that Haydn is going to do something dramatically interesting with the form. Listen for the eventual _modulation back to C major_ and the relief that the return to the home key brings.

#### One-sentence background

**Haydn, String Quartet in C major, Op. 76 No. 3 "Emperor," Hob. III:77** — composed 1797 in Vienna, published 1799; the third of six quartets in the Op. 76 set commissioned by Count Joseph Erdődy of Galántha; the second movement is a theme-and-variations on Haydn's own _Gott erhalte Franz den Kaiser_ (the Austrian Imperial anthem of 1797–1918, which later became the German national anthem). Total duration ~25 minutes across four movements.

The Mosaïques are a period-instrument string quartet (gut strings, classical bows, no chin rests) that produces a transparent, expressive sound particularly suited to Haydn's textures. The Takács, Tátrai, and Amadeus alternates are all modern-instrument quartets representing different traditions (American-Hungarian-international, Hungarian, Anglo-Austrian).
