### 12.2 The Listening Window

#### "Der Hölle Rache" — the Queen of the Night's aria (~3 minutes)

The aria is in D minor, marked Allegro assai, and runs about three minutes. Most performances are very close to this duration; the aria is rhythmically tight and does not admit much expressive elongation.

* **0:00–0:30.** **Orchestral introduction and opening vocal line.** The orchestra plays a fast, urgent D-minor figure that establishes the aria's atmospheric urgency. The soprano enters with the opening text _Der Hölle Rache kocht in meinem Herzen_ — "Hell's vengeance boils in my heart." The vocal line is declamatory, with the rhythm of the words tightly fitted to the rhythm of the music.

* **0:30–1:00.** **First coloratura passage.** The soprano launches into the first of two extended _coloratura_ (rapid running-note) passages, climbing through her high register. The text here is fragmentary — _Tod, Tod und Verzweiflung_ (death, death and despair) — with the words punctuating fast vocal figures.

* **1:00–1:15.** **The first high F.** The coloratura reaches its first climactic peak with a sustained high F (F6 — two octaves and a fourth above middle C). This is one of the most-famous moments in the soprano repertoire. The high F is held briefly; the soprano must execute it cleanly while sustaining the dramatic intensity. Some Queens are _thrilling_ on the high F (an audible explosion of vocal power); others are _cleanly accurate_ but less thrilling. The best Queens combine both.

* **1:15–1:50.** **Middle declamatory section.** The soprano returns to syllabic singing — text closely fitted to notes — with the orchestra continuing its urgent accompaniment. The text describes the consequences of the Queen's demand: if Pamina does not kill Sarastro, the Queen will disavow her daughter, and the bond between them will be broken.

* **1:50–2:20.** **Second coloratura passage.** A second climb through the high register, with the text _Hört, hört, hört, Rachegötter, hört der Mutter Schwur_ (Hear, hear, hear, ye gods of revenge, hear a mother's vow).

* **2:20–2:40.** **The second high F.** The aria's second high F appears here, more sustained than the first, holding the listener at the soprano's most extreme range. This is the climactic structural moment of the aria.

* **2:40–3:00.** **Closing.** The soprano descends from the high F, the orchestra plays a few closing chords, the aria ends with a definitive D-minor cadence.

The Queen of the Night aria is _the_ primer for what opera does. Spoken language could not express the Queen's vengeance; ordinary song could not express it; the only adequate vehicle is the highest extremity of the soprano's voice, in a key that signals tragedy, with an orchestra that supports the urgency at every level. _This is why opera exists_ : certain dramatic states require vocal-and-orchestral resources that no other art form possesses. The Queen aria is a three-minute demonstration of why opera matters.

#### Requiem Dies Irae (Gardiner reading, ~2 minutes)

* **0:00–0:10.** **The orchestral hammer.** Strings and woodwinds begin fast running figures in D minor; trumpets and trombones enter with sharp, declarative blasts. The energy is apocalyptic.

* **0:10–0:30.** **Chorus entry.** The chorus enters fortissimo on _Dies irae, dies illa_ (Day of wrath, that day) — the four-voice texture singing in tight declamation, with the orchestra hammering underneath. The dynamic is at maximum.

* **0:30–1:00.** **Continued chorus.** _Solvet saeclum in favilla, Teste David cum Sybilla_ (Will dissolve the world into ash, As prophesied by David and the Sibyl). The chorus continues at full intensity; the orchestra's running figures continue.

* **1:00–1:30.** **Brief quieter section.** _Quantus tremor est futurus, Quando judex est venturus, Cuncta stricte discussurus_ (How great the trembling shall be, when the Judge shall come, to strictly examine all). The chorus drops to a hushed unison for a few bars — the trembling text setting itself reflected in the hushed dynamics — then builds back.

* **1:30–2:00.** **Final climactic section.** The chorus and orchestra return to full intensity, with the _Solvet saeclum_ text repeated and the music driving toward a definitive cadence. The movement ends on a strong D-minor chord.

This is one of the most-theatrical settings of the _Dies Irae_ in the standard repertoire. Mozart is treating the medieval text as a _dramatic operatic moment_ — chorus and orchestra in full intensity, the apocalyptic imagery embodied in the sound. This is the _Mozart Dies Irae_ — the Latin sequence text set by Mozart in his own musical language. The medieval _plainchant_ melody for the _Dies Irae_ (Chapter 16's launch) is a different, older, monophonic melody; Mozart does not quote it here. The text is the same; the music is Mozart's.

#### Requiem Lacrimosa (Gardiner reading, ~3 minutes)

* **0:00–0:15.** **The opening weeping figure.** The strings play a slow, falling sigh — a _lamenting_ gesture in 12/8 time (a meter that produces a rocking, rocking-cradle quality). The figure is in D minor.

* **0:15–0:40.** **Chorus entrance.** The chorus enters softly, almost in tears, with the text _Lacrimosa dies illa_ (Mournful that day). The four voices sing in close harmony, with the rhythm of the words gently lifted by the music. The dynamic is _piano_ throughout this opening section.

* **0:40–1:00.** **First climb.** The chorus's melodic line rises gradually; the orchestra's weeping figures continue underneath. The text describes the day when the dead shall rise from their ashes (_qua resurget ex favilla_).

* **1:00–1:15.** **The Mozart-Süssmayr transition.** Mozart wrote the first eight bars of the Lacrimosa in his own hand before he died; from bar 9 onward, the music is by Süssmayr, completing what Mozart had begun. The transition is around 1:00 in most readings; some listeners hear a _subtle character shift_ here (a slight reduction in harmonic richness, a slight conventional turn in the phrasing) — but the shift is subtle, and many listeners do not detect it. Süssmayr was an attentive student.

* **1:15–2:15.** **Continued chorus.** The choral writing continues to develop, with sopranos taking the melodic lead and the lower voices providing harmonic support. The dynamic remains primarily _piano_ with occasional brief swells.

* **2:15–3:00.** **Final climb to the Amen.** The chorus rises to its emotional peak with the text _Huic ergo parce, Deus_ (Therefore spare him, O God) and concludes with a sung _Amen_ — a final, accepting cadence on a D-major chord (a Picardy third — closing a minor-key movement on a major chord, traditional in Baroque and Classical sacred music for the final cadence).

The Lacrimosa is one of the most-loved movements of the Requiem and one of the most-loved choral movements in the standard repertoire. The weeping figure, the gentle chorus, the slow climb, the major-key resolution — the music's structure embodies the text's theology: mourning that opens toward acceptance, sorrow that opens toward grace.

The fact that Mozart wrote only the first eight bars before dying gives the Lacrimosa an added layer of legend. _Mozart died composing the Lacrimosa_ , the story goes — leaving the tears unfinished, the resurrection-from-ashes literally unwritten when he lost the strength to write. The legend is dramatic and partly true; what is documented is more complicated, and we will get to it in the Stories section.

### 12.3 What's Happening in the Music

#### Definition: Opera

_Opera_ is a multi-movement musical drama for solo singers, chorus, and orchestra, with a libretto (a poetic-dramatic text) sung throughout or with sung sections interspersed among spoken dialogue. Most opera includes acting, costumes, sets, and theatrical staging. The form was developed in Italy in the early seventeenth century (Monteverdi's _L'Orfeo_ of 1607 is sometimes considered the first surviving great opera) and spread across Europe over the next two centuries.

In plain language: opera is _theater set to music_. The actors are also singers; the dialogue is sung; the orchestra provides continuous musical support; the audience watches a play in which every word is delivered in song.

The main types of operatic vocal writing alternate within the form:

* **Recitative** — sung dialogue close to natural speech rhythm; used for plot advancement, narrative content, conversation. Either _secco_ (with sparse continuo accompaniment) or _accompagnato_ (with full orchestra).
* **Aria** — a fully developed melodic setting in which a character expresses an emotion or reflection. The Queen of the Night aria is an aria.
* **Ensemble** — multiple singers performing together (duet, trio, quartet, quintet, sextet). Ensembles are often the dramatic high points of operas because they let multiple characters express different feelings simultaneously.
* **Chorus** — the operatic chorus singing collectively, often as commentary on the action or as part of a crowd scene.

_Die Zauberflöte_ is a _Singspiel_ — a German-language opera with _spoken dialogue_ rather than recitative between the musical numbers. The Italian _opera seria_ tradition (which Handel worked in, Chapter 9) uses recitative; the Singspiel tradition uses spoken dialogue. The two traditions produced different aesthetics — Italian _seria_ feels continuous and lofty; German _Singspiel_ feels closer to theatrical drama, with the music interrupted by direct spoken exchange. The Singspiel tradition produced not only _Die Zauberflöte_ but also Beethoven's _Fidelio_ (1814) and Weber's _Der Freischütz_ (1821), and indirectly the German operetta (Lehár's _The Merry Widow_) and the American musical (Rodgers and Hammerstein).

#### Definition: Coloratura

_Coloratura_ (Italian for "coloring") is a style of operatic vocal writing characterized by elaborate, rapid, ornamental passages — runs, trills, leaps, fast figurations, extreme high notes. Coloratura is most associated with the soprano voice and especially with eighteenth- and nineteenth-century opera. The Queen of the Night aria is one of the most-famous coloratura passages in the soprano repertoire.

Coloratura serves several functions: it is _vocal display_ (showing off the singer's technique), it is _dramatic intensification_ (expressing extreme emotional states that ordinary syllabic singing could not convey), and it is _characterization_ (the Queen of the Night's coloratura signals her _superhuman_ nature, her connection to the realm of night and magic, her unnatural rage).

The vocal Fach (German term for a singer's specific vocal category) that handles coloratura at its highest range is the _coloratura soprano_ — a soprano whose voice is light, agile, and capable of extreme high notes (high E, F, F#, sometimes higher). Famous coloratura sopranos in the recorded era include Joan Sutherland, Beverly Sills, Diana Damrau, Sumi Jo, and many others. The Queen of the Night is one of the standard repertoire test pieces for the coloratura-soprano voice.

#### Definition: Requiem

A _Requiem_ is a Latin Mass for the Dead — a setting of the Catholic Mass with the variable texts replaced by texts specific to a funeral or memorial. The standard Requiem text includes the _Introitus_ (_Requiem aeternam_ — Eternal rest), the _Kyrie eleison_ (Lord have mercy), the _Sequentia_ (the _Dies Irae_ — Day of Wrath), the _Offertorium_ , the _Sanctus_ , the _Benedictus_ , the _Agnus Dei_ , and the _Communio_ (_Lux aeterna_ — Eternal light). Most settings also include the _Pie Jesu_ (a brief intercession) and the _Libera me_ (Deliver me).

The Requiem as a _concert-music genre_ (rather than as actual liturgical music for a funeral) emerged in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries. Major Requiem settings include those by Mozart (1791), Cherubini (two settings, 1816 and 1836), Berlioz (1837, with massive orchestral forces), Verdi (1874, operatic in style), Brahms (a _German Requiem_ in 1868, on Lutheran rather than Latin texts), Fauré (1888, a consoling setting that omits the _Dies Irae_), Duruflé (1947), Britten (a _War Requiem_ in 1962, interleaving Latin texts with Wilfred Owen's English war poetry, see Chapter 24). The Requiem is one of the central choral genres in Western art music.

The _Mozart Requiem_ is particularly central because it is _unfinished_ — Mozart died mid-composition — and because it has a _complicated authorship situation_ (the completion by Süssmayr, the question of how much Mozart wrote vs how much Süssmayr extended). The work has accumulated legend in a way few other Requiems have, and the legend is intertwined with the actual music.

#### Common Misconception

People sometimes treat opera as _elitist_ — fancy theaters, expensive tickets, foreign-language libretti, aristocratic conventions. Some opera is elitist, in the sense of being institutionally inflected toward wealthy audiences. But the form itself is not inherently elitist, and historically _opera was popular entertainment_ for centuries.

_Die Zauberflöte_ is a useful corrective. Schikaneder's Freihaus-Theater was a _suburban popular theater_ for working-class and middle-class Viennese audiences who could not afford the court opera. The opera's mixture of fairy tale, comedy, magic, and music was designed to entertain a broad audience, not a narrow elite. The Queen of the Night aria is a virtuoso showcase — but the bird-catcher Papageno's songs are folk-style, the choral hymns are accessible, and the comedy is broad. _Die Zauberflöte_ was _Mozart's most-performed opera in his lifetime_ not in court theaters but in popular venues, and its enduring appeal is part of why opera in the German-speaking world has retained broader audiences than opera in some other countries.

Similarly, _La Bohème, Carmen, Madama Butterfly, La Traviata_ were popular hits in their time. The elitist reputation that has accumulated around opera in the twentieth century is partly a function of how the form has been institutionalized (large fancy houses, formal-dress conventions, expensive ticket prices), not of the form itself. The amateur listener who encounters opera through _Die Zauberflöte_ — and especially through the popular Mozart-Schikaneder mixture of high and low elements — has access to the form in its most-accessible mode.

### 12.4 The Stories

#### Mozart's last year

Mozart began 1791 in difficult circumstances. He had been borrowing money from Michael Puchberg since 1788; his subscription concerts in Vienna had not been profitable for several years; his wife Constanze had been in poor health (six pregnancies across the previous eight years, and recurring leg ulcers requiring treatment at the Baden spa). He had two surviving children — Karl Thomas (age 7) and the newborn Franz Xaver Wolfgang Mozart (born July 1791). His income depended on commissions, and commissions had been irregular.

Then, in the spring and summer of 1791, four commissions arrived nearly simultaneously:

  1. **Die Zauberflöte** — Schikaneder's commission for the Freihaus-Theater, which Mozart had begun composing in early 1791.
  2. **La clemenza di Tito** — commissioned by the Bohemian estates for the coronation of Leopold II as King of Bohemia, to be performed in Prague in September 1791. The commission arrived in July; Mozart had about two months to compose a complete two-act opera.
  3. **The Requiem** — commissioned anonymously through Walsegg's gray-clad steward in mid-July 1791.
  4. **The Clarinet Concerto K. 622** — for Anton Stadler, completed in October 1791.

Plus various other works: piano concertos, a string quintet, a Masonic cantata, _Eine kleine Freimaurer-Kantate_ K. 623, performed at his Masonic lodge on 18 November 1791 with Mozart conducting (his last completed conducting engagement).

Mozart was composing at a pace that, in retrospect, looks unsustainable. He traveled to Prague in late August, conducted the _Tito_ premiere on 6 September, returned to Vienna in mid-September, conducted the _Magic Flute_ premiere on 30 September, attended a few more _Flute_ performances in early October, completed and saw Stadler off to Prague with the Clarinet Concerto in early October. By late October he was complaining of fatigue and ill health; by mid-November he was bedridden.

He died on the night of 4–5 December 1791, around midnight. The cause of death is uncertain — eighteenth-century medical reporting cannot identify it with confidence — but the _most-likely_ cause is _rheumatic fever_ (an inflammatory condition following a streptococcal throat infection), with secondary kidney failure. He had been ill for about three weeks. The story of Mozart being _poisoned_ — by Salieri, by Masonic enemies, by Walsegg, by anyone else — is a nineteenth-century legend with no eighteenth-century documentary support, dramatized famously in Pushkin's 1830 verse drama _Mozart and Salieri_ , then in Rimsky-Korsakov's 1898 opera based on Pushkin, then in Peter Shaffer's 1979 _Amadeus_. The Salieri-poisoning story is fiction; Salieri was a respected court composer who outlived Mozart by 34 years and did not, by any documented evidence, harm him.

Mozart was buried in a _common grave_ in St. Marx Cemetery on 7 December 1791. This was _not_ an indignity. Common graves in Vienna in 1791 were the standard practice for _anyone except aristocracy_ , including comfortable middle-class people. (The Habsburg-era _Josephinian reforms_ in the 1780s had restructured Viennese burial practice toward common graves for hygienic reasons.) Mozart's burial was _normal for his social class_ , not the secret pauper's grave the nineteenth century romanticized. The legends of mysterious unmarked graves, of bodies never recovered, of unexplained absence of mourners — most of this is later embellishment. What is documented: he was buried in the standard Viennese manner for his time and social position, in a section of St. Marx Cemetery that has been built over since, so the exact grave location has been lost.

Constanze was 29 when Mozart died. She had two young children and significant debts. The Requiem was unfinished. Walsegg, the commissioner, had paid half the fee in advance; he expected delivery of a complete Requiem, with Mozart's authorship. If the work could not be delivered, Constanze would have to return the advance and lose the second half of the fee. If the work could be delivered as Mozart's complete authorship, Walsegg would pay the rest and Constanze could keep both halves.

So Constanze hid the fact that the Requiem was unfinished. She gathered the partial manuscript and asked first Joseph Eybler (one of Mozart's students) and then Franz Xaver Süssmayr (another, closer student) to complete the work. Eybler made some sketches and then withdrew. Süssmayr completed the work in early 1792, drawing on Mozart's sketches where they existed and writing entirely new music where they did not. The completed Requiem was delivered to Walsegg in 1792 as Mozart's work; Constanze received the rest of the fee. Walsegg performed the work at his country estate in 1793 under his own name. Mozart's authorship was kept secret as Walsegg had requested.

The Requiem's _true_ authorship was widely known to Mozart's family and close friends but was not publicly acknowledged. After Constanze's authorized 1800 publication of the Requiem under Mozart's name, controversy began about what was Mozart and what was Süssmayr. The controversy continues. Modern scholarship has produced _alternative completions_ — Robert Levin (1991, 2024 revision), Duncan Druce, Richard Maunder, Robert Snow, and others have completed the Requiem in different ways, drawing on Mozart's sketches and on the conjectured Mozart style. The Süssmayr version remains the most-performed, but conductors and choirs increasingly choose alternative completions. The "real" Mozart Requiem is, in some sense, plural: a set of works derived from Mozart's incomplete manuscript by various editors over two centuries.

#### The Magic Flute as Masonic opera

_Die Zauberflöte_ is sometimes called Mozart's _Masonic opera_ — its libretto is full of Masonic symbolism: the trials of fire and water (echoing Masonic initiation rites), the temple of Wisdom and Reason (echoing Masonic philosophical aspirations), the brotherhood of the Priests of Isis and Osiris (Egyptian-mystical Masonic imagery), the three-flat key signature of many key passages (three flats = the Masonic number three), the contrast between the night (the Queen) and the day (Sarastro and his temple) (Masonic light-dark imagery).

Mozart had been a Mason since December 1784 (he was initiated into the Zur Wohltätigkeit lodge in Vienna). Schikaneder was also a Mason, in a different lodge. The Vienna of the 1780s and 1790s had a substantial Masonic community among educated middle-class men — composers, writers, doctors, civil servants. Masonry was suspected by the Habsburg court (especially after the French Revolution made _Liberty, Equality, Fraternity_ dangerously close to Masonic vocabulary), and several lodges were forced to merge in 1785 by imperial decree. The Masonic community in Vienna was therefore _socially significant but politically suspect_ — a thriving subculture under official surveillance.

_Die Zauberflöte_ is an _advertisement_ for Masonic ideals: brotherhood, enlightenment, the conquering of irrational forces by reason, the moral education of human beings through trials. The Queen of the Night represents the _irrational_ and the _vengeful_ (her aria is the most-extreme statement of operatic rage); Sarastro represents the _rational_ and the _humane_ (his "In diesen heil'gen Hallen" is the opposite — slow, dignified, forgiving). The opera's moral arc is the _triumph of Reason over Unreason_ , embodied in Tamino's successful trials and his union with Pamina.

This Masonic framework is part of what gives the opera its philosophical depth beneath the fairy-tale surface. It is also why some twentieth-century productions have struggled with the libretto's gender politics — the Queen is the _bad_ feminine principle to be overcome, the Priests of Sarastro's brotherhood are explicitly male, Pamina has to _prove herself worthy_ before being admitted to the trials. The Masonic eighteenth-century world view does not always translate well into twenty-first-century gender politics. Productions vary in how they handle this — some reinterpret, some preserve, some reframe.

#### Süssmayr and the Requiem completion

Franz Xaver Süssmayr (1766–1803) was a Salzburg-born composer who studied with Mozart in Vienna in 1790–1791. He was about twenty-five years old when Mozart died; he had been a copyist for Mozart, helping to prepare the Magic Flute and other late works. He was therefore _the closest available musical hand_ to Mozart's own style — someone who had been in Mozart's working environment and who knew the late-Mozart musical idiom intimately.

Constanze gave him the partial Requiem manuscript in December 1791 or January 1792 and asked him to complete it. Süssmayr worked through the following months and delivered the completed score in summer 1792. What Mozart had left:

* **Complete in Mozart's hand** : the Introitus and Kyrie (the first two movements).
* **Sketched in Mozart's hand with substantial completion needed** : most of the Sequentia (the _Dies Irae_ , _Tuba Mirum_ , _Rex Tremendae_ , _Recordare_ , _Confutatis_) and the Offertorium (_Domine Jesu Christe_ and _Hostias_).
* **Mostly or entirely unfinished** : the Sanctus, Benedictus, Agnus Dei, Communio (the last four movements).
* **The Lacrimosa** : the first eight bars in Mozart's hand; the rest unfinished.

Süssmayr's contribution:

* **Continuing where Mozart had sketched** : he wrote out the harmonization, orchestration, and counter-melodies for movements Mozart had sketched.
* **Composing where Mozart had not started** : he wrote the Sanctus, Benedictus, Agnus Dei, and parts of the Communio.
* **Reusing Mozart's earlier material** : for the Communio's final _Lux aeterna_ and _Cum Sanctis tuis_ , Süssmayr reused the music Mozart had written for the opening Introitus and Kyrie — a structural choice that lets the work close as it began. This may have been Mozart's intention (sketched at some point) or Süssmayr's invention.

The result is _the Mozart Requiem we have_. It is in part Mozart, in part Süssmayr, in part Mozart-via-Süssmayr-as-interpreter. The work is one of the great choral masterworks of the Western tradition despite — or perhaps partly because of — its complex authorship.

#### The recordings

**John Eliot Gardiner, English Baroque Soloists, Monteverdi Choir, 1986 (Philips Classics)** — period-instrument, smaller ensemble, sharply articulated. Gardiner's reading was a landmark when released and remains a benchmark; it uses the Süssmayr completion but with attention to period-instrument balance.

**Karl Böhm, Vienna Philharmonic and Vienna State Opera Chorus, 1971 (Deutsche Grammophon)** — modern-instrument, large-scale, traditional Viennese Romantic-grand. The Böhm reading is one of the great mid-twentieth-century Mozart Requiems; the slow movements are deeply felt in the _late-Viennese_ tradition.

**Karl Richter, Munich Bach Choir and Orchestra, 1961 (Deutsche Grammophon Archiv)** — modern-instrument, German-tradition, with the slightly heavier choral writing characteristic of mid-century German Bach-Handel-Mozart performance.

**Nikolaus Harnoncourt, Concentus Musicus Wien, Arnold Schoenberg Choir, 2003 (DG/Archiv)** — period-instrument with a more dramatic, theatrically inflected approach than Gardiner's; uses the Süssmayr completion.

For the **Queen of the Night aria** , recordings span the recorded era:

**Diana Damrau** has recorded the aria several times; her readings are dramatically intense, vocally precise, and theatrically engaged. She is often considered the leading contemporary Queen.

**Edda Moser** 's 1972 recording (with Sawallisch / Bavarian State Opera) is a classic mid-twentieth-century reading.

**Sumi Jo** has recorded the aria with an unusually clean coloratura technique; her readings emphasize precision over dramatic intensity.

**Cristina Deutekom** 's 1969 recording is sometimes singled out for the high F's.

The work-vs-interpretation muscle in the Queen of the Night aria is largely about _vocal personality_ — different sopranos bring different specific combinations of dramatic intensity, technical precision, vocal color, and high-note thrill. The aria sounds substantially different in different sopranos' readings; the differences are at the singer level rather than at the orchestral or conductorial level.

#### Cross-piece links

* For more _Magic Flute_ , listen to **Sarastro's aria "In diesen heil'gen Hallen"** (Act II) — the opposite of the Queen of the Night, slow and forgiving and dignified; **Papageno's "Der Vogelfänger bin ich ja"** (Act I) — the folk-style bird-catcher's song; **the great Act II Finale** — the trials, the union of Tamino and Pamina, the triumph of Reason.
* For more **Mozart Requiem** , listen to **the Tuba Mirum** (the bass-trombone solo introducing the bass aria — one of the great moments of Baroque-Classical brass writing surviving into Mozart's idiom), the **Confutatis** (with its alternating loud male-chorus and soft female-chorus passages), and the **closing Communio** (with the Lux aeterna's return of the Introitus material).
* For **alternative Requiem completions** , listen to the **Robert Levin completion** (1991, revised 2024) on the **John Butt / Dunedin Consort 2014 recording** (Linn Records). The Levin completion handles the Sanctus and Benedictus differently from Süssmayr and is one of the most-recorded alternatives.
* For the **operatic Singspiel tradition Mozart inherited and contributed to** , listen to **Mozart's _Die Entführung aus dem Serail_ (The Abduction from the Seraglio, 1782)** — his earlier German-language Singspiel — and to **Beethoven's _Fidelio_ (1814)**, **Weber's _Der Freischütz_ (1821)**, and the operetta tradition descending from these.
* For the **Berlioz Requiem (1837)** and the **Verdi Requiem (1874)** , see Chapter 16 (Berlioz) cross-references; for the **Britten War Requiem (1962)** , see Chapter 24. These three nineteenth- and twentieth-century Requiems carry forward the Latin-Requiem tradition Mozart inherited.

#### Conversation Seeds

* _Tell the companion which of the two famous high F's in the Queen of the Night aria you found most thrilling, and ask her about the singers who have most-defined the aria across the recording era (Edda Moser, Cristina Deutekom, Diana Damrau, Sumi Jo, others)._
* _Ask the companion about the Walsegg story — what the documented commission was, why Walsegg wanted the work composed secretly, and how the gray-clad messenger became, in Constanze's later telling, an emissary of death._
* _Tell the companion which moment of the Requiem moved you most (the Dies Irae's apocalyptic chorus, the Lacrimosa's weeping figure, the Tuba Mirum's bass solo, the Confutatis's alternating dynamics, the Lux aeterna's return), and ask her about the structural reason that moment works._
* _Ask the companion about the question of _Mozart's authorship_ of the Requiem — what is Mozart, what is Süssmayr, what is in between. Then ask her about Robert Levin's 1991 alternative completion and how it differs from Süssmayr's._
* _Ask the companion about the _Masonic_ dimension of _Die Zauberflöte_ — what the trials of fire and water mean, what Sarastro's temple represents, why the three-flat key signature matters. Then ask her how twenty-first-century productions handle the opera's eighteenth-century gender politics._

### 12.5 Exercises

#### Concept Check

**Q1.** What is _opera_ , and what is _Singspiel_?

Hint

Two modes of musical drama. One uses recitative; the other uses spoken dialogue.

**Answer:** Opera is a multi-movement musical drama for solo singers, chorus, and orchestra, with a libretto sung throughout or with sung sections interspersed among other elements. Most opera includes acting, costumes, sets, and staging. _Singspiel_ (literally "singing-play") is a specifically German-language operatic form that uses _spoken dialogue_ between the musical numbers, rather than recitative. _Die Zauberflöte_ is a Singspiel; most Italian opera (Handel's Italian operas, most of Mozart's Italian operas, Verdi, Puccini) uses recitative. The Singspiel tradition produced _Die Zauberflöte_ , Beethoven's _Fidelio_ , Weber's _Der Freischütz_ , and indirectly the operetta and the American musical.

**Q2.** What is _coloratura_?

**Answer:** A style of operatic vocal writing characterized by elaborate, rapid, ornamental passages — runs, trills, leaps, fast figurations, extreme high notes. Most associated with the soprano voice and especially with eighteenth- and nineteenth-century opera. The Queen of the Night's "Der Hölle Rache" is one of the most-famous coloratura passages in the soprano repertoire, with two sustained high F's at climactic moments. The vocal Fach that handles coloratura at the highest range is the _coloratura soprano_ — a soprano whose voice is light, agile, and capable of extreme high notes.

### Chapter Summary

This chapter introduced Mozart's last year through two works: _**Die Zauberflöte**_ (premiered 30 September 1791) — focusing on the **Queen of the Night aria "Der Hölle Rache"** as a primer for what opera does — and the **Requiem K. 626** (commissioned anonymously by Count Walsegg in July 1791, left unfinished at Mozart's death on 5 December 1791, completed by Mozart's student Franz Xaver Süssmayr in early 1792) — focusing on the **Dies Irae** and the **Lacrimosa**.

You learned **opera** as a multi-movement musical drama with sung text, **Singspiel** as the German-language variant with spoken dialogue, **coloratura** as the elaborate-virtuoso soprano writing of the Queen of the Night aria, and **Requiem** as the Latin Mass for the Dead. You learned the four operatic vocal types: recitative, aria, ensemble, and chorus.

You met **the Walsegg story** — the documented commission for a memorial Requiem for Walsegg's young wife, the gray-clad steward Leitgeb who carried out the logistics, the legend of the messenger-of-death that grew in Constanze's later telling. You learned that **Mozart did not die a pauper** — the common-grave burial in St. Marx Cemetery was standard Viennese practice for his social class — and that **Salieri did not poison Mozart** — the legend is a nineteenth-century Romantic invention dramatized famously in Pushkin and Shaffer.

You met **Süssmayr's completion** — what Mozart had finished (Introitus, Kyrie), what he had sketched (most of the Sequentia and Offertorium), what was unfinished (the last four movements), and what Süssmayr added. You learned that **alternative completions** (Robert Levin 1991/2024, others) have produced different versions of the Requiem from Mozart's surviving fragments; the "real" Mozart Requiem is plural.

You learned about **the Masonic dimension of _Die Zauberflöte_** — the trials of fire and water, the temple of Wisdom and Reason, the brotherhood of the Priests of Isis — and about how this dimension shaped the opera's moral arc (the Queen's defeat, Sarastro's vindication, Tamino and Pamina's union).

You met three readings of the Requiem (Gardiner 1986 period-instrument, Böhm 1971 traditional-Viennese, Karl Richter 1961 German-tradition) and the four representative readings of the Queen of the Night aria (Damrau, Edda Moser, Sumi Jo, Cristina Deutekom).

**Composer Protagonist Mozart culminates in this chapter.** Three Mozart chapters total: Chapter 6 (_Eine kleine Nachtmusik_ , the sonata-form anchor), Chapter 11 (Piano Concerto 23 and Clarinet Concerto, the Classical concertos), Chapter 12 (Magic Flute and Requiem, his last year). He has accumulated into a three-dimensional figure — the prodigy, the freelance experimenter, the family man with his scatological letters and his Masonic loyalties, the composer who died at 35 with the Requiem unfinished. The chapter concludes Mozart's contribution to the book.

The next chapter takes you to **Beethoven's Symphony No. 3 "Eroica"** (1803–1804) — the hinge from the Classical period to Romanticism. The torn-up dedication to Napoleon, the seventeen-minute first movement that breaks every Classical-period scale convention, the funeral march at the symphonic center, the heroic style that transformed what symphonic music could be. Chapter 13 begins the Romantic-period section of the book.

## Chapter 13: Beethoven, Symphony No. 3 "Eroica"

In May 1804, Beethoven's pupil and friend Ferdinand Ries returned to Beethoven's apartment in Vienna with news from a Paris newspaper. Napoleon Bonaparte, the First Consul of the French Republic — the man who, since the late 1790s, had been Beethoven's political hero, the embodiment of post-revolutionary republican ideals — had crowned himself Emperor of the French at Notre-Dame on 2 December 1804. Actually, in May 1804 the coronation had not yet happened; what Ries reported was the news that Napoleon had been proclaimed Emperor by the French Senate on 18 May 1804 (the coronation itself would follow in December). The substantive event was the same: the republican general had made himself a monarch.

Beethoven, who was thirty-three years old and at his desk working on a new symphony, exploded. According to Ries's later memoir, he tore the title page off the manuscript score of the symphony in front of him — a title page that bore the inscription _"Sinfonia grande — intitolata Buonaparte"_ ("Grand Symphony — entitled Bonaparte") — threw it on the floor, and shouted (in some version of the words Ries remembered): "_So is he too nothing more than an ordinary man! Now he too will trample on all human rights and indulge only his own ambition. He will exalt himself above all others, become a tyrant!_ "

The Ries memoir is not unimpeachable (it was published in 1838, more than thirty years after the events; Ries had reasons to make Beethoven dramatically heroic in his recollections). But the _physical fact_ of the torn-off title page is supported by other evidence: a surviving manuscript copy of the symphony's score, now in the collection of the Vienna Society of the Friends of Music, shows the original "Bonaparte" dedication scratched out so violently that the page is punctured through. Beethoven did, somehow, in some manner, retract his dedication. When the symphony was published in 1806, it bore the dedication "_Sinfonia eroica, composta per festeggiare il sovvenire di un grand'Uomo_ " — "Heroic Symphony, composed to celebrate the memory of a great Man." The "great Man" was Napoleon-as-republican-ideal — the figure Beethoven had wanted to honor. Napoleon-the-Emperor was a different person.

The _Eroica_ Symphony, completed in 1804 and premiered privately at Prince Lobkowitz's palace in late 1804 and publicly at the Theater an der Wien in April 1805, is the hinge between the Classical period and Romanticism. Almost every dimension of the symphony breaks Classical-period scale conventions: the first movement is seventeen minutes long (most Haydn-Mozart symphonic first movements run eight to twelve); the second movement is a full-scale funeral march fifteen minutes long (most Classical-period slow movements are five to eight); the orchestra is larger; the harmonic argument is more dramatic; the _expressive ambition_ of the work as a whole exceeds anything Beethoven or anyone else had previously attempted in the symphonic form.

This chapter is about the _Eroica_ 's first movement (~17 minutes) and second movement Marcia funebre (~16 minutes). Together they take more than half an hour — most of an LP side, by the time recording technology arrived. They are the symphony's main listening focus; the third and fourth movements are great in their own right but receive briefer treatment here.

### 13.1 Before You Listen

#### Hook anecdote — the size of the first movement

Imagine you are a Viennese music-lover in 1805. You have heard most of Haydn's late symphonies (the twelve "London" symphonies plus most of the earlier ones), and you know what to expect from a symphony's first movement: a clear sonata-form Allegro, perhaps eight to twelve minutes, with two themes, a brief development, and a satisfying recapitulation. The orchestra is medium-sized — maybe forty players. The dramatic intensity is real but contained within Classical-period proportions.

You go to the Theater an der Wien on 7 April 1805 to hear a new symphony by Beethoven. The first movement begins with two sharp chords. Then a melody enters in the cellos — graceful, almost dance-like, in E♭ major. You think: ah, classical first-movement Allegro, in a noble key, sensible opening figure. You settle in for what you expect.

Twelve minutes later, you are still in the first movement. The development section, when it finally arrived, was not the brief contrasting episode you expected; it was a vast structural region in which the opening theme was developed through what felt like every possible harmonic and rhythmic transformation, including a passage where two violins seemed to enter early on the dominant chord before the rest of the orchestra was ready — a brief moment of harmonic dissonance that critics afterward called _the horns enter before the recapitulation_ and that some early critics interpreted as a misprint. Eventually the recapitulation arrived; the music played through the first themes again; the coda began; the coda _continued_ for another two minutes; the movement finally ended seventeen minutes after it began.

You and your fellow audience members are exhausted. Some are exhilarated; some are confused. A Viennese music critic the next week writes that the symphony is _"too long, too difficult, with too many random ideas"_. A Berlin review the following month concedes that _"the new symphony is exceedingly elaborate, of unusual length, and uses too many instruments,"_ but admits that _"in it shine forth bursts of original musical genius."_ The reviews are mixed. The work is _unprecedented in scale_. Some listeners will need a generation to catch up.

By 1830, the _Eroica_ is canonical. By 1850, it is the model that every nineteenth-century symphonist (Schumann, Brahms, Bruckner, Tchaikovsky, Mahler) is responding to. The Classical-period symphony has been left behind; the Romantic-period symphony has begun.

#### What to notice

For the **first movement** (~17 minutes): listen for three things.

  1. **The opening two chords.** The symphony begins with two short, fortissimo E♭-major chords. The first is a quarter note; the second is a quarter note. Then the cellos begin the main theme. _Most symphonies do not announce themselves this way._ The two chords function as a kind of _clearing of the throat_ — Beethoven announcing that _something is about to begin_ , with maximum dramatic emphasis. Listen for them at 0:00–0:03.

  2. **The main theme.** The cellos play a graceful, dance-like figure in E♭ major. It is not a _heroic_ theme in the way later Romantic-period heroic themes would be (no fanfare, no dotted rhythms, no fortissimo declamation). It is a _Classical-period theme_ that Beethoven is about to put through Romantic-period treatment. _Hold the theme in your ear; it is going to be transformed across the next seventeen minutes._

  3. **The "horn enters early" passage.** Around 14:30 (in the Gardiner recording), near the end of the development section, you hear two violins playing softly on the dominant chord (B♭) while a French horn enters playing the main theme in E♭ — a clash that some early audiences found bizarre and some early critics thought was a misprint. _It is not a misprint._ It is Beethoven deliberately staging a moment of harmonic instability before the resolution to the recapitulation. Listen for this brief strange moment.

For the **second movement Marcia funebre** (~15 minutes): listen for three things.

  1. **The slow, dragging tread.** The movement opens with strings playing a slow tread — _quietly, in C minor, in 2/4 time with dotted rhythms_. This is a _funeral march_ — a march for slow procession, with the _dotted-rhythm pattern_ (long-short-long-short) characteristic of the form. The dynamic begins soft (_piano_); the texture is heavy with bass weight. Listen for the slow tread.

  2. **The C-major middle section.** About four minutes in, the music shifts to C major and a new, lighter theme appears — _almost pastoral_ , a brief moment of consolation in the midst of the funeral. This is the _Trio_ of the funeral-march form (analogous to the Trio of a Minuet — a contrasting middle section). The Trio runs about two minutes before the funeral march returns.

  3. **The fugal development.** After the Trio returns to C minor, Beethoven launches into a fugal section — the main theme of the funeral march treated as a fugue subject, with each voice entering in turn. This is one of the most-extraordinary passages in the symphonic literature: the funeral march becomes _intellectually_ dense, almost Bachian, while remaining emotionally heavy. Listen for the fugal entries around 9:00 onward.

For the **third movement Scherzo** (~6 minutes) and **fourth movement Finale** (~12 minutes): the Scherzo is fast, energetic, in 3/4 time, with hunting-horn calls in the Trio middle section. The Finale is a _theme-and-variations_ on a theme Beethoven had used in three earlier works (his ballet _The Creatures of Prometheus_ finale, his Op. 35 "Eroica Variations" for piano, and the contredanse WoO 14 No. 7) — Beethoven reusing his own material across multiple genres, treating the theme as a kind of compositional signature.

#### One-sentence background

**Beethoven, Symphony No. 3 in E♭ major "Eroica," Op. 55** — composed 1803–1804 in Vienna and Heiligenstadt; originally dedicated to Napoleon Bonaparte; dedication withdrawn after Napoleon's self-coronation as Emperor in May 1804; premiered privately at Prince Lobkowitz's palace in late 1804, publicly at the Theater an der Wien on 7 April 1805; ~45 minutes in four movements (Allegro con brio — Marcia funebre — Scherzo — Finale).

Gardiner uses period instruments and the smaller ensemble size more historically accurate to Beethoven's Vienna; tempi are brisk, the energy is sharp. The Kleiber live recording is one of the great twentieth-century _Eroica_ readings (modern instruments, full Vienna Philharmonic, dramatic and intense). The Furtwängler 1944 wartime recording is a historical document — Wilhelm Furtwängler conducting the Vienna Philharmonic in 1944, in the last months of the Reich, in a reading of extraordinary emotional weight that has caused continuing controversy about the relationship between Furtwängler's art and the regime he played under. (We will return to Furtwängler in Chapter 19.) Norrington is the period-instrument alternative to Gardiner.

### 13.2 The Listening Window

#### First Movement Allegro con brio (Gardiner, ~17 minutes)

* **0:00–0:03.** **Two opening chords.** Two fortissimo E♭-major chords. Then silence. Then the cellos begin.

* **0:03–0:45.** **The main theme.** The cellos play a graceful, dance-like melodic line outlining the E♭-major chord — almost a triadic figure, gently rising. The second violins answer; the violas join; the violins add. The texture is _Classical-period clear_ — voices separate, intelligible.

* **0:45–2:30.** **First-theme group development.** The opening figure is taken through several modulations, treated motivically, passed among the orchestral families. Already, in the first two minutes, Beethoven is doing more development than a Haydn-Mozart first-theme group would normally contain.

* **2:30–4:30.** **Transition and second theme.** The music modulates to B♭ major (the dominant). A second theme appears — more lyrical, with a memorable rising figure. The second theme is itself developed in unusual depth before the exposition closes.

* **4:30–6:00.** **Codetta.** A long closing passage that wraps up the exposition. In some readings (Gardiner included) the exposition repeats from 0:00 at about 6:00; in some readings it does not.

* **8:30** (after the exposition repeat in Gardiner). **The development section begins.** The development of the _Eroica_ is one of the most-extensive in the symphonic literature — about six minutes long, which is longer than many _entire_ Classical-period first movements. Beethoven takes the opening theme and the second theme and develops them through key after key, fragment after fragment. New themes briefly appear that did not exist in the exposition (a hushed, lyrical line that some commentators call the _third theme_); the music passes through major and minor keys; the orchestration thickens and thins.

* **12:00–13:30.** **The development's climactic central section.** The music reaches its most dissonant and rhythmically intense moment. Beethoven uses _sforzato_ (sudden accents) on weak beats, producing a sense of off-balance urgency. The harmonic landscape is unstable.

* **14:00–14:30.** **The "horn enters early" passage.** As the music settles toward the recapitulation, two violins play softly on the dominant chord (B♭) — a sustained quiet — while the French horn enters playing the main theme in E♭. The horn's entry sounds _premature_. The two-key effect lasts only a few seconds before the rest of the orchestra arrives with the full E♭-major recapitulation. This brief moment is one of the most-discussed dissonances in the symphonic literature.

* **14:30–15:00.** **The recapitulation begins.** The cellos restate the main theme in E♭ major. We are home. The remaining material from the exposition passes through, now all in the home key.

* **15:00–17:00.** **The coda.** Beethoven's _Eroica_ coda is longer than any prior Classical-period coda — about two minutes, with substantial new developmental work, not just a closing tag. The movement ends with definitive E♭-major cadences.

The first movement is enormous, and the _enormity_ is part of its meaning. Beethoven is signaling that the symphony, as a form, can carry an expressive weight Haydn and Mozart had not asked it to carry.

#### Second Movement Marcia funebre (Gardiner, ~15 minutes)

* **0:00–0:30.** **The slow tread.** Strings begin a slow, dotted-rhythm pattern in C minor — the _funeral march_ opening. The dynamic is _piano_ ; the bass is heavy; the rhythm is _long-short-long-short_. _This is a march for slow procession._ The mood is grave.

* **0:30–1:30.** **The main funeral-march theme.** A melody in C minor develops above the slow tread. The melody is _plaintive_ ; the harmonization is austere. The strings carry the melody; the woodwinds reinforce; the brass plays sparingly.

* **1:30–3:30.** **Continued funeral march.** The theme is restated, transformed slightly, taken through related keys. The slow tread continues underneath throughout.

* **3:30–4:00.** **Transition to the C-major Trio.** The music shifts toward C major. A new texture appears: slower, lighter, more pastoral.

* **4:00–6:00.** **The C-major Trio.** A contrasting middle section in C major, almost a _moment of consolation_ in the midst of the funeral. The theme is lyrical; the orchestration is lighter (with prominent oboe and flute solos). This is the funeral march's brief vision of _hope_ — the kind of relief that a funeral procession sometimes briefly admits before the heavy work continues.

* **6:00–6:30.** **Return to C minor.** The slow tread resumes; the main funeral-march theme returns.

* **6:30–9:00.** **Continued funeral march, building.** The music intensifies. The orchestration thickens. The dynamic grows.

* **9:00–11:00.** **The fugal section.** Beethoven launches into a _fugue_ on the funeral-march theme. Each voice in the orchestra enters in turn with the theme, treating it contrapuntally — strings first, then woodwinds, then brass. _The funeral march has become a fugue._ This is one of the most-extraordinary moments in the symphonic literature: a Bachian contrapuntal density imposed onto a march-form movement. The music's intellectual weight matches its emotional weight.

* **11:00–13:00.** **Return to the funeral march and climactic build.** The fugal section gives way to a fuller, louder restatement of the funeral march. The orchestra is at its most extensive; the funeral march reaches its emotional peak.

* **13:00–14:00.** **Gradual withdrawal.** The music dims. The funeral procession draws away. The dynamic drops; the orchestration thins.

* **14:00–15:00.** **The disintegrating ending.** The final pages of the Marcia funebre are some of the most-unusual closing passages Beethoven wrote. The music does not end with a definitive cadence; it _disintegrates_ — the funeral-march theme is heard in fragments, broken phrases, hesitations, with silences between. The movement closes on a quiet, almost exhausted C-minor cadence. The funeral has been observed; the music withdraws without claiming resolution.

The Marcia funebre is the _Eroica_ 's emotional center. It is also, in its disintegrating ending, one of the most-modern moments in early-nineteenth-century music — Beethoven refusing to close on a heroic gesture, refusing to give the listener the easy uplift, instead letting the music exhaust itself into silence. The funeral has been faced; the music acknowledges what it has seen; the closing is honest about loss rather than triumphant over it.

This kind of _honest closing_ — refusing the conventional final triumph — is something Beethoven returns to repeatedly in his later work (the _Heiliger Dankgesang_ from Op. 132, the closing of the _Missa Solemnis_ , the slow movement of the Ninth Symphony, the closing of the late piano sonatas Op. 109 and Op. 111). The _Eroica_ funeral march is the first major instance, and it announces something about what Beethoven's music will increasingly be willing to do.

### 13.3 What's Happening in the Music

#### Definition: The Heroic Style

The _heroic style_ in Beethoven scholarship refers to the dramatic-expressive style Beethoven developed in his _middle period_ (roughly 1802–1812), most-famously embodied in the _Eroica_ Symphony, the Fifth Symphony, the _Coriolan_ Overture, the _Fidelio_ opera, and the Fourth and Fifth Piano Concertos. Characteristics include:

* **Larger scale** : longer movements, longer codas, larger development sections, larger orchestra.
* **Dramatic-narrative ambition** : the music is doing a _story_ — struggle to triumph, death to consolation, conflict to resolution. _Per aspera ad astra_ (through hardships to the stars) is the recurring narrative arc.
* **Motivic development at unprecedented depth** : ideas are transformed across long structural spans (the four-note cell of Beethoven 5, the opening figure of the _Eroica_).
* **Expressive intensity** : dynamics, accents, rhythmic urgency, harmonic instability all pushed beyond Classical-period norms.
* **Identification with specific subjects** : heroic, military, civic, philosophical. The _Eroica_ is about _the great Man_ ; the Fifth is about _fate / triumph_ ; _Fidelio_ is about _political liberty_ ; the _Choral Symphony_ (No. 9) is about _the brotherhood of humanity_.

The heroic style is one of three Beethoven styles. The _early period_ (roughly 1792–1802) extends Haydn and Mozart in a recognizably Classical idiom. The _middle period_ (1802–1812) is the heroic style. The _late period_ (1815–1827) is the introverted, contrapuntally-dense, sometimes-eccentric style of the late piano sonatas, the late quartets, the Ninth Symphony, the _Missa Solemnis_ , and the _Diabelli Variations_ — the style we will encounter in Chapter 14.

The _Eroica_ is the first major heroic-style work and is therefore often dated as _the beginning of Beethoven's middle period_. The middle period in turn is often dated as _the beginning of Romanticism in the symphonic literature_. The two datings overlap; the _Eroica_ is the symphonic hinge.

#### Definition: Funeral March

A _funeral march_ is a slow, processional movement designed to accompany or evoke a funeral procession. The characteristic features:

* **Slow tempo** (Adagio or Largo).
* **Dotted rhythm** (long-short-long-short), evoking the heavy tread of a procession.
* **Minor key** (often C minor or another somber key).
* **Heavy, low-orchestrated texture** (with bass and lower strings emphasized).
* **Often in march form** (A — B — A, with a contrasting Trio middle section) or in funeral-march variation form.

Famous orchestral funeral marches: Beethoven's _Eroica_ second movement (this chapter); Beethoven's Piano Sonata No. 12, Op. 26 second movement (titled "Marcia funebre sulla morte d'un Eroe" — "Funeral March on the Death of a Hero," written 1801 and predating the _Eroica_); the funeral march from Mahler's Symphony No. 5 first movement (Chapter 21); Wagner's _Siegfried-Idyll_ funeral music from _Götterdämmerung_ ; Chopin's Piano Sonata No. 2 in B♭ minor third movement (the "Marche funèbre" Chopin himself called the most-famous funeral march in music); Mendelssohn's _Songs without Words_ funeral march. The form has continued through the twentieth century into the present (Shostakovich, Britten, John Adams have all written funeral-march style movements).

The _Eroica_ 's funeral march is unusual in its _scale_ (fifteen minutes — longer than most stand-alone funeral marches), its _fugal development_ (no other funeral march has the contrapuntal density Beethoven imposes on his), and its _disintegrating ending_ (no other funeral march refuses the conventional final cadence so explicitly).

#### Common Misconception

People sometimes think the _Eroica_ is _Beethoven's tribute to Napoleon_ — that is, a piece written in admiration of Napoleon and that Beethoven changed his mind about. This is too simple. The _Eroica_ 's relationship to Napoleon is more complex:

* The original dedication ("Bonaparte") was to _the republican general_ — Napoleon-as-embodiment-of-post-revolutionary-ideals (citizen-army, civil law, religious tolerance, the rule of reason over hereditary privilege). Beethoven, who had grown up in Bonn (a Rhineland city briefly under French revolutionary occupation in his teenage years) and who absorbed Enlightenment republican ideals during his Vienna years, saw Napoleon as the political hero of the Enlightenment.
* When Napoleon crowned himself Emperor in 1804, Beethoven saw this as _the betrayal_ — the embrace of hereditary monarchy by the very figure who was supposed to embody republican alternatives. The withdrawn dedication is a _political reaction_ , not a personal grudge.
* The published 1806 dedication ("to celebrate the memory of a great Man") is _not_ a re-dedication to Napoleon. It is a dedication to _the heroic figure in general_ — the kind of person Napoleon had once seemed to be. The symphony commemorates an _ideal_ , not a particular politician.

This matters because the music's _heroic_ dimension is _political-philosophical_ rather than military-personal. The _Eroica_ is not a Napoleon-victory symphony; it is a _symphony about what heroism in the Enlightenment sense looks like_ — the courage of the citizen, the struggle of the great soul, the funeral that honors a death without enemy hatred. The Marcia funebre's _consoling_ C-major Trio in the middle of the funeral march is the moment where the symphony is _most clearly philosophical_ — the work is reflecting on death generally, on the _condition_ of mortality, rather than on a specific funeral.

This makes the _Eroica_ unlike most subsequent Romantic-period "heroic" symphonies (Tchaikovsky's "Pathétique" — Chapter 20 — is _deeply personal_ ; Mahler's symphonies are _philosophical-spiritual_ but in different ways). The _Eroica_ sits in its own category: _political-philosophical-heroic_. The republican-ideal dedication is part of what gives the work its specific character.

### 13.4 The Stories

#### Beethoven in 1803–1804

Beethoven was thirty-two when he began the _Eroica_ in 1803 and thirty-three when he completed it in 1804. He had moved to Vienna in 1792, eleven years earlier; he had established himself as a pianist of extraordinary technique and as a composer of growing reputation; he had been Beethoven the _successor to Haydn and Mozart_ in the early years of the new century. But the year 1802 had been a personal crisis: Beethoven's hearing, which had been deteriorating for several years, had reached a point where he could no longer ignore it. In the summer of 1802 he had retreated to the Vienna suburb of Heiligenstadt to consult a specialist. The consultations did not help. In October 1802 he wrote the _Heiligenstadt Testament_ — a letter addressed to his two brothers, never sent, found among his papers after his death — in which he described his despair at his deafness and his decision to live for his art despite it.

The _Heiligenstadt Testament_ is one of the most-quoted documents in Beethoven biography. Two passages are particularly relevant:

> _...how grievous was the sad sound which struck me cruelly, of someone calling me into a battle while I would fain hide... Forced to be a philosopher at six and twenty, oh it is not easy, less easy for the artist than for any one else._

> _... But I would not let myself give in. I will grapple with fate... it shall never wholly drag me down. — Oh how beautiful is it to live a thousandfold..._

The _Eroica_ was composed in the year after the _Heiligenstadt Testament_. The symphony's expansive ambition — the seventeen-minute first movement, the fifteen-minute funeral march, the heroic-style narrative arc — is in part _Beethoven's response_ to the personal crisis. The composer who in 1802 had contemplated suicide and decided against it for art's sake was in 1803–1804 composing the most ambitious work in his life so far. The work was _the artistic answer_ to the personal despair.

This is part of why the _Eroica_ feels personal beyond its political-philosophical dimensions. Beethoven was _grappling with fate_ (his deafness, his mortality) at the same time as the symphony was grappling with heroism, death, and the _per aspera ad astra_ arc. The work's funeral march in the second movement — the burial of a hero — is also, in some interpretive sense, Beethoven's burial of the version of himself who had imagined a normal hearing-life. The work's continued movement into the third and fourth movements — the scherzo's energy, the finale's variation set — is the continued life _after_ the burial. The whole symphony is the composer working through, in art, what he had worked through in despair in 1802.

This is not a _programmatic_ reading (the symphony is not depicting Beethoven's autobiography), but it is a _biographical context_ that helps us understand the symphony's emotional weight. The _Eroica_ is not just political philosophy; it is also personal philosophy. Both readings can be held at once.

#### The Lobkowitz premiere

The _Eroica_ was first performed _privately_ — at the Vienna palace of Prince Joseph Franz Maximilian Lobkowitz, the symphony's eventual dedicatee, in August or September 1804. Lobkowitz was a young aristocratic patron (he was twenty-five in 1804, only seven years younger than Beethoven) who maintained a private orchestra at his Bohemian palace and at his Vienna residence. He paid Beethoven for the symphony's first performance rights — about 400 florins for six months of exclusive performance access — and Beethoven dedicated the symphony to him.

The Lobkowitz premiere was for a small audience: the prince's family, his musical-aristocratic circle, a few invited Vienna composers and critics. The reception was respectful but uncertain. The work's scale exceeded what the audience knew what to make of. Beethoven himself conducted (or led from the keyboard).

The _public_ premiere came on 7 April 1805 at the Theater an der Wien — an open-ticket concert in which Beethoven was the featured composer and conductor. The public reaction was the mixed reaction described in the opening of this chapter: critics divided, audiences puzzled, some enthusiastic, some put off by the work's length and difficulty. The _Eroica_ did not become an immediate sensation; it became canonical _gradually_ , over fifteen or twenty years, as composers (Schubert, Mendelssohn, Schumann) and critics (E. T. A. Hoffmann — see Chapter 3) recognized that Beethoven had opened up a new symphonic territory.

#### Three readings

**John Eliot Gardiner, Orchestre Révolutionnaire et Romantique, 1993 (DG Archiv).** Period-instrument, smaller ensemble (about 60 players), faster tempi than the modern-instrument tradition (Gardiner's first movement runs about 16 minutes). The reading is _crisp, urgent, with sharp articulation and bright orchestral colors_. The funeral march is taken at a brisk pace that emphasizes the dramatic-narrative content over the contemplative weight.

**Carlos Kleiber, Vienna Philharmonic, 1989 (live, multiple releases including Orfeo).** Modern-instrument, full Vienna Philharmonic, dramatic and intense. Kleiber recorded few Beethoven symphonies (only the Fifth and Seventh commercially); the _Eroica_ live recording from a 1989 Vienna concert is one of the supplementary documents of his Beethoven approach. The reading is _electric_ , with extraordinary tempo flexibility and dynamic range. The funeral march is taken slightly slower than Gardiner; the dramatic intensity is sustained throughout.

**Wilhelm Furtwängler, Vienna Philharmonic, December 1944 (Music & Arts / EMI historical archives).** Modern-instrument, traditional Romantic-large, full Vienna Philharmonic. Furtwängler conducted the _Eroica_ across his career; the 1944 wartime Vienna recording is the most-historically-resonant. It was made in December 1944 — the Reich's last months, with Allied bombing of Vienna intensifying, with the political situation collapsing — and the reading has an emotional weight that has been read many ways. Some hear it as _the symphony as defiance against the regime_ ; others hear it as _Furtwängler's complicity_. The Furtwängler reading is _slow_ (the first movement runs over 18 minutes; the funeral march is the slowest of the three readings); the funeral march in particular is _devastatingly slow and weighted_. The recording is a historical document of the most fraught kind — beautiful, troubling, irreducible. (We will return to Furtwängler in Chapter 19 in the context of Wagner.)

The work-vs-interpretation muscle: three readings, three approaches. _Period-historical-crisp_ (Gardiner), _modern-electric-dramatic_ (Kleiber), _modern-weighted-historically-fraught_ (Furtwängler). The differences in tempo alone are substantial: the first movement runs about 16 minutes in Gardiner, 18 in Kleiber, 19 in Furtwängler. The differences in _emotional temperature_ are even larger. The _Eroica_ admits all three readings and many more.

#### Cross-piece links

* The _Eroica_ is the first of Beethoven's nine symphonies. The remaining eight: No. 4 in B♭ major (1806, often heard as a _lighter_ companion to the _Eroica_); No. 5 in C minor (1808, the iconic _fate_ symphony, Chapter 3); No. 6 in F major "Pastoral" (1808, the _programmatic_ symphony, depicting countryside scenes); No. 7 in A major (1813, the "Dance Symphony"); No. 8 in F major (1814, the _small_ late symphony); No. 9 in D minor "Choral" (1824, Chapter 14, the late summit).
* For more _Beethoven heroic style_ , listen to the **Fifth Symphony** (Chapter 3 — the iconic example); **the _Coriolan_ Overture, Op. 62** (1807); **the _Egmont_ Overture, Op. 84** (1810); **Piano Concerto No. 5 in E♭ major "Emperor," Op. 73** (1809–1811, premiered 1811).
* For _funeral marches by Beethoven_ , listen to the **Piano Sonata No. 12 in A♭ major, Op. 26** (1800–1801) — the second movement is titled "Marcia funebre sulla morte d'un Eroe" and predates the _Eroica_ 's funeral march. The piano-sonata funeral march is shorter (~6 min) and less ambitious than the _Eroica_ 's, but the two are clearly related.
* For _other heroic-style symphonies of the early Romantic period_ , listen to **Schumann's Symphony No. 3 in E♭ major "Rhenish"** (1850, in the same key as the _Eroica_ , with a similarly ambitious first movement), and **Brahms's Symphony No. 1 in C minor** (1876, the symphony Brahms struggled with for twenty years partly because of the _Eroica_ 's shadow).
* For _Furtwängler's continuing controversy_ , see Chapter 19 (Wagner) — Furtwängler's wartime conducting and his relationship with the Nazi regime is one of the central no-verdict cases in the book.

#### Conversation Seeds

* _Ask the companion about the Heiligenstadt Testament of October 1802 — what Beethoven wrote, who it was addressed to, why it was never sent, and how it relates to the _Eroica_ composed the following year._
* _Tell the companion which of the three readings (Gardiner 1993 period-crisp, Kleiber 1989 modern-electric, Furtwängler 1944 wartime-weighted) you preferred for the funeral march, and ask her what the differences in tempo (15 vs 16 vs 18+ minutes) actually do to the music's effect._
* _Ask the companion about the "horns enter early" passage at about 14:30 in the first movement — why nineteenth-century critics thought it was a misprint, what Beethoven was actually doing, and how the passage relates to the broader pattern of his harmonic boundary-pushing._
* _Ask the companion about the Furtwängler 1944 recording specifically — what it sounds like, what we know about the political context, why some listeners find it the most-moving _Eroica_ and some find it morally compromised, and what the case is for and against listening to it today._
* _Ask the companion to walk you through the fugal section in the funeral march (around 9:00 onward) — why a funeral march would become a fugue, and what Beethoven is signaling about the relationship between intellectual structure and emotional weight._

### 13.5 Exercises

#### Concept Check

**Q1.** What is the _heroic style_ in Beethoven scholarship, and which period of his career does it characterize?

Hint

Three periods: early, middle, late. The heroic style is the middle one.

**Answer:** The _heroic style_ is the dramatic-expressive style Beethoven developed during his _middle period_ (roughly 1802–1812), characterized by larger-scale movements, dramatic-narrative ambition (often the _per aspera ad astra_ arc — through hardships to the stars), motivic development at unprecedented depth, expressive intensity beyond Classical-period norms, and frequent identification with specific subjects (heroic, military, civic, philosophical). The _Eroica_ Symphony (1803–1804) is the first major heroic-style work; the Fifth Symphony, the _Coriolan_ Overture, _Fidelio_ , and the Fourth and Fifth Piano Concertos are other major examples. Beethoven's _early period_ (1792–1802) extends Haydn and Mozart; the _late period_ (1815–1827, Chapter 14) is introverted and contrapuntally dense.

**Q2.** Why did Beethoven withdraw his original dedication of the _Eroica_ to Napoleon?

**Answer:** When Napoleon crowned himself Emperor of the French in May–December 1804, Beethoven saw this as a betrayal of the republican ideals that had made Napoleon, in Beethoven's earlier eyes, a political hero. Beethoven's republican ideals — citizen-army, civil law, religious tolerance, the rule of reason over hereditary privilege — had been embodied (in his view) by Napoleon-the-republican-general; Napoleon-the-Emperor was the opposite figure, embracing hereditary monarchy. Beethoven scratched out the original "Bonaparte" dedication so violently that the surviving manuscript copy is punctured through. The 1806 published dedication ("to celebrate the memory of a great Man") refers to _the heroic figure in general_ , not to Napoleon specifically.

### Chapter Summary

This chapter introduced **Beethoven's Symphony No. 3 in E♭ major "Eroica," Op. 55** (1803–1804) — the hinge between the Classical period and Romanticism, the first major work of Beethoven's heroic-style middle period, and one of the most-influential works in the symphonic literature.

You learned the **Beethoven three-period framework** (early ~1792–1802 extending Haydn-Mozart; middle ~1802–1812 the heroic style; late ~1815–1827 the introverted, contrapuntally dense final style — Chapter 14), the **heroic style** characteristics (larger scale, dramatic narrative, motivic development, expressive intensity, identification with subjects), and the **funeral march** as a Beethoven sub-form (slow tread, dotted rhythms, minor key, often A-B-A with contrasting C-major Trio).

You met the **Napoleon dedication story** — Beethoven's original "Bonaparte" dedication for Napoleon-the-republican-general, the dedication's withdrawal after Napoleon's 1804 self-coronation as Emperor, the published 1806 dedication "to celebrate the memory of a great Man" referring to the heroic figure in general. The political-philosophical content of the _Eroica_ — republican-ideal heroism rather than military-personal celebration — was clarified.

You met the **Heiligenstadt Testament** (October 1802) — Beethoven's private letter to his brothers describing his despair at his progressive deafness and his decision to live for his art — and saw how the personal crisis of 1802 fed into the composition of the _Eroica_ in 1803–1804.

You met three readings (Gardiner 1993 period-crisp, Kleiber 1989 modern-electric, Furtwängler 1944 wartime-weighted) and learned that the _Eroica_ 's funeral march admits substantially different tempo and emotional approaches — 15 minutes in Gardiner, 16 in Kleiber, 19+ in Furtwängler. The Furtwängler 1944 wartime recording was previewed as a historical document of fraught moral complexity, to which the book will return in Chapter 19.

The next chapter takes you to **Beethoven's Symphony No. 9 "Choral"** (1824) and the **late string quartets** (1825–1826) — the introverted late style, the choral finale of the Ninth (with the Ode to Joy), the Heiliger Dankgesang from Op. 132 (which Beethoven called "the high point of my life as an artist"), the Cavatina from Op. 130. Composer Protagonist Beethoven culminates in Chapter 14.
