## Chapter 14: Beethoven — Symphony No. 9 + Late String Quartets

A Vienna concert hall, the Kärntnertortheater, the evening of 7 May 1824. Beethoven is fifty-three years old, almost totally deaf, no longer performing publicly, working in seclusion in his apartment on his last great works. Tonight is the premiere of his Ninth Symphony — the symphony he has been thinking about since the 1810s, sketching since 1817, composing intensively since 1822. The orchestra is the largest he has ever called for; the chorus is the largest in Viennese concert practice; the four vocal soloists are the leading singers of the city. The fourth movement is something no symphony has ever included before: a full chorus, four vocal soloists, and the orchestra together, setting Friedrich Schiller's _An die Freude_ (Ode to Joy) — a 1785 poem in which Schiller had imagined a brotherhood of all humanity united in joy.

The conductor of record for the premiere is Michael Umlauf, the Theater's resident music director. Beethoven sits beside him at the front of the stage, with the score open, beating time with hand gestures the orchestra has been instructed to ignore. He cannot hear what the orchestra is playing. He can read the score visually; he can feel the music's pulse through the floor; he cannot hear it as the audience hears it. At the end of the symphony's final movement — after the choral Ode to Joy has reached its triumphant fortissimo conclusion and the audience has erupted into applause — Beethoven is still beating time, facing the orchestra. The alto soloist Caroline Unger reaches forward and turns him toward the audience so that he can see the standing ovation he cannot hear.

The premiere is a triumph. The audience demands five curtain calls (the Imperial protocol allowed three even for the Emperor; the audience insists on more for Beethoven). The Ninth Symphony — and especially its choral finale — is recognized within weeks as one of the central works of European music. Three years later Beethoven is dead; thirty years later the Ninth is performed in every major capital in Europe; by the centenary of Beethoven's birth in 1870 the Ninth has become the work that orchestras perform at moments of civic ritual. In the twentieth century it becomes the music played at the fall of the Berlin Wall in 1989 (Bernstein in Berlin), at every New Year's Eve concert in Japan (a tradition begun in the 1940s), and the official anthem of the European Union (since 1985, with Schiller's text translated or in the original German). The Ode to Joy melody is, by 2026, among the most-recognized melodies in the history of Western music.

This chapter is about the late Beethoven — the Beethoven of the introverted, contrapuntally dense, sometimes-eccentric late style. We focus on the **fourth movement of the Ninth Symphony** (the Ode to Joy, ~25 minutes), on the **Heiliger Dankgesang from String Quartet Op. 132** (the slow movement Beethoven himself called the high point of his artistic life), and briefly on the **Cavatina from String Quartet Op. 130**. Composer Protagonist Beethoven culminates here.

### 14.1 Before You Listen

#### Hook anecdote — the alto soloist turning the deaf composer

The Caroline Unger story is one of the most-told anecdotes in Beethoven biography. It comes to us from multiple sources — Unger's own later recollections, contemporary accounts of the premiere, several Vienna newspapers — and is one of the more reliably documented Beethoven anecdotes. Beethoven, at the Kärntnertortheater premiere on 7 May 1824, sat beside conductor Umlauf at the front of the stage with the score open. He had been almost totally deaf for several years by this point; his hearing aids of various designs (ear-trumpets, special pianos with resonance plates) helped little. He could read the score visually and follow the music through internal hearing of what he had composed; he could not hear what was actually being played. The orchestra and soloists had been instructed by Umlauf and others to follow Umlauf and to ignore Beethoven's tempo cues.

At the end of the Scherzo (the second movement, exuberant and rhythmic — Beethoven's symphonies in this period frequently placed the Scherzo before the slow movement rather than after, reversing the Haydn-Mozart order), the audience burst into applause. Beethoven, still reading the score and beating time for the next movement, did not realize the audience was applauding. Caroline Unger — the alto soloist for the choral finale, standing at the front of the stage — reached out and gently turned Beethoven by the shoulders toward the audience. He saw the standing ovation. He bowed.

This sequence happened again at the end of the third movement and again at the end of the choral finale. By the end of the symphony, the audience had been applauding repeatedly while Beethoven, deaf, had been turned each time by Unger or by others to see the response.

This is one of the most-affecting moments in concert history. It is also part of why the Ninth Symphony, from its first performance onward, has carried an emotional weight beyond its musical content. The premiere is one of the few documented moments in music history where _the audience's reception is itself a profound part of the work's meaning_ — the audience honoring the deaf composer, the deaf composer not hearing the honor, the alto soloist mediating between them.

The Ninth Symphony, from that first night on, has been _both a work of music and a cultural-historical event_. Its choral finale in particular has become the music of public ritual — civic gatherings, political moments, anniversaries, memorials. The work's cultural weight is so substantial that approaching it for the first time as _just music_ is almost impossible. The chapter will try to do so anyway.

#### What to notice

The Ninth Symphony has four movements: first (Allegro ma non troppo, sonata form, ~16 min), second (Scherzo, ~12 min), third (Adagio molto e cantabile, slow movement, ~16 min), fourth (Presto / Allegro / Ode to Joy choral finale, ~25 min). The first three movements are entirely orchestral; the fourth introduces vocal soloists and chorus halfway through. The chapter focuses on the **fourth movement**.

For the **fourth movement** (~25 minutes), listen for five things:

  1. **The opening dissonance.** The movement opens with a _fortissimo dissonant chord_ — sometimes called the _Schreckensfanfare_ ("terror fanfare") — that announces the movement is going to be a _response_ to what came before. The dissonance is unusual for an opening; it signals discontinuity with the previous movements.

  2. **The _recall_ of earlier movements.** Beethoven, in the orchestral prelude to the choral entry, _quotes_ fragments from each of the first three movements — first the opening of the first movement (briefly), then the Scherzo, then the Adagio. _Each is rejected_ by an instrumental recitative (low strings playing in a speech-like rhythm). Beethoven is _staging a debate_ : the music is asking _what kind of resolution to seek_ , and the answer is _none of the previous movements has been adequate_. The recitative finally introduces the _Ode to Joy_ melody — first quietly, in the cellos and basses.

  3. **The Ode to Joy melody.** Once the recitative has settled on the Ode to Joy theme, the orchestra introduces it in a slow build — first the low strings alone, then the violas, then the violins, then the full orchestra, each statement adding voices and dynamic weight. _This is the symphony's first proper presentation of its main melody._ Listen for the build.

  4. **The choral entry.** The baritone soloist enters with _"O Freunde, nicht diese Töne!"_ (Oh friends, not these tones!) — words Beethoven himself wrote to introduce Schiller's text. Then the chorus joins. The chorus's first statement of the Ode to Joy is one of the most-immediate moments in symphonic literature: a full chorus singing a memorable melody in unison, accompanied by the orchestra. _This is the moment the symphony tips into the public, civic, communal mode._

  5. **The _Turkish March_ and the final fugue.** Across the fourth movement's twenty-five minutes, Beethoven includes a _Turkish March_ section (Schiller's text _"Froh, wie seine Sonnen fliegen"_ — "Joyful as His suns fly" — set with Janissary percussion: triangle, cymbals, bass drum). Then a long instrumental fugue, then a final choral climax. The movement closes with the chorus and orchestra at full intensity, with Schiller's vision of _the brotherhood of humanity_ given musical embodiment.

For the **Heiliger Dankgesang** from String Quartet Op. 132 (~17 minutes — yes, a 17-minute slow movement, longer than many entire Classical-period symphonies): this is the third movement of Beethoven's Quartet No. 15 in A minor, Op. 132, composed in 1825. Beethoven titled the movement _"Heiliger Dankgesang eines Genesenen an die Gottheit, in der lydischen Tonart"_ — "Sacred Song of Thanksgiving from a Convalescent to the Divinity, in the Lydian Mode." Beethoven had been seriously ill in early 1825 (probably an intestinal disorder, possibly an early flareup of the liver condition that would kill him two years later) and recovered enough to complete this quartet. The slow movement is his musical thanksgiving for recovery.

Listen for three things:

  1. **The Lydian mode.** The movement is in the _Lydian mode_ — a medieval church mode with an _F major scale that omits B♭_ (so it has B natural rather than B♭, giving it a distinctive "raised fourth" sound). The mode is ancient, pre-Renaissance; Beethoven is reaching back to Renaissance and medieval sacred music for his thanksgiving. _Listen for the modal quality_ — the music sounds slightly _archaic_ , like an old hymn, because the Lydian mode is not standard major or minor.
  2. **The alternation of two textures.** The movement alternates between a _slow, hymn-like sacred song_ (in Lydian mode) and a _faster, more energetic section_ marked _Neue Kraft fühlend_ ("Feeling new strength"). The two textures alternate: hymn — new strength — hymn — new strength — hymn. The slow sections grow more sublime each return; the fast sections more energetic. The movement is _theme-and-variations on two themes_ held in alternation.
  3. **The final hymn statement.** The closing hymn statement is the deepest moment. It is _quiet, sustained, suspended in time_. Beethoven himself called this movement _the high point of my life as an artist_. The closing minutes are the proof.

For the **Cavatina** from String Quartet Op. 130 (~7 minutes): the fifth movement of Beethoven's Quartet No. 13 in B♭ major, Op. 130, composed 1825–1826. _Cavatina_ is a vocal-style movement, usually slow and song-like. Beethoven's Op. 130 Cavatina is in E♭ major, slow, lyrical, and contains a passage (around 4:00 in most recordings) in which the first violin enters in _broken, fragmented sobbing rhythm_ — Beethoven marked this passage _beklemmt_ ("oppressed" or "anguished"). Beethoven reportedly wept when revising this passage; he told his friend Karl Holz that _"never had any of his own pieces, even in writing, so moved him."_ This is _the most personal moment in Beethoven's late string-quartet output_.

#### One-sentence backgrounds

**Beethoven, Symphony No. 9 in D minor "Choral," Op. 125** — composed 1822–1824 (sketched since 1817), premiered 7 May 1824 at the Kärntnertortheater in Vienna; ~70 minutes in four movements; the fourth movement introduces four vocal soloists and chorus singing a setting of Schiller's _An die Freude_ (Ode to Joy, 1785).

**Beethoven, String Quartet No. 15 in A minor, Op. 132** — composed 1825 in Vienna, premiered November 1825; ~45 minutes in five movements; the third movement _Heiliger Dankgesang_ is ~17 minutes and is the work's emotional center.

**Beethoven, String Quartet No. 13 in B♭ major, Op. 130** — composed 1825–1826 in Vienna, premiered March 1826; originally in six movements with the _Grosse Fuge_ (Op. 133) as the finale, later revised with a lighter finale; the fifth movement _Cavatina_ is ~7 minutes.

### 14.2 The Listening Window

#### Ninth Symphony, Fourth Movement (Bernstein / VPO 1979, ~25 minutes)

* **0:00–0:08.** **The Schreckensfanfare.** A sudden, dissonant fortissimo chord from the entire orchestra. This is the _terror fanfare_ that announces the fourth movement.

* **0:08–1:30.** **The instrumental recitative.** Low strings (cellos and basses) play a _speech-like_ recitative — fast, rhetorical, unmetered. The recitative is _commenting_ on the symphony so far; Beethoven later wrote in his sketches that these passages mean things like _"No, this would remind us of our despair. Let us sing of joy."_ The recitative is interspersed with brief orchestral recalls of the first three movements — each recall _rejected_ by another recitative passage. _The symphony is debating with itself._

* **1:30–2:30.** **The Ode to Joy melody is introduced quietly.** The cellos and basses play the Ode to Joy theme alone, very softly, in a long lyrical line. This is the _first true presentation_ of the melody that will dominate the rest of the movement.

* **2:30–3:30.** **The orchestral build.** Each voice in the orchestra picks up the theme in turn — violas join, then violins, then woodwinds, then horns. The dynamic builds; the texture thickens.

* **3:30–4:30.** **Full orchestral statement.** The entire orchestra at fortissimo plays the Ode to Joy melody in full. _This is the orchestra's complete statement_ before the voices enter.

* **4:30–5:00.** **The Schreckensfanfare returns.** A renewed dissonant chord — same as the opening. The recitative voice is now ready to _speak_.

* **5:00–5:45.** **The baritone enters.** Bass-baritone soloist enters with Beethoven's own added text: _"O Freunde, nicht diese Töne! Sondern laßt uns angenehmere anstimmen und freudenvollere!"_ (Oh friends, not these tones! Let us begin instead more pleasant ones, more joyful ones!). Then he begins Schiller's text: _"Freude, schöner Götterfunken, Tochter aus Elysium..."_ (Joy, beautiful divine spark, daughter of Elysium...).

* **5:45–7:00.** **First chorus statement of Ode to Joy.** The chorus enters at full force singing the Ode to Joy melody to Schiller's words. This is the moment of _public revelation_ — the symphony has reached the music that will define its meaning.

* **7:00–10:00.** **Verses two and three.** The four vocal soloists and the chorus alternate, with the orchestra accompanying. The text moves through Schiller's vision of the brotherhood of humanity.

* **10:00–12:30.** **The "Turkish March" section.** A change of meter and a _military_ texture, with Janissary percussion (triangle, cymbals, bass drum). The text is _"Froh, wie seine Sonnen fliegen"_ (Joyful as His suns fly through the splendid heavens). The tenor soloist sings; the chorus responds. The Turkish March is in some sense the _celebratory-military_ embodiment of the brotherhood.

* **12:30–15:00.** **Long instrumental fugue.** A purely orchestral fugue on the Ode to Joy melody — the chorus is silent for several minutes while the orchestra develops the theme contrapuntally. _The orchestra is doing what fugue does_ : building intellectual-emotional density on a melody we now know intimately.

* **15:00–17:00.** **Choral return with new text.** _"Seid umschlungen, Millionen!"_ (Be embraced, millions!) — the chorus enters with a new text on a new (more solemn, slower) melodic line. This is _the brotherhood vision at its most sublime_ — the chorus invoking universal embrace.

* **17:00–20:00.** **Double fugue.** Beethoven combines the Ode to Joy melody with the _Seid umschlungen_ melody in a _double fugue_ — two themes treated simultaneously in counterpoint. This is one of the most-elaborate contrapuntal moments in the symphonic literature.

* **20:00–23:00.** **Final builds.** The chorus and orchestra alternate; the energy grows; the dynamics climb.

* **23:00–25:00.** **Coda.** A final acceleration into Presto, with the chorus singing _"Götterfunken!"_ (Divine spark!) on a final triumphant cadence. The symphony closes in D major (the parallel major of D minor, the symphony's overall home key).

The fourth movement is _enormous_. It is also unprecedented in including a chorus and vocal soloists in a symphony. The structural device — instrumental recitative debating the previous movements, then introducing the Ode to Joy melody, then building to the choral entry — was Beethoven's invention. No previous symphony had attempted anything like it.

#### Heiliger Dankgesang from Op. 132 (Quartetto Italiano, ~17 minutes)

This is one of the most extraordinary movements in the string-quartet literature.

* **0:00–2:30.** **First Lydian hymn statement.** The quartet plays a slow, hymn-like passage in F Lydian mode — F major with B natural rather than B♭, giving the music an _archaic, modal_ quality. The texture is mostly chordal; each chord is sustained; the voices weave slowly. _Listen for the modal sound_ — it does not sound like ordinary major or minor; it sounds like medieval church music.

* **2:30–5:00.** _**Neue Kraft fühlend**_ ("Feeling new strength") — first contrasting section. The music shifts to D major (a normal major key, no longer Lydian) and to a _faster, more energetic_ rhythmic pattern. The convalescent is _recovering_ ; the music's vitality grows. The two violins exchange running figures; the viola and cello provide energetic accompaniment.

* **5:00–7:30.** **Second Lydian hymn statement.** Return to the slow F Lydian hymn. The texture is similar to the opening but slightly fuller; the music now feels _known_ — the listener recognizes the hymn's character.

* **7:30–9:30.** _**Neue Kraft fühlend**_ — second contrasting section. The energetic D-major music returns, with slightly fuller writing and greater intensity.

* **9:30–17:00.** **Third and final Lydian hymn statement.** The longest of the three hymn sections — about seven minutes of sustained, quiet, Lydian-modal hymn-writing. The music is _suspended_ : tempi very slow, dynamics consistently soft, harmony moving by small steps. The four voices weave the hymn into ever-deeper sustained chords. _Beethoven is sustaining a state of grace for seven minutes_ , without dramatic incident, without crisis, without conventional musical activity. The music simply _is_. The closing pages are the deepest moment in his string-quartet output and one of the deepest moments in the entire chamber-music literature.

Beethoven called this movement _"Heiliger Dankgesang eines Genesenen an die Gottheit, in der lydischen Tonart"_ — "Sacred Song of Thanksgiving from a Convalescent to the Divinity, in the Lydian Mode." The title is autobiographical: Beethoven had been seriously ill in early 1825, recovered, and wrote the movement as a thanksgiving for the recovery. The Lydian mode (medieval, sacred, pre-Renaissance) was chosen for its associations with the old church repertoire. The movement is one of the most explicit instances of _Beethoven's late introverted style_ — long, slow, contrapuntally dense, refusing dramatic incident, asking the listener to enter a sustained state rather than to follow a narrative.

#### Cavatina from Op. 130 (Quartetto Italiano, ~7 minutes)

* **0:00–3:30.** **The Cavatina proper.** A slow, lyrical, song-like movement in E♭ major. The texture is _vocal_ — the four instruments singing together as if they were a vocal quartet. The melodic writing is some of the most-beautiful Beethoven wrote.

* **3:30–4:30.** _**Beklemmt**_ ("oppressed" / "anguished") section. The first violin enters in _broken, sobbing rhythm_ — fragmented phrases, hesitations, silences between the fragments. The other three voices play hushed sustained chords underneath. _This is the most personal moment._ Beethoven marked the passage _beklemmt_ in the score — an unusual marking suggesting _constricted breathing, choked emotion, the difficulty of speaking through grief_. Beethoven reportedly wept while revising this passage.

* **4:30–7:00.** **Return to the main Cavatina.** The lyrical music returns; the _beklemmt_ moment passes; the movement closes on a long sustained E♭-major chord.

The Cavatina is in some ways the _most personal_ moment in Beethoven's late quartet output — a moment of audible vulnerability, briefer than the _Heiliger Dankgesang_ but more wounded. Listeners often describe the _beklemmt_ passage as _the moment when Beethoven's own grief becomes audible_. The composer who could write the public triumph of the Ode to Joy could also write the private suffering of the Cavatina. Both are him.

### 14.3 What's Happening in the Music

#### Definition: Late Style

In Beethoven scholarship, _late style_ refers to the works composed roughly 1815 onward — the last twelve years of Beethoven's life. The late style is characterized by:

* **Introversion** : turning inward, away from public-civic ambition toward private-philosophical reflection. (The Ninth Symphony is partially a late-style work but retains the public-civic dimension; the late quartets are pure late style.)
* **Contrapuntal density** : extensive use of fugue and complex contrapuntal weaving. The _Heiliger Dankgesang_ is contrapuntally dense in a sustained way the middle-period Beethoven rarely attempted.
* **Eccentric formal structures** : movements that depart from Classical and Romantic norms — five-movement quartets, slow movements that take seventeen minutes, fugues that interrupt scherzos. The form is rebuilt for each work.
* **Long contemplative spans** : extended slow sections without dramatic incident, asking the listener to enter a state rather than to follow a narrative.
* **Use of older idioms** : Lydian mode in the _Heiliger Dankgesang_ ; archaic Baroque counterpoint in the late fugues; references to Bach, Palestrina, the Renaissance polyphonic tradition.
* **Idiosyncratic notation** : unusual time signatures, atypical performance markings, _beklemmt_ -like emotional indications that have no clear musical translation.

The late style is widely considered the _summit_ of Beethoven's output, more so than the heroic middle period. Pianist Alfred Brendel, conductor Daniel Barenboim, and many other musicians have described the late piano sonatas and late quartets as _the deepest music Beethoven wrote_. The works are not always immediately accessible — they ask more of the listener than the middle-period heroic-narrative works — but the depth that rewards the patience is substantial.

The Ninth Symphony is a partial exception. It is composed in the late period (premiered 1824) and contains late-style elements (the eccentric fourth-movement structure, the contrapuntal fugue, the long slow movement), but it is _also_ the culmination of the public-civic heroic narrative of the middle period. The Ode to Joy finale is _not_ introverted; it is the most-public statement Beethoven ever made. The Ninth is therefore in some sense _both_ late and middle Beethoven — the transitional work that closes one period and opens another.

#### Definition: Lydian Mode

The _Lydian mode_ is one of the seven _modes_ — the seven possible diatonic scales that can be built by starting on a different note of the major scale. The Lydian mode starts on the fourth degree: F to F using only the white keys of the piano, which gives F-G-A-B-C-D-E-F. The defining feature is the _raised fourth_ — B natural rather than B♭ — which gives the mode a distinctive sound (almost like F major but with that one note shifted up a half step).

In Western art music, the seven modes (Ionian, Dorian, Phrygian, Lydian, Mixolydian, Aeolian, Locrian) were the basis of Renaissance and earlier sacred music. By the late Baroque, the modes had largely been replaced by _major and minor scales_ (which themselves derive from Ionian and Aeolian modes). After 1700, modal writing became rare in art music; composers used major and minor almost exclusively.

Beethoven's choice of Lydian for the _Heiliger Dankgesang_ is therefore unusual and historically meaningful. He is reaching back to Renaissance and medieval sacred music for his thanksgiving — using an idiom that listeners of 1825 would have recognized as _ancient, ecclesiastical, sacred_. The choice gives the movement its specifically _otherworldly_ sound.

Modal writing returns in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries — Vaughan Williams uses modes extensively, as do Holst, Sibelius, and many British folk-influenced composers. Debussy uses modal scales (Chapter 22). The modal idiom has continued in the twentieth and twenty-first centuries through folk-influenced music, jazz modal improvisation, and various contemporary composition.

#### Common Misconception

People sometimes think the Ninth Symphony is _just the Ode to Joy_ — that the fourth movement is the symphony and the first three are preliminaries to it. This misreads what Beethoven did.

The first three movements are major works in their own right. The first movement (sonata-form Allegro in D minor, ~16 min) is one of the most-extensive opening movements Beethoven wrote, with dark dramatic content and substantial development. The second movement (Scherzo, ~12 min) is in 3/4 time with extraordinarily energetic rhythmic content. The third movement (Adagio molto e cantabile, ~16 min) is a _Theme and Variations_ of extraordinary lyrical depth, sometimes considered the deepest slow movement Beethoven wrote — a _late-style_ slow movement in the symphony.

The fourth movement is the _destination_ , not the _whole_. The instrumental recitative that opens the fourth movement _quotes_ and _rejects_ fragments of the first three movements — Beethoven himself signals that the previous movements have been _inadequate_ to the symphony's eventual subject (the brotherhood of humanity). But the rejection is not dismissal; it is _the move that gives the Ode to Joy its meaning_. The Ode to Joy _answers_ the first three movements; it does not _replace_ them. A listener who hears only the fourth movement gets the answer without the question — and the answer means less without the question.

The mature engagement with the Ninth Symphony is to hear all four movements in sequence. The first movement's D-minor darkness, the Scherzo's restless energy, the Adagio's lyrical depth, and the fourth movement's revelation — these are the four parts of a single argument. The chapter has focused on the fourth movement because it is the cultural touchstone, but the listener who wants to encounter the symphony properly should give it its full seventy minutes.

### 14.4 The Stories

#### Beethoven's late years

Beethoven was forty-five in 1815, when his late period is usually dated to begin. By that point his hearing was profoundly impaired; he had largely stopped performing publicly; his finances were unstable (the patron payments from Lobkowitz and Kinsky and Rudolph had been disrupted by Habsburg economic crises of the 1810s); his personal life had not produced a marriage despite several attempted attachments. He was a difficult man — temperamentally explosive, frequently in disputes with publishers and friends, increasingly isolated by his deafness.

He was also the most-famous composer in Europe. His middle-period works (the symphonies, the concertos, the chamber music, _Fidelio_) were performed regularly across Europe; his music was the touchstone for the next generation of composers. He had financial difficulties but he was not poor.

The 1815–1820 years were productive but difficult. He composed less than in the heroic middle period; he was working through stylistic transitions; he had not yet found the late voice that would emerge in the late piano sonatas (Op. 109, Op. 110, Op. 111, composed 1820–1822), the _Diabelli Variations_ (1819–1823), the _Missa Solemnis_ (1819–1823), the Ninth Symphony (1822–1824), and the late string quartets (1825–1826).

In 1815, Beethoven's brother Carl died, leaving a nine-year-old son named Karl. The will named Beethoven and Carl's widow Johanna as co-guardians. Beethoven, who profoundly disliked Johanna, immediately sued for sole custody. The custody dispute consumed years of Beethoven's energy — court appearances, legal filings, the boy's emotional involvement, Johanna's countersuits. Beethoven won and lost custody several times. Karl himself attempted suicide in 1826 (he survived). The relationship between Beethoven and Karl is one of the most-painful aspects of Beethoven biography — the deaf, intensely controlling uncle attempting to raise a teenage nephew, both of them substantially damaged by the relationship. The story is part of the late-life Beethoven context: the great works of 1820–1826 were composed against the background of substantial personal turmoil.

The Galitzin commission — three string quartets commissioned in 1822 by Prince Nikolai Galitzin of Saint Petersburg — gave Beethoven the financial occasion to write the late quartets. He composed Op. 127, Op. 132, and Op. 130 (with the _Grosse Fuge_ Op. 133 as its original finale) for Galitzin in 1825–1826. He also composed Op. 131 (1826) and Op. 135 (1826) without commission. These five late quartets are now the heart of his late chamber-music output.

He died in Vienna on 26 March 1827 at age 56, after a long final illness. The cause of death was probably _cirrhosis of the liver_ (Beethoven had been a heavy drinker for many years); the secondary cause was lead poisoning (from the medicines administered by his doctors, which contained substantial lead). His funeral on 29 March was attended by an estimated _ten to twenty thousand mourners_ — one of the largest funerals in Vienna's history. Schubert (Chapter 15) was a torchbearer at the funeral, walking in the procession; Schubert himself would die the following year, age 31.

#### The Galitzin commission and the late quartets

Prince Nikolai Galitzin (1794–1866) was a Russian aristocrat, amateur cellist, and major Beethoven admirer. In 1822 he wrote to Beethoven from Saint Petersburg offering to commission _one, two, or three quartets, the price of which I will leave to your decision._ Beethoven accepted the commission and set a price: 50 ducats per quartet, plus expenses, payable in advance.

The first quartet (Op. 127 in E♭ major) was delivered in 1825. The second (Op. 132 in A minor, which contains the _Heiliger Dankgesang_) was completed in 1825 and delivered late in the year. The third (Op. 130 in B♭ major, originally with the _Grosse Fuge_ Op. 133 as finale) was completed in 1825–1826.

Galitzin's payments to Beethoven were irregular — partly because Russian aristocratic finances of the 1820s were unstable, partly because of communication problems between Vienna and Saint Petersburg. The full payment owed to Beethoven was not received until 1853, after Beethoven's death; Galitzin's son finally paid the remaining 125 ducats to Beethoven's estate. The commission's financial completion took two generations.

The five late string quartets (Op. 127, Op. 130, Op. 131, Op. 132, Op. 135) are now widely considered the summit of Beethoven's output. The middle-period quartets (Op. 18, the three "Razumovsky" quartets Op. 59, Op. 74, Op. 95) are great. The late quartets are _different in kind_ — longer, more introverted, contrapuntally denser, structurally more eccentric, emotionally more demanding. The _Heiliger Dankgesang_ and the Cavatina are two of the most-personal moments in the entire string-quartet literature.

#### The premiere story revisited

The Caroline Unger anecdote, mentioned in the opening of this chapter, was widely reported in Vienna newspapers in May 1824 and was retold by Anton Schindler (Beethoven's biographer-confidant) for the rest of his life. The basic outline — Beethoven sitting beside Umlauf, beating time, unable to hear, turned by Unger to see the ovation — is corroborated by multiple sources. Some details (the specific moment, the exact words spoken) vary between accounts.

What is well-documented:

* Beethoven was almost entirely deaf by 1824.
* He sat at the front of the stage with the score, beating time, while Umlauf actually conducted.
* The audience applauded enthusiastically; the applause exceeded the imperial protocol of three curtain calls; some sources say five, some seven.
* The Vienna police reportedly tried to restore order, citing the protocol limit, but the audience persisted.
* Beethoven, deaf, did not realize the applause was happening until turned to see it.

The premiere is one of the most-documented moments in concert history. The combination of Beethoven's deafness, the work's unprecedented scale, the audience's overwhelming response, and the alto soloist's quiet act of turning the composer to see the response makes this one of the few moments in music history where _the human conditions of art_ are visible in the act of premiere itself.

#### The Ninth Symphony as cultural-political object

The Ninth Symphony has been _more politically used_ than any other piece of music in the Western art-music tradition. A selective timeline:

* **1830s onward** : standard repertoire piece, performed widely in Europe; the choral finale becomes the music of civic ritual.
* **1870 (Beethoven centenary)** : performed in every major European capital, often at civic anniversary events.
* **1933 onward (Nazi Germany)** : appropriated by the Nazi regime as a German cultural artifact; Hitler's birthday in 1942 was marked by a Furtwängler performance of the Ninth.
* **1945 onward** : deliberately _de-Nazified_ ; performances were used in postwar reconciliation events (Bernstein in Berlin in December 1989 to celebrate the fall of the Berlin Wall is the most-famous example, with Bernstein conducting and the chorus singing "Freedom" — _Freiheit_ — in place of "Joy" — _Freude_ — for that performance).
* **1980s onward (Japan)** : an annual tradition began in postwar Japan of performing the Ninth at New Year's Eve concerts; by the 2000s, between two hundred and three hundred Ninth Symphony performances occur in Japan annually, with a participatory tradition of audience members joining the chorus from the audience for the _Ode to Joy_ — _Daiku_ (literally "Big Nine") culture.
* **1972 onward** : the Council of Europe adopted the Ode to Joy melody (without Schiller's text) as its anthem.
* **1985 onward** : the European Union adopted the Ode to Joy melody as its anthem.
* **1989** : Bernstein-Berlin performance celebrating the Wall's fall.
* **2003** : UNESCO added the manuscript of the Ninth Symphony to its Memory of the World Register.
* **Present** : the Ninth Symphony's choral finale is the music of public ritual across the Western world — civic anniversaries, political moments, memorials, openings of new institutions.

This is more politically resonant use than any other work in this book or in the Western art-music tradition. The Ninth has become _the music of brotherhood and reconciliation_ — the universal-civic music. The work earns the role; the Ode to Joy melody is genuinely a great melody, and Schiller's text is genuinely a great poetic vision. But the work has also been used in ways Beethoven could not have anticipated, and some of those uses (the Nazi appropriations, the marketing-jingle deployments) have been problematic. The Ninth, like the Mozart Requiem, has accumulated a complex social-ritual existence that is intertwined with but not identical to its musical content. The mature listener can hold both.

#### Recordings

**Leonard Bernstein, Vienna Philharmonic, 1979 (Deutsche Grammophon)** for the Ninth Symphony. Bernstein conducted the Ninth more than any other single work in his career; he recorded it five times commercially. The 1979 Vienna recording is the most-celebrated. The reading is _intense, expansive, dramatically committed_ — Bernstein at his most musically generous, with the Vienna Philharmonic at its full late-Romantic sound. The fourth movement runs about 24 minutes; the whole symphony about 70.

**Wilhelm Furtwängler, Bayreuth Festival Orchestra and Chorus, 1951 (EMI)** — the 1951 Bayreuth Festival concert performance of the Ninth, conducted by Furtwängler in his postwar return to Bayreuth (the Festival had been closed since 1944). This is one of the most-historically-resonant Ninth recordings — Furtwängler in a postwar Bayreuth gesture of reconciliation, with the Beethoven Ninth as the symbolic central work. The reading is slow, weighted, sometimes idiosyncratically inflected, deeply Romantic in scale. The recording quality is monaural (1951), but the performance has been treasured for sixty years.

**John Eliot Gardiner, Orchestre Révolutionnaire et Romantique and Monteverdi Choir, 1992 (DG Archiv)** — period-instrument reading, smaller forces (about 60 in the orchestra, about 40 in the chorus), brisker tempi than Bernstein or Furtwängler. The fourth movement runs about 22 minutes. The reading restores the work to _Beethoven's Vienna scale_ — smaller chorus, period winds and strings, sharper articulation. Some listeners find this _thrillingly fresh_ ; others find it _under-weighted_ for the work's cultural mass. Either response is defensible.

**Quartetto Italiano, complete Beethoven cycle 1968–1975 (Philips)** for the late quartets. The Quartetto Italiano was a Naples-based ensemble founded in 1945 that maintained an unchanged personnel for over forty years — Paolo Borciani (first violin), Elisa Pegreffi (second violin), Piero Farulli (viola), and Franco Rossi (cello). The continuity gave them an ensemble unity few other quartets matched. Their Beethoven cycle is one of the great recorded chamber-music projects of the twentieth century; the late quartets in their hands are _warm, deeply musical, structurally clear_.

**Takács Quartet, complete Beethoven cycle 2003–2004 (Decca)** — the contemporary alternative. Recorded in concert sequence over an intensive period; the readings are _brisk, focused, conversational, technically immaculate_. The Takács late quartets have been widely praised; their _Heiliger Dankgesang_ is somewhat brisker than the Quartetto Italiano (about 15 minutes versus the Italians' 17–18 minutes) but equally probing.

**Busch Quartet, late quartets 1936–1942 (HMV / EMI historical archives)** — the great prewar quartet, with Adolf Busch as first violin. The Busch readings have a _spiritual seriousness_ and _direct emotional engagement_ that distinguishes them from later, more technically polished recordings. The recording quality is historical (mid-1930s) but the performances are extraordinary.

#### Cross-piece links

* For more **late Beethoven** , listen to the **Piano Sonata No. 32 in C minor, Op. 111** (1822) — Beethoven's last piano sonata, in two movements; the second movement is an _Arietta and Variations_ of sustained transcendent character (sometimes called _anticipation of jazz_ because of the rhythmic syncopation in one variation). Listen also to the **Missa Solemnis in D major, Op. 123** (1819–1823) — Beethoven's last great choral work, composed alongside the Ninth Symphony.
* For **Schubert's response to Beethoven** , listen to **Schubert's String Quartet No. 14 in D minor "Death and the Maiden," D. 810** (1824) — composed during Schubert's first deep engagement with Beethoven's late quartets, demonstrating Schubert's own quartet writing taking on the late-Beethoven scale and ambition. We will meet Schubert in Chapter 15.
* For **the Brahms response to Beethoven** , listen to **Brahms's Symphony No. 1 in C minor, Op. 68** (1876) — the symphony Brahms struggled with for twenty years partly because of the Ninth's shadow. The fourth-movement chorale-melody (sometimes called _Brahms's Ode to Joy_) is in direct dialogue with Beethoven's choral finale.
* For **Mahler's response to Beethoven** , listen to **Mahler's Symphony No. 8 "Symphony of a Thousand"** (1906–1907) — the largest-scale symphonic-choral work in the standard repertoire, with eight vocal soloists, double chorus, children's chorus, and massive orchestra. Mahler is responding to and extending what the Ninth opened up. We will meet Mahler in Chapter 21 (different Mahler symphonies — No. 2 and No. 5).
* For **modern political uses of the Ninth** , listen to **the Bernstein Berlin 1989 recording** (DG) — the live recording from the Berlin Wall celebration with the substituted _Freiheit_ (Freedom) text. The performance has its own cultural significance.

#### Conversation Seeds

* _Ask the companion about the Caroline Unger story of the May 1824 premiere — what is well-documented, what may be embellished, and what the moment of the alto soloist turning the deaf composer to see the ovation tells us about the work's reception from the first._
* _Ask the companion about the _Heiliger Dankgesang_ — what the Lydian mode is, why Beethoven chose it for this movement, and how the alternating slow-hymn and _Neue Kraft fühlend_ sections structure the seventeen-minute span._
* _Tell the companion which of the late-style moments struck you most — the Ode to Joy's revelation, the _Heiliger Dankgesang_ 's sustained Lydian-modal grace, the Cavatina's _beklemmt_ breaking-of-voice — and ask her what each reveals about what Beethoven was trying to do in his last six years._
* _Ask the companion about the Ninth Symphony's _political afterlife_ — the Nazi appropriations, the Bernstein 1989 Berlin performance with the _Freiheit_ substitution, the Japanese New Year's Eve _Daiku_ tradition, the EU anthem adoption. What does it mean for a piece of music to become this politically used?_
* _Bring the late piano sonatas (Op. 109, Op. 110, Op. 111) into the conversation with the companion. What does the late piano style do that the late quartet style cannot — and what does the quartet style do that the piano cannot?_

### 14.5 Exercises

#### Concept Check

**Q1.** What is the _late style_ in Beethoven scholarship?

**Answer:** The style Beethoven developed in his final twelve years (roughly 1815 onward), characterized by introversion, contrapuntal density, eccentric formal structures, long contemplative spans without dramatic incident, use of older idioms (Lydian mode, Renaissance counterpoint), and idiosyncratic notation (_beklemmt_ , unusual time signatures). The late piano sonatas (Op. 109, 110, 111), the _Diabelli Variations_ , the _Missa Solemnis_ , the Ninth Symphony, and especially the late string quartets (Op. 127, 130, 131, 132, 135) are the main late-style works. The late style is widely considered the summit of Beethoven's output.

**Q2.** Why is the Ode to Joy melody introduced _quietly in the low strings_ before the chorus enters?

**Answer:** Beethoven structures the fourth movement as a _gradual revelation_. The instrumental recitative _debates_ the previous three movements, _rejecting_ fragments of each. The Ode to Joy melody is then introduced as the _answer_ — first quietly, in the cellos and basses alone, as if the music is _finding its way_ to the right melody. Then the orchestra builds it up across several minutes, adding voices and dynamics, before the chorus finally enters at full force. This gradual revelation gives the Ode to Joy its specific dramatic weight: the listener has been with the orchestra as it searched for the right melody, and the chorus's eventual public statement feels _earned_ rather than _announced_. A direct choral entry without the orchestral build would be far less dramatically effective.

### Chapter Summary

This chapter introduced **Beethoven's late style** through three masterworks: the **fourth movement of Symphony No. 9 in D minor "Choral," Op. 125** (premiered 7 May 1824, ~25 minutes); the **Heiliger Dankgesang from String Quartet No. 15 in A minor, Op. 132** (1825, ~17 minutes, in the Lydian mode); and the **Cavatina from String Quartet No. 13 in B♭ major, Op. 130** (1825–1826, ~7 minutes, with the _beklemmt_ central passage).

You learned **late style** characteristics (introversion, contrapuntal density, eccentric formal structures, long contemplative spans, use of older idioms, idiosyncratic notation) and met the **Lydian mode** (the medieval church mode with the raised fourth that gives the _Heiliger Dankgesang_ its archaic-sacred sound). You learned that the late style is widely considered the summit of Beethoven's output and that the Ninth Symphony is partly late-style and partly culmination of the middle-period heroic style.

You met the **Caroline Unger anecdote** from the May 1824 premiere — Beethoven sitting beside Umlauf at the front of the stage, beating time deaf, turned by the alto soloist to see the standing ovation he could not hear. The premiere as one of the most-documented moments in concert history.

You met the **Galitzin commission** (1822, three quartets from Prince Nikolai Galitzin of Saint Petersburg) and the resulting **late string quartets** (Op. 127, 130, 131, 132, 135). The _Heiliger Dankgesang_ came from Beethoven's recovery from serious illness in early 1825; the Cavatina's _beklemmt_ passage made Beethoven weep when he revised it.

You met the **Ninth Symphony's political afterlife** — the Nazi appropriations, the Bernstein 1989 Berlin performance celebrating the Wall's fall (with _Freiheit_ substituted for _Freude_), the Japanese New Year's Eve _Daiku_ tradition, the EU anthem adoption. The work's cultural-ritual weight as one of the most-politically-resonant pieces in the Western art-music tradition.

You met four readings: Bernstein 1979 (modern-Romantic, expansive), Furtwängler Bayreuth 1951 (postwar-historic, weighted), Gardiner 1992 (period-instrument, brisk) for the Ninth; Quartetto Italiano 1968–1975 (warm, deeply musical), Takács 2003–2004 (brisk, technically immaculate), Busch 1936–1942 (spiritually serious, historical) for the late quartets.

**Composer Protagonist Beethoven culminates here.** Three Beethoven chapters total: Chapter 3 (Symphony 5 first movement, motif-and-development), Chapter 13 (_Eroica_ , the Classical-Romantic hinge), Chapter 14 (Ninth and late quartets, the late style). He has accumulated into a three-dimensional figure — the proud, prickly, progressively deaf composer who wrote his way through despair (Heiligenstadt 1802), built the heroic-style symphonic tradition (1803–1812), and ended his life in the introverted, contrapuntally dense, philosophical-cosmic late style (1815–1827).

The next chapter takes you to **Schubert** — the inheritor of Beethoven and one of the great composers of the early Romantic period. Chapter 15 anchors on **Schubert's _Winterreise_** (the song cycle for voice and piano on Wilhelm Müller texts) and the **Trout Quintet** (chamber music as friends-around-the-piano). The book is now in the Romantic-period section.

## Chapter 15: Schubert — _Winterreise_ and the _Trout_ Quintet

Schubert was thirty-one years old when he died of typhoid fever in his older brother Ferdinand's apartment in Vienna on 19 November 1828, twenty months after Beethoven. He had been a torchbearer at Beethoven's funeral the previous March, walking in the procession of ten or fifteen thousand mourners; he had asked, on his own deathbed, to be buried near Beethoven, and the request was honored — Schubert's grave was placed three plots from Beethoven's in Vienna's Währing Cemetery. In the eight years between his first major works (around 1815) and his death (1828), Schubert composed approximately one thousand works: more than six hundred songs (called _Lieder_), nine symphonies (some incomplete), fifteen string quartets, twenty-one piano sonatas, several operas, the _Mass in E♭_ , two song cycles (_Die schöne Müllerin_ and _Winterreise_), and large amounts of chamber music for unusual combinations. Most of this was unpublished and unperformed during his lifetime. He was paid almost nothing for what was published. He lived hand-to-mouth, supported by close friends in the small Viennese musical circle that knew him.

Schubert was the great composer of _intimacy_. He did not compose for the Theater an der Wien or for the Esterházy court orchestra; he composed for the _Schubertiade_ — informal evenings at the homes of his friends, where Schubert would sit at the piano and his circle would gather to hear new songs sung by his friend Johann Michael Vogl (a retired tenor from the court opera), to play through new chamber music in a music room of twenty or thirty people, to drink wine and argue about poetry. The _Schubertiade_ was Vienna's most-personal music-making tradition of the 1820s, and it produced what is now the heart of Schubert's output: the late piano sonatas, the late chamber music, the great song cycles, the _Trout_ Quintet, the late string quartets, the _Octet_ for winds and strings, the _Quintet in C_ for two cellos.

This chapter is about Schubert's intimate art in two specific forms. The first is _Winterreise_ (_Winter Journey_) — a cycle of twenty-four songs for voice and piano, composed 1827, on poems by Wilhelm Müller about a young man rejected in love wandering through winter landscapes. The cycle is one of the deepest works in the song repertoire and one of the most-devastating extended works of musical sadness in the Western canon. We focus on two songs: **"Der Lindenbaum"** (No. 5, ~4 min) and **"Der Leiermann"** (No. 24, ~4 min). The second is the _Trout_ Quintet — Piano Quintet in A major, D. 667, composed 1819 in a happier period for Schubert, anchored in the fourth movement on a theme from Schubert's earlier song "Die Forelle" ("The Trout"). The _Trout_ Quintet is the great instance of _chamber music as friends-around-the-piano_ — the genre's most-warmly communal exemplar.

### 15.1 Before You Listen

#### Hook anecdote — the rejected manuscript and the _Schubertiade_

In November 1827, Schubert finished the second half of _Winterreise_ — twelve songs to complete a cycle whose first twelve he had composed earlier the same year. He had been intensely focused on the cycle for most of 1827; it consumed his energy in ways he himself acknowledged were unusual. He gathered his closest friends — including Joseph von Spaun, Franz Lachner, Eduard von Bauernfeld, the painter Moritz von Schwind — in his apartment on a winter evening to perform the completed cycle for them. He sang the songs himself in his light voice (he was not a trained singer but he could carry the songs adequately), accompanying himself on the piano.

The friends listened in silence for the entire cycle — about seventy minutes. At the end, several of them were in tears. Spaun, in a memoir written decades later, wrote that the songs had been _"strangely melancholy"_ and that Schubert himself had been profoundly affected by composing them. He recalled Schubert saying: _"I like these songs more than all the rest, and you will come to like them as well."_

A few months later, Schubert was dead. _Winterreise_ was published in two installments — the first twelve songs in January 1828, the second twelve posthumously in December 1828. The cycle entered the song repertoire gradually over the following decades. By the late nineteenth century it was recognized as one of the central works of the German lieder tradition; by the twentieth century it was a touchstone for every great baritone and tenor who wanted to demonstrate the seriousness of the song repertoire.

The cycle is _unrelentingly sad_. The protagonist, a young man rejected by the woman he loved, walks out of her village in winter and wanders through a series of snow-bound landscapes — frozen rivers, weather-beaten signposts, abandoned mailcoaches, will-o'-the-wisps, dogs barking, an inn with no room, a crow following him. The twenty-four songs trace his progressive estrangement from human connection. The cycle ends with him meeting a hurdy-gurdy man playing in the snow with no one listening, asking the hurdy-gurdy man if he should follow him. There is no resolution, no redemption, no consoling return. The protagonist disappears into the winter.

This is what the chapter is asking you to listen to. Two of the cycle's most-loved songs. After that, the _Trout_ Quintet, as a contrast — the _other_ Schubert, the happier Schubert, the chamber-music Schubert of the Schubertiades.

#### What to notice

For **"Der Lindenbaum"** (_The Linden Tree_ , No. 5 in _Winterreise_ , ~4 min) — the most-known song in the cycle:

  1. **The opening piano figure.** The piano introduces a rocking, gentle rhythmic pattern in E major — _almost a lullaby_. Hold this in your ear; it is the _welcoming voice_ of the linden tree, calling the wanderer to rest.
  2. **The change to minor.** Around 1:30 (in most recordings), the music shifts to E minor for the second verse. _The wanderer remembers passing the linden tree on his way out of the village_ ; the memory turns dark. The contrast between the welcoming E major of the opening and the troubled E minor of the second verse is the song's emotional engine.
  3. **The return to major.** The song returns to E major for the closing verses, with the linden tree's _Komm her zu mir, Geselle, hier findst du deine Ruh_ — "Come here to me, friend, here you will find your rest." The wanderer keeps walking, but the linden tree's call lingers. The song closes with the same gentle piano figure that began it.

For **"Der Leiermann"** (_The Hurdy-Gurdy Man_ , No. 24 — the last song in _Winterreise_ , ~4 min):

  1. **The piano's _drone_.** The piano plays a sustained drone on two notes — _A and E_ — that persists throughout the entire song. This is the imitation of the _hurdy-gurdy_ (a medieval-Renaissance instrument with a wheel that bows the strings continuously, producing a sustained sound underneath the melody). _Listen for the drone._ It does not stop.
  2. **The vocal line's plainness.** The singer's melody is _almost monotone_ — narrow in range, slow, hesitant, with long sustained notes. The wanderer is _almost too exhausted to speak_.
  3. **The final question.** At the end of the song, the wanderer asks the hurdy-gurdy man: _Wunderlicher Alter, soll ich mit dir geh'n? Willst zu meinen Liedern deine Leier dreh'n?_ — "Strange old man, shall I go with you? Will you turn your hurdy-gurdy to my songs?" The song does not answer. The drone fades. The cycle ends in silence.

For the **Trout Quintet, Fourth Movement** (Andantino, theme and variations, ~8 min):

  1. **The opening of the theme.** The violin plays a graceful melody — _"Die Forelle"_ ("The Trout") — that Schubert had composed as a song in 1817. The theme is in D major; cheerful, walking, almost dance-like.
  2. **The variations.** Five variations follow the theme. Each variation features a different instrument: variation 1 violin, variation 2 viola, variation 3 cello, variation 4 piano (with all four strings), variation 5 a slower, more lyrical variation across all instruments. _Listen for which instrument carries the melody in each variation._
  3. **The coda.** A closing passage in 6/8 time that brings the movement to a brisk, joyful close.

#### One-sentence backgrounds

**Schubert,_Winterreise_ (Winter Journey), D. 911** — song cycle for voice (originally tenor) and piano, on twenty-four poems by Wilhelm Müller (1794–1827); composed 1827 in two installments; first half premiered at a Schubertiade in spring 1827, complete cycle assembled later in 1827, published in two installments 1828; complete cycle ~70 minutes.

**Schubert, Piano Quintet in A major "Trout," D. 667** — chamber music for violin, viola, cello, double bass, and piano (an unusual quintet scoring); composed 1819 in Steyr in Upper Austria, premiered at a Schubertiade in 1820; ~35 minutes in five movements; the fourth movement is the famous theme-and-variations on Schubert's earlier song "Die Forelle."
