## Chapter 21: Mahler — Symphony No. 5 Adagietto + Symphony No. 2 "Resurrection"

Gustav Mahler is the late-Romantic symphonic giant. Born in 1860 in a Bohemian village to Jewish parents (Iglau, then in the Austrian Empire, now Jihlava in the Czech Republic), he studied at the Vienna Conservatory in the 1870s, worked as an opera conductor across the German-speaking world in the 1880s and early 1890s (Bad Hall, Olomouc, Leipzig, Hamburg), and from 1897 to 1907 served as Director of the Vienna Court Opera — the most-prestigious operatic position in Europe. He composed _only on summer holidays_ , building small composing huts at his country estates (Steinbach, then Maiernigg, then Toblach) where he would work for two or three months each year while the opera houses were closed. The result was nine completed symphonies (Symphonies Nos. 1–9, composed 1888–1909), a substantial unfinished tenth, two major song cycles (_Lieder eines fahrenden Gesellen_ , _Kindertotenlieder_), and the song-symphony _Das Lied von der Erde_ (1908–1909). He died in Vienna on 18 May 1911 at age 50, of subacute bacterial (streptococcal) endocarditis — a heart-valve infection.

His symphonies are _enormous_. Most run 60–90 minutes; the Symphony No. 8 ("Symphony of a Thousand") requires over 1000 performers and runs 90 minutes; the Symphony No. 3 is the longest standard-repertoire symphony at over 100 minutes. The orchestras are large (Mahler often calls for 80–120 players); the choral and vocal-soloist forces are large in the choral symphonies (Nos. 2, 3, 4, 8). The emotional ambition is _as expansive as the scale_ : each symphony attempts a _world_ — a complete philosophical-emotional cosmos contained in a single multi-movement work.

This chapter focuses on two of Mahler's most-loved single movements: the **Adagietto from Symphony No. 5** (~10 min, one of the most-popular Mahler movements, the soundtrack of _Death in Venice_ , the music played at funerals of people who loved this music) and the **finale of Symphony No. 2 "Resurrection"** (~33 min, the choral-orchestral cosmology whose apocalyptic opening alludes to the _Dies Irae_ 's expressive territory and that ends in a _Resurrection_ affirmation in post-Beethoven 9's central inheritance).

### 21.1 Before You Listen

#### Hook anecdote — the Freud consultation

In August 1910, Mahler was at his summer composing hut at Toblach in the Dolomites, working on his Symphony No. 10, when his wife Alma confessed that she had been having an affair with the architect Walter Gropius (who later founded the Bauhaus). The marriage had been strained for years; Alma was 19 years younger than Mahler; she had given up her own composing career at his insistence when they married in 1902; she had borne him two daughters (one of whom, Maria, had died of scarlet fever in 1907, age 4); she had felt creatively suffocated for nearly a decade.

Mahler was devastated. Through their mutual friend Bruno Walter, he obtained an emergency appointment with **Sigmund Freud** in Leiden, Netherlands (where Freud was vacationing). On 26 August 1910, Mahler met Freud and walked with him for four hours through Leiden. The conversation was the only documented contact between the two men. Freud later wrote (in a 1925 letter to Mahler's biographer) that Mahler had impressed him deeply; that they had discussed Mahler's mother fixation (a recurring theme in Mahler's psychology); that they had explored Alma's name (Mahler's mother had been named Marie, and Mahler had been distressed when his wife wanted to call their second daughter Anna rather than the maternal Marie); and that Mahler had reportedly recognized his own situation in Freud's analysis and had been somewhat relieved.

Whether the consultation helped is uncertain. Mahler and Alma resumed their marriage; Alma broke off the affair with Gropius (briefly); the marriage continued. But Mahler's health declined rapidly through the autumn of 1910 and winter of 1910–1911. He died in May 1911 of the streptococcal bacterial endocarditis described above. The Symphony No. 10 was left unfinished; Alma in 1924 commissioned several composers (Ernst Krenek, Deryck Cooke later in the 1960s) to complete the symphony. The Cooke completion is the most-performed version today.

The Freud consultation is part of the Mahler-Alma story that has been retold in biographies for over a century. The story sometimes overshadows the music. What is _documented_ is the August 1910 walking conversation; what is _legend_ is the precise content of what was discussed. The music — the late symphonies, _Das Lied von der Erde_ , the Tenth Symphony's first movement — speaks for itself; the Freud-Alma story is part of the biographical context but is not the music.

#### What to notice

For the **Adagietto from Symphony No. 5** (~10 minutes):

  1. **The instrumentation.** The Adagietto is scored for _strings alone with harp_ — no woodwinds, no brass, no percussion. The texture is the _softest_ in the symphony. _This is the chamber moment_ in a symphony that elsewhere uses full late-Romantic orchestra.

  2. **The opening melody.** First violins begin a _long, breath-suspended_ melodic line in F major. The melody is _slow_ — adagietto, slightly faster than adagio but still slow — and _singing_. The harp plays _gentle pizzicato chords_ underneath; the lower strings provide sustained harmonic support. _Listen to the harp_ — it is the texture's heartbeat.

  3. **The arch shape.** The Adagietto is essentially _one long arch_ — rising gradually from the opening to a climactic peak around 6:30, then descending back to the opening's quiet character. The structural shape is _not_ sonata form; it is _not_ A-B-A; it is _single-arch lyrical development_. The shape is one of the most-direct emotional architectures in late-Romantic symphonic music.

  4. **The major-minor uncertainty.** Throughout the Adagietto, the music _seems_ to be settling into F major but _keeps_ slipping toward F minor or D minor. The harmonic ambiguity is part of the music's _emotional character_ — _tenderness with longing_ , not pure consolation.

For the **finale of Symphony No. 2 "Resurrection"** (~33 minutes):

  1. **The opening orchestral interlude (~8 minutes).** The finale begins with a _long orchestral interlude_ of _apocalyptic_ character. The full late-Romantic orchestra plays _fast, urgent, fortissimo_ music — distant trumpet calls (sometimes from offstage), heavy timpani, dramatic dynamics. _This is the music of the Last Judgment_. The opening of the finale connects musically to the _Dies Irae_ 's expressive territory (Thread B!) without quoting the chant directly.

  2. **The _Dies Irae_ allusion.** Across the finale's first ten minutes, the brass writing — heavy, descending, austere — has been heard by some musicologists as alluding to the _Dies Irae_ contour, particularly around 6:00–7:00 in most readings. The connection is debated: Mahler does not quote the chant melody directly the way Berlioz does, but the apocalyptic character and some of the melodic shapes are in the chant's lineage. _This is your third encounter with Thread B — at the level of allusion rather than quotation_.

  3. **The _Auferstehen_ (Resurrection) chorus.** Around 23:00 in most readings, after extended orchestral and brief vocal-soloist passages, the _chorus enters_ singing _Auferstehen, ja auferstehen wirst du_ — "Rise again, yes you shall rise again." The choral entrance is _pianissimo_ (hushed, almost whispered) — a deliberate contrast with the apocalyptic loud orchestral writing of the previous twenty minutes. _The chorus's quiet entry_ is one of the most-affecting moments in the symphonic literature.

  4. **The build to the final climax.** From the choral _pianissimo_ entry, the music builds slowly across about ten minutes to a _fortissimo final cadence_ in E♭ major. The chorus and soprano and alto soloists sing through Friedrich Klopstock's _Auferstehen_ hymn (which Mahler had heard at Hans von Bülow's 1894 funeral and which inspired the finale's choral text), with additional verses by Mahler himself. The symphony ends in a triumphant E♭-major _Resurrection_ affirmation.

This is _post-Beethoven 9 choral cosmology_. Beethoven 9 ended in choral universal-brotherhood; Mahler 2 ends in choral _Resurrection_. The lineage is direct — Beethoven was the model, and Mahler is consciously extending the post-Classical choral-symphony tradition. The Mahler 2 finale is _larger in scale_ than Beethoven 9's (the chorus is bigger, the orchestra is bigger, the duration is longer) and _more-explicit in its theological content_ (Beethoven 9 is _Schiller's Enlightenment universal brotherhood_ ; Mahler 2 is _Christian-and-also-cosmic Resurrection_).

#### One-sentence backgrounds

**Mahler, Symphony No. 5 in C♯ minor** — composed summer 1901 and summer 1902 in Maiernigg on the Wörthersee; premiered 18 October 1904 in Cologne with Mahler conducting; ~70 minutes in five movements (Trauermarsch — Stürmisch bewegt — Scherzo — Adagietto — Rondo-Finale). The Adagietto (fourth movement) runs ~10 minutes and is scored for strings and harp alone.

**Mahler, Symphony No. 2 in C minor "Resurrection"** — composed 1888–1894 in various locations; premiered 13 December 1895 in Berlin with Mahler conducting; ~80 minutes in five movements (Allegro maestoso — Andante — Scherzo — _Urlicht_ with mezzo-soprano — Finale with full chorus, soprano and alto soloists, organ). The finale (fifth movement) runs ~33 minutes.

### 21.2 The Listening Window

#### Adagietto from Symphony No. 5 (Bernstein / VPO 1987, ~10 minutes)

* **0:00–0:30.** **Opening.** Harp begins with pizzicato chord; first violins enter with the slow, sustained opening melody in F major. The texture is _strings only with harp_ — no winds, no brass, no percussion. The dynamic is _pianissimo_.

* **0:30–2:00.** **First melodic statement and development.** The opening melody is stated and developed; the lower strings provide harmonic support; the harp adds _gentle harmonic punctuation_ (chords on specific beats rather than continuous accompaniment).

* **2:00–4:00.** **Continued development.** A second melodic idea emerges briefly; the harmonic territory expands (modulations through related keys); the dynamic builds slightly but remains in the _piano to mezzo-piano_ range.

* **4:00–6:00.** **The build toward climax.** The melodic line ascends gradually; the texture grows fuller (more string voices active simultaneously); the dynamic climbs.

* **6:00–7:00.** **The climax.** The first violins reach their highest tessitura; the dynamic is _mezzo-forte to forte_ (the loudest the Adagietto goes — the movement does not have a fortissimo); the harmonic content reaches its peak intensity.

* **7:00–9:00.** **The descent.** The music gradually withdraws — dynamics decrease, tempo settles, melodic line descends.

* **9:00–10:00.** **The closing.** Return to the opening's hushed character. The Adagietto ends on a long sustained F-major chord — _pianissimo_. The harp plays a final pizzicato note. The movement closes.

The Adagietto's structural simplicity is part of its power. Most Mahler movements are _complex_ — long, structurally ambitious, with multiple themes and developmental sections. The Adagietto is _short and simple_ — a single melodic line, an arch shape, no formal complications. This makes it _immediately accessible_ to amateur listeners (it is the most-popular Mahler movement and the entry point for many listeners) and _condensed_ in its emotional content (ten minutes of sustained tenderness without contrast).

The Adagietto is also widely understood as _Alma's love letter from Gustav_ — composed in summer 1902, the same summer Gustav and Alma married. There is no documented evidence that Mahler wrote the Adagietto specifically _as_ a love letter, but Bruno Walter (Mahler's friend and the first major Mahler conductor) wrote in his memoirs that this is what the music was; and Alma herself in her 1940 memoir _Gustav Mahler: Erinnerungen und Briefe_ recounted that Gustav delivered the movement to her _without a note_ and that she understood it to be the love-message it appeared. The biographical reading has shaped how generations have heard the Adagietto.

The Adagietto is also widely heard as _Mahler's elegy to himself_ — composed during a period when he had recovered from a serious illness (a near-fatal hemorrhage in 1901) and was facing mortality more directly than before. The two readings (love letter to Alma / elegy to mortality) are not mutually exclusive; both contribute to the music's emotional weight.

The Adagietto became famous outside the symphonic context after **Luchino Visconti** used it as the central musical theme of his 1971 film _Death in Venice_ (based on Thomas Mann's 1912 novella). The film made the Adagietto pop-culturally famous; from 1971 onward, many amateur listeners encounter the music first through the film. The film also _retrospectively assigned_ a different meaning to the Adagietto — _the dying composer in the Venice cholera epidemic_ — which has competed with the _Alma love letter_ and _Mahler elegy_ readings.

#### Finale of Symphony No. 2 "Resurrection" (Bernstein / NYPO 1987 live, ~33 minutes)

* **0:00–8:00.** **Orchestral interlude.** Long apocalyptic-character opening. Distant trumpet calls (Mahler specifies offstage horns and trumpets, played from outside the concert hall); heavy timpani; full late-Romantic orchestra. The music is _the Last Judgment in symphonic form_ — the trumpet calls are _Wagner-derived_ (echoing Wagner's _Ring_ trumpets) and Berlioz-derived (echoing Berlioz's _Symphonie Fantastique_ trumpets).

* **6:00–7:00 (within the orchestral interlude).** **The _Dies Irae_ allusion.** The medium-low brass writing here — heavy, descending, austere — has been heard by some musicologists as alluding to the _Dies Irae_ contour. The connection is at the level of _expressive territory and melodic shape_ rather than direct quotation: Mahler does not state the chant the way Berlioz does, but the music is unmistakably in the lineage of apocalyptic-funereal writing the chant defined. _This is your third encounter with Thread B from Chapter 16 — at allusion-level rather than quotation-level._

* **8:00–14:00.** **Continued orchestral development.** The apocalyptic material is taken through long developmental passages. The music is _enormously loud at peaks_ and _briefly hushed in transitions_. The orchestra is in its most-active state.

* **14:00–22:00.** **Increased intensity and brief vocal-soloist passages.** The dynamics continue at high levels. The music reaches several climactic peaks. Mahler's _Wachet auf_ (literally "Awaken") motif appears in the orchestra. The vocal soloists (soprano and alto, plus chorus) make brief appearances but are not yet fully introduced.

* **22:00–23:00.** **Sudden pianissimo.** The orchestra drops to _almost-silence_. _This is the moment of transition_.

* **23:00–25:00.** **The choral entrance.** The chorus enters at _pianissimo_ singing _Auferstehen, ja auferstehen wirst du, mein Staub, nach kurzer Ruh!_ — "You shall rise again, yes you shall rise again, my dust, after brief rest!" The chorus's quiet entry — after twenty-two minutes of fortissimo apocalyptic orchestral writing — is one of the most-moving moments in the symphonic literature. The text is Klopstock's _Resurrection Hymn_ (the first two stanzas) plus additional verses by Mahler himself.

* **25:00–28:00.** **Chorus and orchestra develop the _Auferstehen_ theme.** The chorus continues with Klopstock's text; the orchestra builds underneath; the soprano and alto soloists enter briefly.

* **28:00–32:00.** **The build to the final climax.** Chorus, soloists, orchestra build together. Mahler adds _organ_ (often played from a separate organ console at the back of the stage), _additional brass_ (offstage), and _bells_. The dynamic climbs to _fortissimo_ ; the harmonic territory moves toward E♭ major (the symphony's home tonal area for resurrection).

* **32:00–33:00.** **The final cadence.** The chorus, soloists, and orchestra sing the final _Sterben werd ich, um zu leben!_ — "I shall die in order to live!" — on a fortissimo E♭-major chord. _Bells_ ring. The symphony ends in a triumphant _Resurrection_ affirmation.

The Mahler 2 finale is _post-Beethoven 9 choral cosmology_. The Beethoven model is direct — Mahler had conducted Beethoven 9 many times and knew the work intimately. The Mahler extension involves _explicit Christian-and-cosmic theology_ (the _Resurrection_ affirmation, the apocalyptic _Last Judgment_ opening) where Beethoven 9 had been _Enlightenment-universal-brotherhood_. The Mahler 2 finale is also _longer_ (33 minutes versus Beethoven 9's 25 minutes), _larger in forces_ (Mahler's orchestra and chorus are bigger), and _more-elaborate in its dramatic structure_ (Mahler's slow build from apocalyptic loud to choral pianissimo to triumphant final climax is structurally more-complex than Beethoven 9's more-direct buildup).

The Mahler 2 finale's choral entry — the _pianissimo_ statement of the _Auferstehen_ text after twenty-two minutes of orchestral storm — is widely considered one of the _most-affecting structural moments in symphonic music_. The dramatic-temporal logic is: build apocalyptic intensity for twenty minutes, suddenly drop to hushed quiet, and let the chorus emerge from the silence with the message of resurrection. The audience experiences _the music's own resurrection_ in real time.

### 21.3 What's Happening in the Music

#### Definition: The Late-Romantic Symphonic Cosmology

By the late nineteenth century, the symphonic form had become _the medium for philosophical statement_ in a way that no other instrumental genre quite reached. Bach's _Mass in B minor_ and the great choral works were philosophically ambitious; Beethoven 9 had pushed the symphony into philosophical territory; Brahms's symphonies were _abstract structurally serious_. But the late-Romantic generation — Mahler, Bruckner, Sibelius, Strauss, and others — treated the symphony as _a complete philosophical cosmos_. Each symphony attempted _a world_ — a complete worldview embodied in 60–90 minutes of music.

For Mahler specifically: each symphony has a _characteristic theme_. Symphony No. 1 (1888): nature, _Wunderhorn_ folk-poetry imagery, the young composer's emotional life. Symphony No. 2 (1894): death and resurrection (this chapter). Symphony No. 3 (1896): nature, animals, angels, eternal love (the most-pantheist of Mahler's symphonies). Symphony No. 4 (1900): childlike heaven, simplicity. Symphony No. 5 (1902): emotional progression from funeral march to ode-to-joy chorale finale, with the Adagietto as emotional center (this chapter). Symphony No. 6 (1904): "tragic" — Mahler's only major-minor symphony, with three blows of fate. Symphony No. 7 (1905): "Song of the Night" — night, supernatural, Romantic-Gothic imagery. Symphony No. 8 (1906): the "Symphony of a Thousand" — Veni Creator Spiritus hymn and Goethe's _Faust_ Part II final scene. Symphony No. 9 (1909): death-acceptance, late-style. Symphony No. 10 (unfinished 1910): post-Alma-crisis, the conjugal-conflict music.

The Mahler symphonies are _cosmologies_. Each one asks _what is the world?_ and answers in 60–90 minutes of music. This level of philosophical ambition was new — Beethoven 9 had reached toward this scale, but Mahler institutionalized it. Subsequent twentieth-century symphonists (Shostakovich's 15 symphonies, Vaughan Williams's 9 symphonies, Sibelius's 7 symphonies, others) extended what Mahler had developed.

#### Definition: Choral Symphony

A _choral symphony_ is a symphony that includes vocal soloists and chorus in one or more movements. The first major instance is Beethoven 9 (1824, the fourth-movement Ode to Joy choral finale — Chapter 14). The form continued: Mahler 2 (1894, Resurrection finale with full chorus and soprano and alto soloists), Mahler 3 (1896, with alto soloist and women's chorus and boys' chorus), Mahler 4 (1900, soprano soloist only in the final movement), Mahler 8 (1906, full chorus throughout, multiple soloists), Mahler 9 (orchestral only), Symphony No. 14 by Shostakovich (1969, eleven songs for soprano, bass, chamber orchestra), and many others.

The choral symphony is _Beethoven's invention_ ; Mahler is the form's leading nineteenth-century extender; the form's twentieth-century extensions continue. The choral element gives the symphony _direct textual content_ — the music can _say something specific_ through the chorus's words — that purely orchestral symphonies do not have. This _textual specificity_ is one of the choral symphony's powers and one of its costs (the audience must understand the language being sung; the music must _handle_ the text without becoming subordinate to it).

#### Definition: Klopstock's _Auferstehen_ Hymn

The choral text of Mahler 2's finale is _Friedrich Gottlieb Klopstock's hymn "Auferstehen, ja auferstehen"_ (Resurrection, yes resurrection). Klopstock (1724–1803) was a major German poet of the eighteenth century, known for his religious-epic poems (especially _Der Messias_ , 1748–1773, in twenty cantos) and his hymns. His _Auferstehen_ hymn was a standard part of late-eighteenth- and nineteenth-century Protestant Lutheran hymnody — sung at funerals and Easter services across German-speaking Europe.

Mahler heard the hymn at Hans von Bülow's 1894 funeral. (Bülow was the conductor who had premiered _Tristan und Isolde_ — Chapter 19; Mahler had known and respected him as a senior figure in the German musical world.) The hymn moved Mahler deeply at the funeral; he subsequently used the first two stanzas of Klopstock's text _plus his own additional verses_ for the Symphony 2 finale's choral text. The Mahler additions extend Klopstock's _resurrection-after-death_ imagery into _cosmic-mythological territory_ — the additions invoke _the seed dying in the earth_ , _the singer rising again_ , _the dying-to-live paradox_. The composite Klopstock-Mahler text gives the symphony's finale its specific theological content.

#### Common Misconception

People sometimes treat Mahler as _the angst-ridden composer_ — the depressive, the death-obsessed, the philosophically tormented. This is partly true (Mahler did suffer from depression, especially in his last years; his music does engage with death extensively) but it is also partly misleading.

Mahler's music is _also_ full of moments of _joy_ , _celebration_ , _child-like simplicity_ , and _pantheist nature-affirmation_. The Symphony No. 3's third movement (the _animal scherzo_) is one of the most-joyful movements in the symphonic literature. The Symphony No. 4's _Wunderhorn_ finale (the soprano-soloist _Heavenly Life_) is _child-like simplicity at its purest_. The Symphony No. 7's _Nachtmusik_ movements are _Romantic-Gothic atmospheric_ but not _angst-ridden_. The Symphony No. 8's _Veni Creator Spiritus_ and _Faust_ finales are _cosmic celebration_.

The amateur listener who _only_ hears the late symphonies (Nos. 6, 9, _Das Lied von der Erde_) or the _Death in Venice_ Adagietto may form the impression of _Mahler-the-melancholic_. The fuller Mahler is _more emotionally diverse_ than that impression suggests. Listening to Symphony No. 3 (especially the final movement Adagio) or Symphony No. 7 (especially the second-movement Nachtmusik) or Symphony No. 8 (the _Veni Creator_ opening) gives access to the _other Mahler_ — the joyful, the cosmic, the celebratory.

This is the same general principle the book has been arguing — _do not let one piece define your sense of a composer's range_. Mahler is large enough to contain the Adagietto's tenderness, the Resurrection finale's apocalyptic-then-triumphant journey, the Third Symphony's pantheist joy, the Seventh's nocturnal magic, and the Sixth's tragic crisis. The amateur listener who explores at least three or four of Mahler's symphonies starts to understand the breadth.

### 21.4 The Stories

#### Mahler's life

Gustav Mahler was born on 7 July 1860 in Kalischt (then in the Austrian Empire's Bohemian crown lands; now Kaliště in the Czech Republic) to Jewish parents. The family was middle-class — his father was a small-businessman who ran a tavern and brewery — but the cultural context was _complicated_ : the family was Jewish in a Catholic-majority German-speaking region of a Slavic-speaking countryside. Mahler grew up speaking German at home, hearing Czech in the streets, learning Hebrew at synagogue, and reading Goethe and Schiller at school. The triple-identity (German-cultured, Jewish-religious, Czech-Slavic-environmental) marked him for life — _I am thrice homeless: as a native of Bohemia in Austria, as an Austrian among Germans, and as a Jew throughout the world_ , he reportedly told a friend.

He showed musical talent young. At age 15 he was sent to the Vienna Conservatory; he studied composition under Anton Bruckner (the major Austrian symphonist) among others. He graduated in 1878 and began the conducting career that would define his professional life — small opera houses in Bad Hall (1880), Olomouc (1881), Kassel (1883), Prague (1885), Leipzig (1886), Budapest (1888), Hamburg (1891), and finally Vienna (1897).

The 1897 Vienna appointment as Director of the Court Opera was the most-prestigious operatic position in Europe. Vienna was the operatic capital of the German-speaking world; the Court Opera was its leading institution. Mahler held the position from 1897 to 1907 — a ten-year tenure that transformed the Vienna Court Opera into one of the world's leading operatic institutions and made Mahler one of the most-famous conductors of the era.

To take the Vienna Court Opera position, Mahler had to _convert to Catholicism_ (1897). Austrian law required all senior court positions to be held by Catholics. The conversion was a _career necessity_ rather than a _religious change_ ; Mahler reportedly maintained his Jewish identity privately while satisfying the formal Catholic requirement. The conversion is part of the difficult biography — a Jewish composer in the increasingly anti-Semitic late-nineteenth-century Austrian Empire, navigating _what he had to do_ to advance his career.

He composed only in summers. Each year, after the Vienna Court Opera season ended (typically in June), he would travel to a summer estate — first Steinbach on the Attersee (1893–1896), then Maiernigg on the Wörthersee (1899–1907), then Toblach in the Dolomites (1908–1910) — and compose for two or three months in small composing-huts he built specifically for the purpose. The huts (which still stand today, preserved as cultural sites) were _deliberately isolated_ — set in the woods, away from family, away from the household. Mahler would work eight or ten hours a day in the hut, composing through the morning into the afternoon. The annual summer composition produced the nine symphonies (Nos. 1–9), the song cycles, and the late works.

In 1902 he married **Alma Schindler** (1879–1964), a 22-year-old Viennese-Jewish-Catholic woman of considerable beauty, intelligence, and musical talent. Alma was 19 years younger than Mahler. She had been composing songs and was studying composition with Alexander Zemlinsky (who would later become Schoenberg's brother-in-law and one of the leading composers of the next generation). Mahler — by all reports including Alma's own — required her to give up her composing career as a condition of marriage. He believed the household could contain only one composer; he was that composer; Alma was to be his support.

The marriage produced two daughters: Maria (Putzi, 1902–1907, who died of scarlet fever at age 4) and Anna (Gucki, 1904–1988, who became a sculptor). Maria's death was _devastating_ for both parents and especially for Mahler, whose Symphony No. 6 (which had included three _blows of fate_ in the finale, completed in 1904) was now read as having _predicted_ the death (Mahler had reportedly told friends after Maria's death that he should have known better than to invite fate by writing such music).

The 1907 Vienna Court Opera resignation came after years of conflict with the Vienna press and aristocracy. Anti-Semitic and conservative-musical critics had attacked Mahler throughout his tenure. He resigned in 1907 and almost immediately accepted positions in New York — at the Metropolitan Opera (1907–1908) and at the New York Philharmonic (1909–1911). The American positions were less politically fraught but were exhausting (the Met had a punishing performance schedule; the Philharmonic required extensive concert tours).

In 1910, Alma's affair with Walter Gropius was discovered. The Freud consultation (described in the chapter opening) was that summer. Mahler's health declined rapidly. He returned to Vienna in February 1911 and died of bacterial endocarditis on 18 May 1911, age 50.

Alma outlived Gustav by 53 years. She subsequently married Walter Gropius (1915, divorced 1920) and the writer Franz Werfel (1929, with whom she lived until his death in 1945). She wrote two memoirs about Mahler (_Erinnerungen und Briefe_ , 1940; _Mein Leben_ , 1960) that are partial — both selective and self-serving in places — but are also irreplaceable as sources for what Mahler said and did in his personal life. Alma is one of the most-dramatic personalities of the early twentieth-century musical world; her _post-Mahler_ career as patron, lover, and cultural-figure has been the subject of multiple biographies.

#### The Mahler-conductor tradition

Mahler's symphonies entered the standard repertoire _gradually_ across the twentieth century. In his lifetime he conducted his own works in major venues, but they were not yet _standard repertoire_ ; many critics and audiences found them too long, too complex, too philosophically ambitious. The Mahler symphonies were heard _occasionally_ in the 1910s and 1920s — Bruno Walter (Mahler's former assistant) and Willem Mengelberg (Concertgebouw, Amsterdam) were major Mahler conductors before World War II, but they were the exceptions.

The _Mahler revival_ of the 1960s and 1970s changed this. **Leonard Bernstein** (New York Philharmonic, 1958–1969 as Music Director) was the central figure in the revival — he conducted all nine Mahler symphonies, recorded them twice with the New York Philharmonic, and made the case publicly through his television appearances that Mahler was _the great twentieth-century symphonist who had been overlooked_. By 1970 Mahler had become standard repertoire; by 2000 he was one of the most-performed symphonists in the orchestral repertoire.

Bernstein's championship is part of why he is _the_ Mahler conductor in the recording era. The 1987 Vienna Philharmonic Mahler 5 and the 1987 New York Philharmonic Mahler 2 (both live recordings made in his late career) are _the recommended primary readings_ for this chapter — they capture Bernstein at his fullest Mahlerian commitment.

Other major Mahler conductors of the recording era: **Otto Klemperer** (Philharmonia Orchestra, 1950s-1960s — austere, monumental); **Bruno Walter** (Vienna and New York, mid-century — the _Mahler pupil_ tradition); **Claudio Abbado** (Berlin Philharmonic and Lucerne Festival Orchestra, 1990s-2010s — refined, structurally precise); **Bernard Haitink** (Concertgebouw and Berlin, late twentieth century — lyrical, controlled); **Pierre Boulez** (Cleveland and other orchestras, 1990s-2000s — analytic, _cool_).

The Mahler conducting tradition is one of the great recorded-music inheritances of the twentieth century. Each major conductor brings a _different sound_ to Mahler; the _work-vs-interpretation muscle_ at the largest scale.

#### Recordings

**Leonard Bernstein / Vienna Philharmonic, 1987 (Deutsche Grammophon)** for the Mahler 5 Adagietto. Bernstein's _late_ Mahler — recorded near the end of his career, with the Vienna Philharmonic (which Mahler himself had conducted as opera director). The Adagietto runs about 11 minutes — _slower than younger Bernstein readings_ , with extreme expressive weight. Some find it the most-moving Adagietto on record; others find Bernstein's tempo too slow.

**Herbert von Karajan / Berlin Philharmonic, 1973 (Deutsche Grammophon)** for Mahler 5. Karajan's only complete Mahler 5 recording, made when he was beginning to take Mahler seriously. The Adagietto is taken at _more moderate_ tempo than Bernstein's late reading.

**Claudio Abbado / Berlin Philharmonic, 1993 (Deutsche Grammophon)** for Mahler 5. The contemporary refined reading — _structurally clear, with extensive attention to inner-voice details_.

**Leonard Bernstein / New York Philharmonic, 1987 live at Avery Fisher Hall (Deutsche Grammophon)** for Mahler 2. The live recording made in 1987 with the New York Philharmonic — _one of the great live Mahler recordings_. The audience's reaction at the close of the Resurrection finale is audible on the recording; the emotional intensity is at full Bernstein-Mahler level.

**Otto Klemperer / Philharmonia Orchestra, 1962 (EMI)** for Mahler 2. The austere monumental reading. _Slower, more deliberate_ , with the Philharmonia Orchestra of the early 1960s at its peak. The Klemperer Mahler 2 is one of the standard _alternative_ readings to the Bernstein.

**Claudio Abbado / Lucerne Festival Orchestra, 2003 (Euroarts DVD / DG)** for Mahler 2. A late Abbado reading, recorded at the Lucerne Festival where Abbado had founded the festival orchestra of leading European musicians. The reading is _radiant, structurally precise, with extraordinary chorus_.

#### Cross-piece links

* For **other Mahler symphonies** , listen to **Symphony No. 1** (the entry-level Mahler — accessible, shorter at ~55 minutes), **Symphony No. 4** (with the heavenly-life soprano finale), **Symphony No. 9** (the slow-ending late-style symphony in dialogue with Tchaikovsky's Pathétique — Chapter 20), and **Das Lied von der Erde** (the song-symphony composed 1908–1909).
* For **Mahler song cycles** , listen to **Lieder eines fahrenden Gesellen** (1885, his first major cycle) and **Kindertotenlieder** (1904, the _Songs on the Death of Children_ , completed before Maria's actual death in 1907).
* For the **post-Mahler symphonic tradition** , listen to **Shostakovich Symphonies Nos. 5, 8, 13, and 14** (Chapter 24 covers Shostakovich's Fifth), **Britten Symphonies and the Spring Symphony** , **Sibelius Symphonies Nos. 5, 6, and 7** , **Vaughan Williams symphonies**. All are in some dialogue with Mahler's symphonic-cosmological project.
* For **Schoenberg's response to Mahler** , listen to **Verklärte Nacht** (1899) and **Pelleas und Melisande** (1903) — Schoenberg's early post-Wagnerian-post-Mahlerian works.
* For **the Mahler-Alma story in music** , listen to **Alma Mahler's surviving songs** — small but real compositions by Alma from the early 1900s, before her marriage to Gustav. Alma's compositional output was substantial in her teens and early twenties; after the marriage Gustav forbade her to compose; some of her early songs survive and have been recorded.

#### Conversation Seeds

* _Ask the companion about the _Dies Irae_ allusion in the Mahler 2 finale's opening orchestral interlude (around 6:00). The connection is debated — some musicologists hear it clearly; others read the brass writing as Mahler's own original Last-Judgment material. What is the case for each reading?_
* _Ask the companion about the Mahler-Alma marriage — Gustav's requirement that Alma give up composing, Alma's affair with Gropius in 1910, the Freud consultation. What is the cost of the marriage to Alma's own work, and how do we hold this alongside Mahler's musical achievement?_
* _Tell the companion which moment in the Resurrection finale moved you most — the apocalyptic orchestral interlude (with its possible _Dies Irae_ allusions), the choral _pianissimo_ entry at 23:00, or the final fortissimo cadence — and ask her about the structural design that makes each moment work._
* _Ask the companion about Bernstein as Mahler conductor — his championing of Mahler in the 1960s and 1970s, his television advocacy, why he was so committed to this composer specifically, and what the relationship between Bernstein and Mahler reveals about how composers find their conductors._
* _Bring up Mahler 3 (the alto-solo _O Mensch_ fourth movement) or Mahler 4 (the soprano-soloist _Heavenly Life_ finale) with the companion as an antidote — a reminder that Mahler is not only angst, that the _other Mahler_ is full of joy, simplicity, and cosmic affirmation._

### 21.5 Exercises

#### Concept Check

**Q1.** What is unusual about the **scoring** of the Mahler 5 Adagietto?

**Answer:** The Adagietto is scored for _strings alone with harp_ — no woodwinds, no brass, no percussion. In a symphony that elsewhere uses full late-Romantic orchestra (roughly 90–100 players), the Adagietto's stripped-down chamber scoring (about 30 string players plus one harp) is a _deliberate contrast_. The texture is the _softest and most intimate_ in the symphony. This is part of what makes the Adagietto _immediately recognizable_ and what gives it its specifically _chamber-vocal_ character.

**Q2.** What is **Klopstock's _Auferstehen_ hymn**, and how did it come into the Mahler 2 finale?

**Answer:** Friedrich Klopstock (1724–1803) was an eighteenth-century German poet who wrote religious-epic poems and hymns; his _Auferstehen, ja auferstehen_ (Resurrection, yes resurrection) was a standard Protestant Lutheran hymn used at funerals and Easter services. Mahler heard the hymn at Hans von Bülow's 1894 funeral; it moved him deeply; he subsequently used the first two stanzas of Klopstock's text _plus his own additional verses_ as the choral text for the Symphony 2 finale. The Mahler additions extend Klopstock's resurrection-after-death imagery into cosmic-mythological territory. The composite Klopstock-Mahler text gives the symphony's finale its specific theological content.

### Chapter Summary

This chapter introduced **Mahler** through two movements from two symphonies: the **Adagietto from Symphony No. 5** (1902, ~10 minutes, scored for strings and harp alone) and the **finale of Symphony No. 2 "Resurrection"** (1894, ~33 minutes, with full chorus, soprano and alto soloists, organ, additional offstage brass, bells).

You learned the **late-Romantic symphonic cosmology** (each Mahler symphony as a complete philosophical world), the **choral symphony** as a Beethoven-9-extended form, and **Klopstock's _Auferstehen_ hymn** as the source for the Mahler 2 finale's choral text.

You met **Thread B for the third time** — at allusion-level rather than direct-quotation level. The Mahler 2 finale's apocalyptic orchestral interlude does not state the _Dies Irae_ chant the way Berlioz does in Chapter 16, but its brass writing is in the chant's expressive lineage; some musicologists hear specific _Dies Irae_ shapes in the music, others read it as Mahler's own original Last-Judgment material. The thread continues across the book.

You met **Mahler** in his single chapter — born 1860 in Bohemia to Jewish parents, the _thrice-homeless_ identity (Bohemian-in-Austria, Austrian-among-Germans, Jew-throughout-the-world), studies at Vienna Conservatory, twenty-year conducting career through small opera houses to the Vienna Court Opera (1897–1907), the conversion to Catholicism required for the appointment, the summer composing-hut tradition, the 1902 marriage to Alma Schindler, the 1907 daughter Maria's death from scarlet fever, the 1907 Vienna resignation, the American positions (Metropolitan Opera, New York Philharmonic), the 1910 Alma-Gropius crisis and Freud consultation, the death from bacterial endocarditis at age 50 in May 1911.

You met the **Mahler-Alma marriage controversy** — Gustav's requirement that Alma give up composing, the cost to Alma's creative life, the larger pattern of major male composers in cultures that suppressed women's work. The book holds this honestly.

You met **the Mahler-conductor tradition** — Bruno Walter's pioneering Mahler conducting in the 1910s-1940s; the post-1960 Mahler revival led especially by Leonard Bernstein; the contemporary Mahler tradition under Abbado, Boulez, Haitink, Rattle, Salonen. The Bernstein 1987 readings (VPO Mahler 5; NYPO live Mahler 2) are the chapter's primary readings.

The next chapter takes you to **Debussy's _La Mer_ and Lili Boulanger's _Du fond de l'abîme_** — the French answer to Mahler's Germanic symphonic weight. Impressionism, color as primary material, French independence from German harmonic tradition. Lili Boulanger as gravitational center of early French modernism alongside Debussy — not as a sidebar.

## Chapter 22: Debussy, _La Mer_ — and Lili Boulanger, _Du fond de l'abîme_

Two French composers, born in different decades. Claude Debussy (1862–1918) is the older — born in Saint-Germain-en-Laye outside Paris, trained at the Paris Conservatoire from age 10, winner of the Prix de Rome in 1884, the leading figure of _what was sometimes called_ Impressionism in music (a label Debussy himself disliked). Lili Boulanger (1893–1918) is the younger — born in Paris, sister of the great composition teacher Nadia Boulanger, the _first woman_ to win the Prix de Rome (1913), and dead at age 24 of intestinal tuberculosis just five weeks before Debussy himself died of cancer. The two composers shared a Paris musical world from Lili's teenage years until both their deaths in spring 1918; they likely encountered each other personally at concerts and Conservatoire events.

This chapter places the two composers _side by side_ as the **gravitational centers of early French modernism**. Debussy is the major canonical figure; Lili Boulanger has been _recovered_ in the past forty years from her undeserved near-erasure (the recovery is part of the larger canonical-recovery work the book has been tracing — Clara Schumann in Chapter 18, Florence Price in Chapter 25 coming, Saariaho and Shaw in Chapter 26 coming). The chapter does not put Boulanger in a _sidebar_ to Debussy; it treats both as composers of their period.

We focus on the **second movement of Debussy's _La Mer_** (1905, "Jeux de vagues" — Play of the Waves, ~7 min) and on **Lili Boulanger's _Du fond de l'abîme_** (Psalm 130 setting, 1917, ~25 min).

### 22.1 Before You Listen

#### Hook anecdote — the _Impressionist_ label

Debussy disliked the _Impressionist_ label that critics applied to his music from the 1880s onward. The label borrowed from the visual-arts movement (Monet, Renoir, Degas, the 1874 Paris exhibition that gave Impressionism its name) and applied it to Debussy's music on the analogy that _Debussy paints with sound the way Monet paints with light_. The analogy is suggestive but partial. Debussy himself reportedly told one critic: _I am trying to do something different — something more like the Symbolists than the Impressionists_. He was thinking of poets like Mallarmé, Verlaine, and Maeterlinck rather than of painters.

The substantive distinction: _Impressionism_ in painting was concerned with _the optical effect of light_ — capturing how light actually strikes the eye. _Symbolism_ in poetry was concerned with _evoking states of mind_ — using verbal images to suggest moods, atmospheres, dreams. Debussy's music is closer to _Symbolism_ than to _Impressionism_ — he is interested in _atmospheric evocation_ more than in _optical accuracy_. The _Prélude à l'après-midi d'un faune_ (1894) is _Symbolist_ (it sets a Mallarmé poem about a faun's afternoon reverie); _La Mer_ (1905) is _Symbolist_ (it evokes the sea's _moods_ rather than depicting waves _literally_); _Pelléas et Mélisande_ (1902) is _Symbolist_ (it sets a Maeterlinck play).

Despite Debussy's resistance, the _Impressionist_ label has stuck. By the early twentieth century _musical Impressionism_ was an established critical category that included Debussy, Ravel (Chapter 23), and others. The label has _partly accurate_ dimensions (the music's evocation of atmosphere, color, mood; the music's use of whole-tone scales and pentatonic colors that give it a _visually-suggestive_ quality) and _partly misleading_ dimensions (the music's Symbolist literary affiliations; the music's structural sophistication that exceeds _optical-impression_ paraphrase). The mature listener can use the label _with awareness of its limits_.

#### What to notice

For **Debussy's _La Mer_ , second movement "Jeux de vagues"** (~7 minutes):

  1. **The _color-based_ orchestration.** Debussy uses the orchestra as a _paint palette_ — different instrumental colors are juxtaposed for _sonic effect_. Listen for: a _celesta_ or _harp_ providing shimmering high-register sound; _flutes_ and _clarinets_ in fluttering figures; _muted strings_ providing harmonic backgrounds; _gentle horn_ calls; _brushed percussion_. The orchestral texture is _highly differentiated_ — each instrumental color is distinct.

  2. **The lack of clear melody.** Most Western symphonic music has _clearly identifiable melodic lines_. _Jeux de vagues_ is _almost melodically continuous_ — short fragments of melody emerge from the texture, develop briefly, fade back. There is no single _tune_ to follow across the movement; instead, the listener follows _the play of colors and short melodic gestures_. This is one of Debussy's signature techniques — _texture-as-content_ rather than melody-as-content.

  3. **The whole-tone scale.** Debussy uses _whole-tone scales_ — scales built entirely on whole-step intervals, with no half-steps. The whole-tone scale gives the music a _floating, unsettled_ quality (because the scale has no clear _tonic_ — no single note feels like the home note). Listen for passages where the music seems to _float_ without obvious harmonic direction; those are likely whole-tone passages.

  4. **The flexible meter.** Debussy frequently changes meter (3/8 to 6/8 to 9/8 to 2/4, sometimes within a single page). The meter changes give the music _fluid rhythmic motion_ — there is no strict pulse the listener can lock onto. _Jeux de vagues_ is in constant rhythmic motion that suggests _the irregular play of waves_.

For **Lili Boulanger's _Du fond de l'abîme_** (~25 minutes):

This is a _substantial choral-orchestral work_ — a setting of Psalm 130 (_De profundis_ — "Out of the depths") for full chorus, soprano and tenor soloists, organ, and large orchestra. The work runs about 25 minutes in three sections.

  1. **The opening descent.** The work opens with a _slow, low-register_ orchestral introduction — _deep bass-register_ writing in the strings and low brass. The texture is _dark, weighted, descending_. The text _De profundis_ (Out of the depths) is being prepared.

  2. **The chorus's first entry.** The chorus enters with the Latin-Hebrew text _Du fond de l'abîme_ (translated French version of _De profundis_). The choral writing is _full-textured_ — eight voice parts in places, with elaborate counterpoint.

  3. **The middle section's intensification.** As the psalm text moves through its expressions of longing, despair, and eventual hope, Boulanger's music builds in intensity. The orchestral writing is _post-Wagnerian, post-Debussian_ — chromatic, modal, with characteristic French color.

  4. **The final section's restraint.** The work closes with a _restrained, almost-resigned_ setting of the psalm's closing verses (about Israel's hope in the Lord). The music does _not_ end in triumph; it ends in a kind of _quiet acceptance_.

#### One-sentence backgrounds

**Debussy,_La Mer_ , three symphonic sketches** — composed 1903–1905 in various locations (Burgundy, Eastbourne in England); premiered 15 October 1905 in Paris, conducted by Camille Chevillard; ~25 minutes in three movements (De l'aube à midi sur la mer — Jeux de vagues — Dialogue du vent et de la mer). The second movement Jeux de vagues runs ~7 minutes.

**Lili Boulanger,_Du fond de l'abîme_** — setting of Psalm 130 for chorus, soprano and tenor soloists, organ, and orchestra; composed 1914–1917 in Paris and at the Boulanger summer estate at Gargenville; not performed in Boulanger's lifetime; premiered posthumously 17 March 1923 in Paris; ~25 minutes.

### 22.2 The Listening Window

#### Debussy, _La Mer_ Second Movement "Jeux de vagues" (Boulez / Cleveland, ~7 minutes)

* **0:00–0:30.** **Opening.** Flutes and harp play hushed, shimmering figures. Muted strings provide gentle harmonic support. The texture is _atmospheric_ — no clear melody yet, no clear pulse.

* **0:30–1:30.** **Brief melodic gestures emerge.** Short melodic fragments (4-6 notes) appear in the flutes, oboes, then violins. The fragments are passed between instruments — _played, then dropped, then picked up by another voice_. The wave-like motion is built into the orchestration.

* **1:30–2:30.** **First climactic gesture.** A brief fortissimo passage from the full orchestra. _Not a climax in the traditional sense_ — not a structural moment that has been built toward. More like _a wave reaching its peak before breaking_.

* **2:30–4:00.** **Continued development.** The texture continues to shift; instrumental colors are juxtaposed; the meter changes frequently; the music _moves like water_.

* **4:00–5:30.** **A larger build.** The orchestra is gradually fuller; the brass enters more prominently; the dynamics climb. This is _the movement's structural climax_ , but it is _not_ the kind of climax Beethoven or Mahler would write — it is _a wave that breaks more substantially than the smaller waves_.

* **5:30–6:30.** **Withdrawal.** The texture thins; dynamics decrease; the orchestration returns to the gentler colors of the opening.

* **6:30–7:00.** **Final settling.** The music quiets to a hushed close. The movement does not end with a definitive cadence; it _settles_ into a final shimmer that fades.

The movement's structural principle: _the play of waves_. There is no traditional sonata form, no theme-and-variations, no rondo. The music _plays with itself_ the way waves play with the shore — building, breaking, withdrawing, building again, all in irregular rhythms and at irregular dynamics. The structure is _aleatoric-seeming_ even though every note is composed; the _effect_ is one of _natural-seeming non-pattern_. This is one of Debussy's central techniques — _the music sounds spontaneous_ because Debussy has _carefully designed_ it to sound that way.

#### Lili Boulanger, _Du fond de l'abîme_ (Markevitch / Lamoureux, ~25 minutes)

This work is more _symphonic-choral_ in scale than _Jeux de vagues_ is _orchestral-color_. The two works represent different French modernist sensibilities — Debussy the _Symbolist atmospheric_ , Boulanger the _neo-tonal sacred-monumental_.

* **0:00–3:00.** **Orchestral introduction.** Slow, low-register strings and brass play descending phrases. The music establishes a _dark, weighted_ atmosphere. Lili's harmonic language is _post-Wagnerian chromatic_ with _French modal colors_ — the orchestration is full but the texture remains heavy.

* **3:00–6:00.** **First chorus entry.** The chorus enters with the Latin text _De profundis clamavi ad te, Domine_ (Out of the depths I have cried to thee, O Lord). The choral writing is _eight-voice_ with elaborate counterpoint. The Latin text is from Psalm 130 (the _De profundis_), one of the _Penitential Psalms_ and a standard sacred text for choral settings.

* **6:00–11:00.** **First development.** The choral text continues through the opening verses of the psalm. The orchestral writing supports the chorus with rich textures; soloists begin to emerge briefly.

* **11:00–15:00.** **The middle section.** A _more lyrical_ second main subject is introduced. The chorus and orchestra develop this material; the music's emotional content shifts from initial despair to _yearning_.

* **15:00–19:00.** **Soprano-tenor duet.** The two vocal soloists sing duet passages with the chorus and orchestra; the texture is _operatic-symphonic_. The text moves through the psalm's expressions of _hope for the Lord_.

* **19:00–22:00.** **The climactic section.** Full chorus, soloists, orchestra at maximum intensity. The dynamics climb to fortissimo; the harmonic territory is _post-Wagnerian extended chromatic tonality_. The setting reaches its _emotional peak_.

* **22:00–25:00.** **The final restrained close.** The music settles to a _restrained, almost-resigned_ closing. The work does _not_ end in triumphant _Resurrection-affirmation_ (compare Mahler 2 in Chapter 21); it ends in _quiet acceptance_. The psalm's final verse — _Et ipse redimet Israel ex omnibus iniquitatibus eius_ (And he shall redeem Israel from all his iniquities) — is set _gently_ , without the triumphal cadences that Mahler or Verdi might have given it.

The Boulanger setting is _substantially different_ from a Verdi Requiem's _operatic-theatrical_ setting or a Mahler 2 Resurrection finale's _post-Beethoven 9 triumphalism_. The French sacred-choral tradition (Fauré Requiem, Duruflé Requiem) has _historically been more-restrained_ than the Italian or Germanic-Austrian traditions. Boulanger's Du fond de l'abîme sits squarely in this French tradition — _honest about the depths_ , _restrained in the consolation_ , _without the triumphalist closing_.

### 22.3 What's Happening in the Music

#### Definition: Impressionism / Symbolism in Music

**Impressionism** (the visual-arts movement of the 1860s and 1870s) and **Symbolism** (the literary movement especially in late-nineteenth-century French poetry) are the two terms most-applied to Debussy's music. The terms have different connotations:

* _Impressionism_ : capturing the optical-visual effect of light, the moment-by-moment perception of reality, the spontaneous-seeming sketch quality. Applied to Debussy because _the music seems to paint with sound_ — orchestral colors are juxtaposed to evoke specific atmospheres (sea, gardens, fauns, moonlight).

* _Symbolism_ : evoking states of mind through verbal images, suggesting moods and dreams rather than depicting external reality directly. Applied to Debussy because _the music shares aesthetic affinities with Symbolist poetry_ — Mallarmé's _L'Après-midi d'un faune_ (1876, set by Debussy in 1894), Maeterlinck's _Pelléas et Mélisande_ (1893, set by Debussy 1902), the Verlaine song-settings.

Debussy himself preferred _Symbolism_. The label _Impressionist_ has nonetheless stuck. The two terms point at _different aspects of the same compositional practice_ — the orchestral-color-as-atmosphere is _Impressionist_ , the philosophical-evocative-mood is _Symbolist_. Both are accurate; both are partial.

#### Definition: Whole-Tone Scale

A _whole-tone scale_ is a scale built entirely on whole-step intervals — no half-steps. Starting from C: C-D-E-F♯-G♯-A♯-C. The scale has six notes (rather than the seven notes of a major or minor scale).

The whole-tone scale has two distinctive properties:

* **No clear tonic.** Because all the intervals are the same size (whole steps), no note in the scale _feels_ like the home note. The scale is _non-functional_ — it does not produce the _tonic-dominant_ relationships that give Western tonal music its sense of direction.
* **A _floating_ quality.** Listeners describe whole-tone-scale passages as _unsettled, dreamlike, suspended_. The lack of clear tonic produces a _placeless_ feeling that is part of why composers (Debussy, Ravel, occasionally others) used the scale for _atmospheric_ effects.

Debussy's _Voiles_ (the second prelude from Book I of his _Preludes_ , 1909–1910) is almost entirely in whole-tone scales — a piano piece that demonstrates the technique at its purest. Many of Debussy's larger works (including _La Mer_ and the _Préludes_) use whole-tone passages alongside other materials. The whole-tone scale is not the only Debussy modal-coloristic technique — he also uses the _pentatonic_ scale (five-note scale, like the Dvořák Largo melody in Chapter 5), _octatonic_ scales (8-note alternating whole-and-half-step scales), and _modal_ writing (medieval modes — Chapter 14's Lydian mode in Beethoven's Heiliger Dankgesang; Debussy also uses Phrygian, Dorian, and others).

#### Definition: The French Modernist Tradition

The _French modernist tradition_ — Debussy, Ravel, Lili Boulanger, Fauré (late works), and the generation that followed (Honegger, Milhaud, Poulenc, Roussel, Messiaen, and Boulez) — represents _a substantial alternative_ to the Germanic-Austrian symphonic tradition of Wagner, Brahms, Bruckner, and Mahler.

Distinctive features of the French modernist tradition:

* **Color and texture as primary content** (rather than melody and motivic development).
* **Modal and pentatonic harmonic language** (rather than the Germanic chromatic tonality of Wagner and beyond).
* **Restraint in expressive register** (rather than the _cosmological-philosophical_ ambition of Mahler).
* **Connection to French literary culture** (Symbolism, Surrealism, Existentialism) more than to Germanic philosophical traditions.
* **Orchestration as compositional foreground** — French composers are widely considered the most-sophisticated orchestrators of the modernist era; Debussy's orchestral writing in _La Mer_ is one of the high points.

The French tradition has been _partially overshadowed_ by the Germanic-Austrian symphonic tradition in twentieth-century musicology. The book has emphasized this throughout — French composers (Berlioz in Chapter 16, Chopin as Paris-resident in Chapter 17, Fauré in Chapter 2, Debussy and Boulanger here) are part of the canon, not sidebars to it. The French tradition has _different aesthetic priorities_ than the Germanic, and listeners who explore the French tradition encounter musical possibilities that the Germanic tradition does not develop.

#### Common Misconception

People sometimes treat _Lili Boulanger_ as _only Nadia Boulanger's younger sister who died young_. This reading erases what Lili did as a composer.

Lili Boulanger (1893–1918) won the _Prix de Rome_ in 1913 — the major French composition prize, awarded annually to a young composer who had not previously won. She was the _first woman_ to win the prize. She had been the favorite for several years (her teachers at the Conservatoire considered her exceptional; her examination compositions had been notable); the 1913 win was _significant for women's place in French music_ and was widely reported.

Lili's output includes _Du fond de l'abîme_ (1914–1917, the chapter's anchor), the larger _Faust et Hélène_ cantata (1913, her Prix de Rome winning composition), the song cycle _Clairières dans le ciel_ (1913–1914), _Vieille prière bouddhique_ (1914–1917), the _Psaume 24_ (1916), and many shorter works. She composed continuously from age 16 until her death at 24 from intestinal tuberculosis — a _brief but substantial_ compositional career.

Her sister **Nadia Boulanger** (1887–1979) was a major _composition teacher_ who taught most of the leading twentieth-century American composers (Aaron Copland — Chapter 25; Roy Harris; Walter Piston; Virgil Thomson; Elliott Carter; David Diamond; and many others). Nadia's influence on American music was enormous. Nadia herself stopped composing in 1922 in favor of teaching; she dedicated her career to teaching others. The two sisters' careers were _intertwined_ — Lili the composer-who-died-young, Nadia the teacher-who-shaped-a-generation.

The recovery of Lili's compositional output has been a major project of the past forty years. Her works are now performed regularly in concert and recording. The chapter places her _as a composer of her period_ — not as a sidebar to Debussy, not as a footnote to her sister, but as _a substantial French modernist whose career was cut short_. The work-vs-interpretation muscle, applied to Boulanger, will continue to develop as more recordings are made.

### 22.4 The Stories

#### Debussy's life

Claude-Achille Debussy was born on 22 August 1862 in Saint-Germain-en-Laye, a suburb west of Paris, the eldest of five children of a _small shop owner_ and a _seamstress_. The family was _not_ prosperous; they moved to Paris when Debussy was a young child; he showed musical talent early.

At age 10 he was admitted to the Paris Conservatoire — a remarkable accomplishment for a child from his class background. He studied piano, composition, and music theory. He won several prizes; he was _not_ a model student (he was famously difficult and impatient with conventional pedagogy); but his talent was recognized.

In 1880 (age 18) he was offered a position as _household musician_ to Nadezhda von Meck — the same wealthy Russian widow who had been corresponding with Tchaikovsky (Chapter 20) since 1877. Debussy spent the summers of 1880, 1881, and 1882 traveling with the Meck household (Italy, Russia, Vienna). The experience exposed him to Russian music (he absorbed Mussorgsky, Borodin, Tchaikovsky) and to international musical worlds.

In 1884 he won the _Prix de Rome_ , which sent him to the Villa Medici in Rome for two years (1885–1887) to compose. He found Rome stifling and returned to Paris before his time was complete.

The 1880s and early 1890s were Debussy's _formative period_. He absorbed Wagner (he made _two_ Bayreuth pilgrimages in 1888 and 1889 and was initially overwhelmed by Wagner's harmonic language); he absorbed Russian music; he absorbed Eastern music (he attended the 1889 Paris World Exposition and heard _Javanese gamelan_ and other non-Western musics; the experience permanently shaped his harmonic and rhythmic thinking); he absorbed Symbolist poetry (his friend Pierre Louÿs introduced him to the Symbolist circle).

The breakthrough came with the _Prélude à l'après-midi d'un faune_ (1894) — a tone poem on Mallarmé's poem. The Prélude is widely considered the _first major work of musical modernism_. The harmonic language, the orchestration, the structural approach — all are _new_ in ways that subsequent composers would build on.

_La Mer_ (1903–1905) extended what _Faune_ had begun, at larger scale. The work was _controversial at its 1905 premiere_ — critics divided about whether it was a _masterpiece_ or a _failure_. Within a generation it was canonical.

The opera _Pelléas et Mélisande_ (1902, on Maeterlinck's 1893 Symbolist play) was Debussy's other major dramatic work — a complete late-Romantic-modernist opera that has remained in the standard repertoire.

In 1909 Debussy was diagnosed with rectal cancer. He underwent surgeries; he continued composing through declining health; he died in Paris on 25 March 1918, age 55, during the German bombardment of Paris in the final months of World War I.

#### Lili Boulanger's life

Marie-Juliette Olga "Lili" Boulanger was born on 21 August 1893 in Paris, the younger of two daughters of Ernest Boulanger (a composer, professor at the Paris Conservatoire) and Raïssa Mychetska (a Russian-born singer). The family was deeply musical — Ernest had been a Prix-de-Rome winner himself in 1835; the household was a meeting place for Paris musicians.

Lili was a _sickly child_. At age two she contracted _bronchial pneumonia_ and was thereafter prone to _recurring respiratory and intestinal infections_. Her health was _fragile throughout her life_ ; she was frequently confined to bed; her compositional life was _constantly interrupted by illness_.

Despite the illness, she showed extraordinary musical talent. By age 4 she was reading music. By age 5 she was studying composition. At age 16 she enrolled at the Paris Conservatoire (initially as a sight-reading student; she added composition study within a year). Her teachers included Gabriel Fauré, Charles-Marie Widor, and Paul Vidal.

In 1913, age 20, she won the _Prix de Rome_ — the major French composition prize — for her cantata _Faust et Hélène_. She was _the first woman_ in the prize's 110-year history to win it. The win was reported across Europe; it was a _substantial moment for women in French music_.

The Villa Medici residency (Rome, 1914–1916) was complicated by World War I — Lili spent only a few months actually in Rome before returning to France in 1914 when war broke out. She continued composing from her family's Paris home and the Boulanger summer estate at Gargenville.

The major works of her final five years (1913–1918) include _Du fond de l'abîme_ (Psalm 130 setting, 1914–1917 — the chapter anchor), _Vieille prière bouddhique_ (a setting of an old Buddhist prayer, 1914–1917), _Psaume 24_ (1916), the _Soir sur la plaine_ (1916), several song cycles, and many shorter works. She also worked on an opera _La princesse Maleine_ (after Maeterlinck) that she did not live to complete.

Her health declined steadily through 1916 and 1917. By late 1917 she was bedridden; she dictated music to her sister Nadia from her bed. She died on 15 March 1918, age 24, of _intestinal tuberculosis_. Debussy died five weeks later, on 25 March 1918, age 55, of cancer. The deaths of the two major French composers within six weeks marked a _generational shift_ in French music.

#### Nadia Boulanger and Lili's recovery

Nadia Boulanger (1887–1979) was six years older than Lili. She had been _the candidate_ for the Prix de Rome before Lili — she had entered the competition multiple times in the 1900s, had reached the final round in 1908, but had not won. After Lili's 1913 win, Nadia _stopped competing_ and focused on teaching.

Nadia became one of the most-influential composition teachers of the twentieth century. From the 1920s onward she taught at the Paris Conservatoire and at the American Conservatory at Fontainebleau. Her American students included Aaron Copland (Chapter 25), Virgil Thomson, Roy Harris, Walter Piston, Elliott Carter, David Diamond, Marc Blitzstein, Quincy Jones, Philip Glass (briefly), and many others. The phrase _Boulangerie_ (literally "bakery" but punning on Boulanger's surname) was sometimes used by American composers to refer to _the network of Boulanger-trained American composers_.

Nadia outlived Lili by 61 years. Throughout those decades she championed Lili's music — making editions of unpublished works, encouraging performers and conductors to program Lili's works, writing about her sister's compositional achievement. The early-twentieth-century neglect of Lili's music was _partially_ counteracted by Nadia's lifelong advocacy.

The full recovery of Lili's music has come _in the past forty years_. From the 1980s onward, Lili's works have been increasingly performed and recorded. _Du fond de l'abîme_ , _Faust et Hélène_ , _Clairières dans le ciel_ , and other Boulanger works are now in the standard repertoire. The recovery is part of the larger canonical-recovery work the book has discussed.

#### Recordings

**Pierre Boulez / Cleveland Orchestra, 1995 (Deutsche Grammophon)** for _La Mer_. Boulez was the leading conductor of French modernist music in the second half of the twentieth century. His Cleveland recording is _structurally clear, with extraordinary attention to inner-voice details_. The orchestration's _color juxtapositions_ are particularly audible in Boulez's reading — each instrumental voice is heard separately as well as in combination.

**Herbert von Karajan / Berlin Philharmonic, 1985 (Deutsche Grammophon)** for _La Mer_. Karajan's reading is _richer, more atmospheric, with full late-Romantic orchestral sound_. Some find this _too Germanic_ for French music; others find it _gorgeously evocative_. The Berlin Philharmonic's late-Karajan sound is on full display.

**Charles Dutoit / Orchestre Symphonique de Montréal, 1989 (Decca)** for _La Mer_. Dutoit's Montreal recording is _bright, clean, with French-color precision_. Dutoit specialized in French repertoire; the Montreal orchestra had developed a particular _French-sound_ under his direction. The Dutoit reading is sometimes considered _the middle path_ between Boulez's structural clarity and Karajan's atmospheric richness.

**Igor Markevitch / Orchestre Lamoureux et Chœurs, 1960 (DG / Mercury Living Presence)** for _Du fond de l'abîme_. The classic recording. Markevitch was a Ukrainian-Russian conductor who specialized in French repertoire (including the Berlioz _Symphonie Fantastique_ — see Chapter 16 cross-reference); his 1960 Lamoureux recording of the Lili Boulanger psalm setting is one of the foundational recordings of the work's modern reception.

**Jonathan Nott / BBC Symphony Orchestra and Chorus, 1995 (Erato)** for _Du fond de l'abîme_. A contemporary reading. Nott's BBC recording is _clear, structurally precise, with attention to text-setting_.

#### Cross-piece links

* For more **Debussy** , listen to the **Prélude à l'après-midi d'un faune** (1894 — the breakthrough work), **Pelléas et Mélisande** (1902 opera), the **Nocturnes** (1899 — three short orchestral works), and the **Préludes for piano** (Books I and II, 1909–1913 — twenty-four piano preludes, each with a poetic title).
* For more **Lili Boulanger** , listen to **Faust et Hélène** (1913 — the Prix de Rome cantata), **Clairières dans le ciel** (1913–1914 — song cycle on Francis Jammes texts), **Vieille prière bouddhique** (1914–1917 — setting of an old Buddhist prayer for tenor, chorus, and orchestra), and **Psaume 24** (1916 — another psalm setting).
* For the **French modernist tradition that descends from Debussy** , see Chapter 23 (Ravel's _Boléro_) and Chapter 26 (John Adams's contemporary American extension of post-Debussian color-based music). Also worth knowing: **Olivier Messiaen** (1908–1992) — the most-influential French modernist composer of the mid-twentieth century, who extended Debussy's modal-harmonic thinking into Catholic-mystical territory.
* For **Symbolist poetry that shaped Debussy** , read **Stéphane Mallarmé** (especially _L'Après-midi d'un faune_), **Paul Verlaine** (especially the _Fêtes galantes_ and _Romances sans paroles_), and **Maurice Maeterlinck** (especially _Pelléas et Mélisande_).
* For **the French sacred-choral tradition Boulanger continued** , listen to **Fauré's Requiem, Op. 48** (1888 — touched in Chapter 2 cross-references) and **Duruflé's Requiem, Op. 9** (1947 — the next great French Requiem after Fauré's).

#### Conversation Seeds

* _Ask the companion to play you a clearly Debussy-impressionist passage (the opening of _La Mer_ 's first movement, or _Clair de lune_ , or the _Prélude à l'après-midi d'un faune_) and then a clearly Boulanger-modernist passage (the opening of _Du fond de l'abîme_ , or _Faust et Hélène_). What do you hear that is _French_ in both? What distinguishes them?_
* _Ask the companion about the _Impressionism_ / _Symbolism_ labels — what each term meant in its respective art movement, why Debussy preferred _Symbolist_ but the world has stuck with _Impressionist_ , and whether the distinction matters for how you listen to the music._
* _Tell the companion about the moment in _Jeux de vagues_ that most-clearly conveyed _waves_ to you, and ask her about how Debussy's orchestrational techniques produce the wave-effect. (She will likely point at the use of harp, the meter changes, the flute-and-clarinet figures.)_
* _Ask the companion about Lili Boulanger — her short life, her win of the Prix de Rome as the first woman in 1913, her death at 24 from intestinal tuberculosis just five weeks before Debussy's death from cancer. What was lost when she died at 24?_
* _Trace with the companion the line that runs from Nadia Boulanger's Paris teaching studio in the 1920s through to twentieth-century American music — Copland, Carter, Glass, and dozens of others studied with her — and ask how Nadia's career was shaped by Lili's brief life and the influence the two sisters had on each other._

### 22.5 Exercises

#### Concept Check

**Q1.** Why did Debussy _dislike_ the _Impressionist_ label?

**Answer:** Debussy felt the label borrowed too literally from the _visual-arts_ movement and missed his actual aesthetic affiliations. He preferred _Symbolism_ (the late-nineteenth-century French literary movement of Mallarmé, Verlaine, Maeterlinck). The substantive distinction: _Impressionism_ in painting was concerned with the _optical effect of light_ ; _Symbolism_ in poetry was concerned with _evoking states of mind_ through verbal imagery. Debussy's music is closer to Symbolism in this sense — interested in _atmospheric evocation_ more than in _optical accuracy_. Despite his resistance the _Impressionist_ label has stuck; both terms point at different aspects of the same compositional practice.

**Q2.** What is a **whole-tone scale** , and why does it sound _unsettled_?

**Answer:** A whole-tone scale is built entirely on whole-step intervals — no half-steps. The scale has six notes (rather than the seven of major or minor scales) and _no clear tonic_ — because all the intervals are the same size, no note feels like the home note. The scale is _non-functional_ — it does not produce the tonic-dominant relationships that give Western tonal music direction. The result is a _floating, dreamlike, suspended_ quality, often described as _placeless_. Debussy used the whole-tone scale (along with pentatonic, octatonic, and modal scales) to create _atmospheric_ effects that conventional major/minor tonality could not produce.

### Chapter Summary

This chapter introduced **Debussy** through the **second movement of _La Mer_** ("Jeux de vagues," 1905, ~7 minutes) and **Lili Boulanger** through _**Du fond de l'abîme**_ (Psalm 130, 1914–1917, ~25 minutes). The two composers are placed _side by side_ as gravitational centers of early French modernism — Debussy the canonical figure, Lili Boulanger the recovered figure whose 24-year life and substantial compositional output have been increasingly recognized over the past forty years.

You learned **Impressionism** and **Symbolism** as labels applied to Debussy's music (with awareness that he preferred _Symbolist_ but the world has used _Impressionist_), the **whole-tone scale** (six-note scale with no clear tonic, producing a floating, atmospheric quality), and the **French modernist tradition** with its distinctive priorities (color and texture as primary content, modal and pentatonic harmonic language, restraint in expressive register, sophisticated orchestration).

You met **Debussy** in his single chapter — born 1862, trained at the Paris Conservatoire, Meck household summers 1880–1882, Prix de Rome 1884, breakthrough with _Prélude à l'après-midi d'un faune_ (1894), _La Mer_ (1905), _Pelléas et Mélisande_ (1902 opera), death from cancer in March 1918 age 55.

You met **Lili Boulanger** in her single chapter — born 1893, fragile health from age 2, talent recognized early, Paris Conservatoire from age 16, Prix de Rome winner 1913 (first woman in 110 years), major works 1913–1918, death from intestinal tuberculosis at age 24 in March 1918 (five weeks before Debussy's death). You met her sister **Nadia Boulanger** , who outlived Lili by 61 years and shaped twentieth-century American music through her teaching of Copland, Carter, and many others.

You met four readings: Boulez / Cleveland 1995, Karajan / Berlin 1985, Dutoit / Montreal 1989 for _La Mer_ ; Markevitch / Lamoureux 1960 and Nott / BBC 1995 for _Du fond de l'abîme_.

The next chapter takes you to **Stravinsky's _The Rite of Spring_ and Ravel's _Boléro_** — the 1913 Paris riot and what happened in it, primitivism and rhythmic revolution, the obsessive crescendo of _Boléro_ (1928) as the rhythmic-revolution sibling. After Debussy's color, the next century's rhythm.
