## Chapter 23: Stravinsky, _The Rite of Spring_ \+ Ravel, _Boléro_

Paris, the Théâtre des Champs-Élysées, the evening of 29 May 1913. The Ballets Russes is premiering a new work by Sergei Diaghilev's company: a ballet titled _Le Sacre du printemps_ (_The Rite of Spring_), choreographed by Vaslav Nijinsky on a scenario by Stravinsky and the Russian-folklorist Nicholas Roerich, with music by the thirty-year-old Russian composer **Igor Stravinsky** (1882–1971), conducted by Pierre Monteux. The audience includes Paris's leading composers, critics, intellectuals, and aristocrats. The performance does not go well. Within minutes of the opening, the audience erupts into shouting — some applauding wildly, some booing loudly, some fighting in the aisles. The conductor cannot hear the music; the dancers cannot hear the conductor; the police are called.

The 1913 _Rite of Spring_ premiere is one of the most-famous scandals in concert-music history. It is also _one of the most-mythologized events in music history_ — the legend has grown across a century into something larger than what happened. What actually happened that night involves audible musical revolution combined with theatrical scandal combined with avant-garde-versus-conservative culture-war combined with the specific physical chaos of a real fight in the theater. The legend simplifies all of this into _the audience rioted because the music was too modern_. The actual event was more complicated.

Fifteen years later, on 22 November 1928, the Paris Opéra premiered another ballet. The choreography was by Bronisława Nijinska (sister of Vaslav); the dancer was Ida Rubinstein; the music was a new commission from another major composer, **Maurice Ravel** (1875–1937). The work was titled _Boléro_. It was a single-movement orchestral piece, seventeen minutes long, built on _a single melody repeated with continuous orchestral elaboration over an unchanging rhythmic figure_. Ravel himself reportedly described it as _an experiment in orchestration without any musical content_ — a single-melody-and-rhythm exercise that should not have succeeded. It became one of the most-loved works in the standard repertoire and the most-recorded Ravel composition.

This chapter places _The Rite of Spring_ and _Boléro_ _side by side_ as **two siblings of the twentieth-century rhythmic revolution**. Both works pioneer _rhythm-and-pulse as primary content_ (rather than melody or harmony). _The Rite of Spring_ (1913) is _the violent rhythmic explosion_ — fast, asymmetric, primitivist. _Boléro_ (1928) is _the obsessive rhythmic crescendo_ — slow, regular, hypnotic. Together they show the _two faces_ of how the twentieth century reorganized music around rhythm.

We focus on **Part I of _The Rite of Spring_ ("Adoration of the Earth," ~17 minutes)** and on **Ravel's _Boléro_ whole (~16 minutes)**.

### 23.1 Before You Listen

#### Hook anecdote — what actually happened at the _Rite_ premiere

The 1913 premiere of _The Rite of Spring_ has accumulated a century of myth. The honest reconstruction:

The audience was _split between two camps_ : a _progressive avant-garde_ (which expected and welcomed the new) and a _conservative aristocratic-establishment_ (which had been increasingly hostile to Diaghilev's Russian-modernist ballets for several seasons). The two camps had been _clashing_ throughout the Ballets Russes's 1913 spring season — the previous performances of _Jeux_ (Debussy) had received boos and protests. The _Rite_ was, in a sense, the culmination of this season's culture war.

Within minutes of the opening of the ballet, the _progressive_ camp began applauding _Nijinsky's choreography_ — which was _anti-classical_ in extreme ways (the dancers stood with feet turned in rather than turned out — the most-basic violation of classical ballet technique; the dancers moved in _primitive_ angular gestures; the body positions evoked _Stone Age_ rather than _Romantic-era_ movement). The _conservative_ camp began booing the same choreography. The two camps began shouting at each other.

The orchestra continued playing. Stravinsky's music was _audible-but-not-the-only-issue_ — the audience was reacting to the _combination_ of _the music_ and _Nijinsky's choreography_ and _Roerich's scenery_ and _Diaghilev's overall provocation_. The shouting was about the _entire Gesamtkunstwerk_ — not just the music.

The police were called; some audience members were ejected; some were arrested; the performance continued. By the end of the ballet, the _progressive_ camp was substantially louder than the _conservative_ camp; the work received what was, on balance, a _positive but contested_ reception.

Within months, _The Rite of Spring_ was being performed in concert (without the choreography) in Paris, London, and other European cities — and was being received as a _masterpiece_. The 1913 scandal was _partly_ about the choreography (Nijinsky's anti-classical movement), partly about the scenario (Russian primitivism), partly about the music (Stravinsky's rhythmic revolution), and partly about the _politics of avant-garde art_ in pre-World War I Paris. Disentangling these dimensions has been the work of a century of musicology.

What the 1913 scandal _did not_ do was _kill_ the work or _destroy_ Stravinsky's career. By 1914 the _Rite_ was the most-discussed concert-music work of the era; by 1920 it was canonical; by 1940 it was being conducted by _every_ major conductor; today it is one of the most-performed twentieth-century works in the standard repertoire.

#### What to notice

For **_The Rite of Spring_ , Part I "Adoration of the Earth"** (~17 minutes):

  1. **The opening bassoon solo.** The work opens with a solo bassoon playing a melodic line in the _very-high register_ — a deliberately _uncomfortable_ range for the instrument that gives the line a _strained, almost-vocal_ quality. Stravinsky was setting a _Lithuanian folk melody_ ; the bassoon's high range was chosen for _atmosphere_ , not for instrumental comfort.

  2. **The _Augurs of Spring_ chord.** After several minutes of folk-flavored opening, the music shifts to a _fast, hammered rhythm_ with a _single repeated chord_. The chord is famously _dissonant_ — combining two different keys (E♭ minor and E major) simultaneously. The _hammered chord_ is played with _irregular accents_ — the pattern is _8 notes then accented, 7 notes then accented, 6 notes then accented_ , with the accents always falling on _unpredictable beats_. _This is the rhythmic revolution in its most-direct form_.

  3. **The rhythmic irregularity.** Throughout Part I, Stravinsky uses _unusual time signatures and changing meters_. The meter changes from 2/4 to 6/8 to 3/4 to 5/4 within single pages; the listener cannot lock onto a steady pulse. The _Rite_ 's rhythm is _fundamentally unpredictable_ — and the unpredictability is part of the _primitive-ritualistic_ atmosphere the music creates.

  4. **The orchestral colors.** Stravinsky uses the orchestra in _new colorings_ — Russian-folk-instrument-inflected sounds (the high bassoon, the alto flute, the contrabassoon), unusual percussion combinations (gourds, _guiros_ , large bass drums), brass and string passages with _unprecedented_ dissonance. The orchestral writing is _as innovative as the rhythmic writing_.

For **Ravel's _Boléro_** (~16 minutes):

  1. **The unchanging rhythmic figure.** From the first measure to the last, _Boléro_ maintains a single rhythmic pattern: a _Spanish dance rhythm_ (bolero) played by side drum, with the same pattern _repeating_ throughout. Listen for the _snare drum from the first note_ — it does not stop until the last fifteen seconds of the piece.

  2. **The single melody.** Ravel uses _one melody_ (with a second, related melodic idea) throughout the work. The melody is played by different solo instruments — flute first, then clarinet, then bassoon, then E♭ clarinet, then oboe d'amore, then trumpet with celesta, then tenor saxophone, then soprano saxophone, then horn with two piccolos, then woodwind ensemble, then full strings, then full orchestra. _The melody does not change_ ; only the orchestration changes.

  3. **The continuous crescendo.** From the first measure to the last, _Boléro_ is _one continuous crescendo_ — the music grows louder _constantly_ across the entire 16 minutes. The work has _no dynamic moments other than the rising arc_. Listen for _how much louder_ each statement of the melody is than the previous.

  4. **The single climax.** The work has _one_ structural climax — the final statement of the melody by the full orchestra, with the rhythm finally accelerating slightly, before the very end. Then the music _snaps_ to its final cadence in C major (a sudden modulation from the work's C-minor home key).

#### One-sentence backgrounds

**Stravinsky,_Le Sacre du printemps_ (The Rite of Spring)** — ballet in two parts on a scenario by Stravinsky and Roerich about prehistoric pagan-Russian rites, choreographed by Nijinsky; composed 1912–1913 in Switzerland and Paris; premiered 29 May 1913 in Paris; ~35 minutes total. Part I "Adoration of the Earth" runs ~17 minutes.

**Ravel,_Boléro_** — single-movement orchestral work for a ballet commissioned by Ida Rubinstein; composed in summer 1928 in Saint-Jean-de-Luz on the French Atlantic coast; premiered 22 November 1928 at the Paris Opéra, choreographed by Bronisława Nijinska, danced by Rubinstein; ~16 minutes.

### 23.2 The Listening Window

#### _The Rite of Spring_ , Part I "Adoration of the Earth" (Boulez / Cleveland, ~17 minutes)

* **0:00–3:30.** **Introduction.** The opening bassoon solo in extreme high register. The _Lithuanian folk melody_ unfolds slowly; gradually other woodwinds enter. The texture is _atmospheric_ — primordial-forest sound effects, irregular meters, woodwind colors that evoke _folk pipes and bird calls_. The _prehistoric atmosphere_ is being established.

* **3:30–5:30.** **Augurs of Spring: Dances of the Young Girls.** The first major rhythmic section. The famous _hammered chord_ (E♭ minor over E major) is repeated _insistently_ with _irregular accents_. The orchestra plays the chord with _no clear pulse_ — the accents fall in patterns of 8, 7, 6 notes; the listener cannot predict where the next accent will land. _This is the rhythmic revolution at its most-direct._

* **5:30–6:00.** **Ritual of Abduction.** A faster, more violent section. The strings play _sliding figures_ ; the brass enters with _fanfares_ ; the percussion grows more intense.

* **6:00–9:00.** **Spring Rounds (Rondes printanières).** A slower section, with _folk-melodic_ materials. The texture is _less violent_ but the meter remains _irregular_.

* **9:00–11:00.** **Ritual of the Rival Tribes.** Fast, conflict-evoking music. The orchestral writing suggests two tribal groups in confrontation.

* **11:00–12:30.** **Procession of the Sage.** A slower, _processional_ section. _Heavy_ orchestral writing — the _Sage_ (the elder) is being brought ceremonially to bless the earth.

* **12:30–13:00.** **The Sage.** A brief moment of stillness — the Sage kisses the earth in the ballet's scenario. The orchestra holds _suspended chords_.

* **13:00–17:00.** **Dance of the Earth.** The climactic section of Part I. Fast, violent, with _full orchestra at maximum intensity_. The rhythmic pattern is _constantly changing_ ; the dynamic is _fortissimo throughout most of the section_. The Part I ends with a final crashing cadence.

The _Rite_ 's Part I (and Part II, the _Sacrifice_ part not covered in this chapter) revolutionized what _orchestral music_ could do. The rhythmic innovations — _unprecedented_ in their irregularity and violence — opened the door to the rest of the twentieth century's rhythmic experimentation. Béla Bartók, Carl Orff, Aaron Copland (Chapter 25), Leonard Bernstein, and many other twentieth-century composers absorbed and extended what Stravinsky had done.

#### Ravel, _Boléro_ (Munch / Boston, ~16 minutes)

* **0:00–0:30.** **Opening.** A side drum begins playing the _bolero rhythm_ — a Spanish dance rhythm with a specific _long-short-long-short-short-long-short_ pattern. The pattern will _repeat without variation_ for the entire 16 minutes. The drum is _very quiet_ (_pianissimo_) at the opening.

* **0:30–1:30.** **First flute statement of melody.** A solo flute plays the main melody — a _single melodic line_ in C minor, with a _Spanish-Arabic_ character. The melody is _not particularly memorable on first hearing_ ; it is _deliberately neutral_. Underneath the flute, the side drum continues its pattern; a _pizzicato_ string accompaniment provides harmonic support.

* **1:30–3:30.** **Second melody (related) on clarinet; first melody returns on bassoon; second on E♭ clarinet.** Different solo woodwind instruments take turns presenting the melody. The dynamics increase _gradually_ — the music is _slightly louder_ with each instrumental change.

* **3:30–6:30.** **First melody on oboe d'amore; second on flute and trumpet with celesta; first on tenor saxophone; second on soprano saxophone.** Ravel uses _unusual_ solo instruments (oboe d'amore, two different saxophones) — the orchestrational variety becomes part of the work's content. The dynamics continue increasing.

* **6:30–10:00.** **Continued solo statements with growing accompaniment.** First melody on horn with two piccolos; second on woodwind ensemble. The accompaniment is now _fuller_ — more strings, more woodwinds providing background. The dynamic continues to climb.

* **10:00–14:00.** **First melody on full first violins; second on full string ensemble; first on full orchestra.** The melody now appears in the _full string section_ and _full orchestra_. The dynamics have reached _forte_ and are climbing toward _fortissimo_.

* **14:00–15:30.** **Final melodic statements with full orchestra.** The melody, with full orchestra at full dynamic intensity, is heard one last time.

* **15:30–16:00.** **The climactic ending.** The music _modulates_ from C minor to E major suddenly — _the only harmonic change in the entire work_. The orchestra plays _one final fortissimo statement_ , then _snaps_ to a close on a final E-major cadence.

_Boléro_ is _the most-extreme test of how-little-musical-material can sustain a 16-minute work_. There is _one melody_ (with a related variant) and _one rhythm_ ; the entire compositional interest is in _orchestrational variation and dynamic crescendo_. The work demonstrates that _the orchestra itself_ can be the primary musical content — that _what instruments are playing the melody_ is as important as _what the melody is_.

The work is also _physically demanding to perform_. The side drummer must maintain _unwavering rhythmic precision_ for sixteen minutes; the soloists must enter at _precise dynamic levels_ in the increasing crescendo; the conductor must shape the _imperceptible-incremental dynamic climb_ across the entire work. _Boléro_ is _deceptively simple_ on the page but _physically difficult_ in performance.

### 23.3 What's Happening in the Music

#### Definition: Primitivism

_Primitivism_ in early twentieth-century art is the _deliberate evocation of pre-civilized, non-Western, or pre-modern aesthetic worlds_ through art that _consciously_ avoids the _refined sophistication_ of late-Romantic European tradition. The movement spans visual arts (Gauguin's Tahitian period, Picasso's African-mask-inspired works), literature (D. H. Lawrence's interest in pre-industrial cultures), and music.

In _music_ , primitivism appeared most directly in:

* **Stravinsky's _Rite of Spring_** (1913, this chapter) — Russian prehistoric pagan rites as compositional material.
* **Stravinsky's _Les Noces_ (The Wedding, 1914–1923)** — Russian peasant wedding rituals.
* **Bartók's _Allegro Barbaro_ (1911) and _The Miraculous Mandarin_ (1918–1924)** — Hungarian folk-inflected primitivism with industrial-urban violence.
* **Orff's _Carmina Burana_ (1937)** — medieval-Latin texts set to _primitive-rhythmic_ music.

Primitivism uses _rhythmic insistence_ , _unison textures_ , _folk-modal harmony_ , and _unconventional orchestration_ to evoke worlds _outside the Romantic-European mainstream_. The aesthetic is _deliberately rough_ — the music _rejects the refinement_ of late-Romantic music in favor of _direct, brutal, ritualistic_ expression.

Primitivism has been _criticized_ in retrospect for its often-idealized and culturally-flattening treatment of non-European cultures (the _Rite_ 's "Russian pagan past" is largely a modernist _invention_ rather than a _recovery_ ; Stravinsky was using _folkloric material_ but constructing a _fictional prehistoric Russia_). The criticism is real; the music is _still_ great. Both can be held.

#### Definition: Rhythmic Revolution

The _twentieth-century rhythmic revolution_ is the reorganization of Western art music _around rhythm_ as primary content, often at the expense of melody and harmony. Before about 1900, rhythm was _subordinate_ to melody and harmony in most Western music. After Stravinsky's _Rite of Spring_ , _rhythm itself_ could be the _primary content_ — and many subsequent composers (Bartók, Copland, Bernstein, Britten, Boulez, Cage) made rhythm central in ways that earlier composers had not.

Key features of the rhythmic revolution:

* **Asymmetric meters** — 5/4, 7/8, 11/16, and other non-standard time signatures.
* **Constantly changing meters** — the meter changes within a single page (the _Rite_ changes meter often).
* **Polyrhythms** — multiple rhythmic patterns happening simultaneously in different orchestral voices.
* **Irregular accents** — accents falling on unpredictable beats rather than on the expected downbeat.
* **Rhythm as melodic content** — the rhythmic pattern itself is what the listener is asked to track, rather than the pitch content.

The revolution continued through the twentieth century. Bartók's _Sonata for Two Pianos and Percussion_ (1937) and _Concerto for Orchestra_ (1943) extended the _Rite_ 's rhythmic innovations. Copland's _Appalachian Spring_ (1944, Chapter 25) uses asymmetric rhythms in a more _folk-derived_ idiom. Bernstein's _West Side Story_ (1957) brings the rhythmic revolution into popular musical theater. Steve Reich's _Music for 18 Musicians_ (1976) and other minimalist works (Chapter 26) extend rhythmic patterning into the late twentieth century.

#### Definition: Crescendo Form (Boléro Form)

_Boléro form_ — the structural design of Ravel's work — is _single-crescendo form_ : a work built around _one sustained, continuous crescendo_ from pianissimo to fortissimo over its entire duration. The form is _unusual_ in classical music; before Ravel, almost no major work was built this way. After Ravel, the form has been used occasionally — Steve Reich's _Drumming_ uses _additive crescendo_ in some sections; Arvo Pärt's _Cantus in Memoriam Benjamin Britten_ (1980) is a _single-descent_ (the opposite of crescendo) form; minimalist music in general often uses _gradual processes_ that share aesthetic kinship with Boléro form.

The form _works_ because:

* **The constant rhythm gives the listener something to lock onto** — the side-drum pattern is constant, predictable, anchoring.
* **The varying orchestration provides interest** — even with a single melody, the changing instrumental colors give the listener constant new sounds.
* **The dynamic crescendo gives the work a clear direction** — the listener can perceive _we are getting louder_ across the sixteen minutes, which provides the sense of _building toward something_.
* **The single climax at the end pays off the crescendo** — the final fortissimo statement _delivers what the crescendo has been promising_.

Without these supporting features, the _Boléro_ form would not work — it would be repetitive and dull. With them, the form is _hypnotic_ and _cumulatively powerful_. The work demonstrates that _radical formal simplicity_ can produce sophisticated musical experience.

#### Common Misconception

People sometimes treat the _Rite of Spring_ premiere as _a riot caused by the music alone_ — the story is that _the music was so shocking_ that audience members rioted in their seats. This reading is partial.

The premiere was a _cultural-political event_ as much as a _musical event_. The Ballets Russes had been provoking conservative Paris audiences for several years; the _Rite_ was the _culmination of an ongoing culture war_. Nijinsky's choreography was _as provocative_ as Stravinsky's music — the anti-classical movement, the _prehistoric_ body positions, the _un-balletic_ gestures all contributed to the disturbance. The _combined_ effect of music, choreography, scenario, and design produced the chaos; _the music alone_ would have been _received differently in a concert hall_ (as it was, within months, when it was performed in concert form).

The honest description: _The Rite of Spring_ combined _unprecedented musical content_ with _unprecedented choreographic content_ in _a culturally-tense theater context_ , producing _a disturbance that has become legendary_. The music _is_ revolutionary; but the _premiere disturbance_ was not caused _solely_ by the music.

This is part of the larger lesson about _historical reception_ — _what audiences saw and heard_ shapes how works are subsequently received. The _Rite_ premiere chaos _did_ contribute to the work's reputation as _revolutionary_. But the _actual revolution_ was in the music itself, and could have been heard differently in different contexts. The 1913 chaos is _part of the work's story_ but _not the whole story_ of its reception.

### 23.4 The Stories

#### Stravinsky's life

Igor Fyodorovich Stravinsky was born on 17 June 1882 in Oranienbaum (now Lomonosov), a summer-resort town near Saint Petersburg, the third of four sons of a _bass singer_ at the Mariinsky Theater (Russia's leading opera house). He grew up in a _musical-theatrical household_ ; his father introduced him to the leading Russian musicians of the late nineteenth century.

He studied law at Saint Petersburg University (his father wanted him to be a lawyer) but increasingly devoted himself to music. From about 1902 he studied composition privately with **Nikolai Rimsky-Korsakov** (1844–1908) — the leading Russian symphonist of the late nineteenth century, who became Stravinsky's musical _father figure_ until Rimsky-Korsakov's death.

In 1909, age 27, Stravinsky was commissioned by **Sergei Diaghilev** (1872–1929) to compose music for the Ballets Russes — the Russian-emigrant ballet company that Diaghilev was building in Paris. The first commission, _L'oiseau de feu_ (_The Firebird_ , 1910), made Stravinsky internationally famous. The second, _Petrushka_ (1911), confirmed it. The third, _The Rite of Spring_ (1913, this chapter), revolutionized music.

Stravinsky lived outside Russia from 1910 onward — first in Switzerland (1914–1920), then France (1920–1939), then the United States (1939–1971). The _exile-pattern_ is similar to Chopin's (Chapter 17) — a Russian composer who could not return to home, who lived the rest of his life in Western Europe and America, and whose music _kept changing_ as he encountered new compositional environments.

Stravinsky's compositional voice changed _substantially_ across his career:

* **Russian period (1910–1920)** : The early ballets — _Firebird_ , _Petrushka_ , _Rite of Spring_ — plus _Les Noces_ and other works. Russian folk-derived material, primitivist rhythms, large orchestras.

* **Neoclassical period (1920–1951)** : _Pulcinella_ (1920, on themes by Pergolesi), the _Octet_ (1923), _Oedipus Rex_ (1927), _Symphony of Psalms_ (1930), _Symphony in C_ (1940), _Symphony in Three Movements_ (1945), _Rake's Progress_ (1951 opera). _Returning to classical-period clarity_ with modernist twist. Smaller forces, clearer textures, sometimes ironic.

* **Serial period (1951–1971)** : After Schoenberg's death in 1951, Stravinsky adopted _twelve-tone serial_ technique. Works include _Agon_ (1957), _Threni_ (1958), the _Requiem Canticles_ (1966). The shift was widely commented on — Stravinsky's late conversion to serialism was _the most-prominent late-style change_ in twentieth-century music.

The _three-Stravinsky_ career is one of the most-discussed patterns in twentieth-century compositional biography. He was _each Stravinsky_ fully — not partially. He kept _revising his own _Rite of Spring__ across his career (with several major revisions through the late 1940s); some of these revisions changed the rhythmic notation, some changed the orchestration. _The Rite_ you hear today is _not exactly the 1913 version_ but a _Stravinsky-revised version_ from the late 1940s.

He died on 6 April 1971 in New York, age 88. He was buried in Venice (the city he had loved most), in the same Russian-Orthodox section of San Michele cemetery where Diaghilev had been buried in 1929.

#### Ravel's life

Joseph Maurice Ravel was born on 7 March 1875 in Ciboure, in the French Basque region near the Spanish border. His mother was Basque-Spanish (Marie Delouart); his father was a Swiss-French engineer (Joseph Ravel). The _Basque-Spanish_ background was important — Ravel's music throughout his life references _Spanish and Basque_ musical traditions.

He studied at the Paris Conservatoire from age 14 (1889). His composition teacher was **Gabriel Fauré** (Chapter 2). Ravel was _not_ a smooth student — he was famously _meticulous, slow, perfectionistic_ , and _sometimes rebellious_. He competed for the _Prix de Rome_ (the same prize Lili Boulanger would win in 1913 — Chapter 22) _five times_ between 1900 and 1905, and was rejected each time. The 1905 rejection caused a public scandal — Ravel was widely considered the most-talented composer of his generation, and the _Prix de Rome_ rejection was treated as scandalous favoritism. _The 1905 Affair_ led to administrative changes at the Conservatoire.

Ravel's compositional output is _small but substantial_. His major works include:

* **Solo piano works** : _Pavane pour une infante défunte_ (1899), _Jeux d'eau_ (1901), _Miroirs_ (1905), _Gaspard de la nuit_ (1908), _Le tombeau de Couperin_ (1917).
* **Orchestral works** : _Daphnis et Chloé_ (ballet, 1909–1912), _Ma mère l'oye_ (Mother Goose, 1908–1911), _La Valse_ (1919–1920), _Boléro_ (1928, this chapter), _Piano Concerto in G major_ (1929–1931), _Piano Concerto for the Left Hand_ (1929–1930, commissioned by the one-armed pianist Paul Wittgenstein).
* **Vocal and chamber music** : many songs, the _String Quartet in F major_ (1902–1903), the _Piano Trio in A minor_ (1914), various sonatas.
* **Orchestrations** : most famously _Pictures at an Exhibition_ (Mussorgsky's piano suite, orchestrated by Ravel in 1922 and now performed almost exclusively in Ravel's orchestral version).

Ravel was _gay_ (the historical evidence is strong though Ravel himself was discreet), _never married_ , and lived a _very private life_. He had a _small circle_ of close friends and was known as _exquisitely polite and reserved_ in public. He was _meticulously dressed_ — small, slight, always _immaculately turned out_ in well-tailored suits.

He developed _aphasia_ (loss of language abilities) and _apraxia_ (loss of motor coordination) in his last years, probably from a brain disorder. He could _hear music in his head_ but _could not write it down_ — one of the most-tragic compositional declines. He died on 28 December 1937 in Paris, age 62, after a final surgery intended to address the neurological condition. He was buried at the Levallois-Perret Cemetery north of Paris.

#### Recordings

**Pierre Boulez / Cleveland Orchestra, 1991 (Deutsche Grammophon)** for the _Rite_. Boulez was one of the leading conductors of twentieth-century music in the second half of the twentieth century. His 1991 Cleveland reading is _structurally precise, with extraordinary attention to inner-voice details and rhythmic accuracy_. Boulez recorded the _Rite_ multiple times; the 1991 is widely considered the most-balanced.

**Leonard Bernstein / Israel Philharmonic, 1982 (Deutsche Grammophon)** for the _Rite_. Bernstein's late reading. _More-Romantically-inflected_ than Boulez's, with the Israel Philharmonic giving the work a _warmer_ string sound than the Cleveland Orchestra's brilliant clarity.

**Esa-Pekka Salonen / Los Angeles Philharmonic, 2006 (Deutsche Grammophon)** for the _Rite_. Salonen is one of the leading contemporary conductors of modernist repertoire; his Los Angeles reading is _vivid, intensely rhythmic, with the Philharmonic at the peak of its 2000s form_.

**Charles Munch / Boston Symphony Orchestra, 1956 (RCA Living Stereo)** for _Boléro_. Munch was the French-trained, Boston-Music-Director conductor we encountered in Chapter 16 (Berlioz). His 1956 _Boléro_ is _the classic Boston reading_ — slightly faster than the modern standard, with extraordinary side-drum precision and orchestral discipline.

**Claudio Abbado / London Symphony Orchestra, 1984 (DG)** for _Boléro_. Abbado's reading is _slower and more deliberate_ than Munch's, with the long crescendo more carefully shaped.

#### Cross-piece links

* For more **Stravinsky** , listen to the **Firebird Suite** (1919 version, his most-accessible work) and **Petrushka** (1911). For the neoclassical Stravinsky, listen to the **Symphony of Psalms** (1930 — choral-orchestral setting of three psalms, in a _neoclassical_ idiom). For the serial Stravinsky, listen to the **Symphony in Three Movements** (1945) and the **Requiem Canticles** (1966).
* For more **Ravel** , listen to **Daphnis et Chloé** (1912 — the great Ravel ballet, with one of the most-beautiful sunrise passages in orchestral music), the **Piano Concerto in G major** (1929–1931), and **Gaspard de la nuit** (1908 piano suite — one of the most-technically-demanding piano works in the repertoire).
* For the **next stage of the rhythmic revolution after the Rite** , listen to **Bartók's _Concerto for Orchestra_** (1943) and **Bartók's _Sonata for Two Pianos and Percussion_** (1937). Bartók extended the rhythmic innovations of the _Rite_ into more _integrated_ compositional idioms.
* For the **Boléro tradition that came after Ravel** , listen to **Steve Reich's _Music for 18 Musicians_** (1976, Chapter 26 cross-reference) and **Arvo Pärt's _Cantus in Memoriam Benjamin Britten_** (1980 — single descent, the opposite of Boléro's single crescendo). Both are _single-process_ works in the larger tradition Ravel opened.

#### Conversation Seeds

* _Ask the companion to play you the opening of the _Rite of Spring_ and to point at three specific moments where the rhythm is _irregular_ or _unpredictable_. Then ask her to play the _Augurs of Spring_ hammered-chord section and to walk you through how Stravinsky combines two keys (E♭ minor and E major) in a single chord._
* _Ask the companion about the actual 1913 premiere of the _Rite of Spring_ — what was happening in the theater, who was shouting at whom, and how much of the chaos was about Stravinsky's music versus Nijinsky's choreography versus Diaghilev's general provocation of conservative Paris._
* _Tell the companion which moment in _Boléro_ most-clearly caught your attention — the orchestrational change to oboe d'amore, to tenor saxophone, to soprano saxophone, to horn with two piccolos — and ask her about the orchestrational logic of Ravel's choices._
* _Ask the companion about Stravinsky's three compositional periods (Russian, Neoclassical, Serial) and how the _Rite of Spring_ 's rhythmic primitivism fits the Russian period — and what Stravinsky thought about the _Rite_ later in his life when he was writing very different music._
* _Ask the companion about Ravel's _Pavane pour une infante défunte_ (his early piano work, with a slow, melancholic melody) and to play it for you. Then ask her about how the same composer who wrote the gentle _Pavane_ also wrote the relentless _Boléro_ — and what the range of Ravel's compositional voice reveals._

### 23.5 Exercises

#### Concept Check

**Q1.** What was actually happening at the **1913 premiere** of the _Rite of Spring_?

**Answer:** The premiere was a _cultural-political event_ combining unprecedented music with unprecedented choreography in a culturally-tense theater. The Ballets Russes had been provoking conservative Paris audiences for several years; the _Rite_ premiere was the culmination of an ongoing culture war. Two camps in the audience — _progressive avant-garde_ and _conservative aristocratic-establishment_ — clashed within minutes of the opening. Some applauded Nijinsky's anti-classical choreography (dancers with feet turned in, primitive angular gestures); some booed loudly; some fought in the aisles; the police were called. The disturbance was about _the entire ballet production_ — music, choreography, scenario, design — not the music alone. Within months the _Rite_ was being performed in concert (without choreography) and was received as a masterpiece. The 1913 chaos is part of the work's mythology but is not the whole reception story.

**Q2.** What is **Boléro form** , and what makes it work?

**Answer:** Boléro form is _single-crescendo form_ — a work built around one sustained, continuous crescendo from pianissimo to fortissimo over its entire duration. Ravel's _Boléro_ (1928) is the form's signature work — sixteen minutes built on one melody (with related variant) and one repeating rhythm, with continuous orchestral variation and dynamic crescendo from start to finish. The form works because: (1) the constant rhythm gives the listener something to lock onto; (2) the varying orchestration provides interest; (3) the dynamic crescendo gives the work a clear direction toward a climax; (4) the single fortissimo climax at the end pays off what the crescendo has been promising. The form was unusual in classical music before Ravel; subsequent minimalist works (Reich, Pärt, others) have used related single-process forms.

### Chapter Summary

This chapter introduced **Stravinsky's _The Rite of Spring_** (1913, Part I focused) and **Ravel's _Boléro_** (1928) as two siblings of the twentieth-century rhythmic revolution.

You learned **primitivism** (the early twentieth-century deliberate evocation of pre-civilized aesthetic worlds), the **rhythmic revolution** (the reorganization of Western art music around rhythm as primary content), and **Boléro form** (single-crescendo form as Ravel's invention).

You met **the actual 1913 _Rite of Spring_ premiere** — the cultural-political event combining music, choreography, scenario, and design in a culturally-tense theater. The disturbance was about the _whole ballet_ and not just the music; the work was canonical within a few years.

You met **Stravinsky** in his single chapter — born 1882 in Russia, studied with Rimsky-Korsakov, Ballets Russes commissions starting 1909 (_Firebird_ , _Petrushka_ , _Rite of Spring_), exile from Russia in 1910, three compositional periods (Russian / Neoclassical / Serial), death in 1971 age 88, buried in Venice. The three-Stravinsky career as one of the most-discussed patterns in twentieth-century compositional biography.

You met **Ravel** in his single chapter — born 1875 in Basque France, Paris Conservatoire from age 14 under Fauré, _Prix de Rome_ rejection scandals 1900–1905, the small but substantial compositional output, gay and private life, neurological decline in his last years, death in 1937 age 62.

You met five readings: Boulez / Cleveland 1991, Bernstein / Israel Philharmonic 1982, Salonen / Los Angeles 2006 for the _Rite_ ; Munch / Boston 1956 and Abbado / London Symphony 1984 for _Boléro_.

The next chapter takes you to **Shostakovich's Symphony No. 5** and **Britten's _War Requiem_** — music under totalitarianism (Shostakovich's "creative answer to just criticism" and the 80-year argument about it) and post-war reckoning in choral form (Britten's _War Requiem_). **Thread B returns explicitly** in the Britten setting.

## Chapter 24: Shostakovich, Symphony No. 5 + Britten, _War Requiem_ — and a Second Viennese School Primer

Moscow, _Pravda_ , the morning of 28 January 1936. An anonymous editorial titled _Sumbur vmesto muzyki_ — "Muddle Instead of Music" — appears on the front page of the Soviet Union's official newspaper. The editorial attacks the composer **Dmitri Shostakovich** (1906–1975) for his opera _Lady Macbeth of the Mtsensk District_ (composed 1932, premiered 1934). The opera, which has been a Soviet sensation for two years and has been performed widely in the USSR and abroad, is denounced as _cacophonous, formalist, vulgar_. The editorial is unsigned but is widely understood to reflect _Stalin's personal view_ (Stalin had attended a performance of the opera on 26 January, two days before; the editorial appears two days later; Shostakovich and most observers understand the connection).

Shostakovich is twenty-nine years old. He has been one of the most-famous young composers in the Soviet Union for over a decade — _Symphony No. 1_ (1925, written when he was 19) had been an international sensation; _The Nose_ (1928 opera) and _Lady Macbeth_ had confirmed his reputation; he had been a _darling of the Soviet cultural establishment_. The _Pravda_ attack reverses this overnight. Performances of _Lady Macbeth_ are canceled across the USSR; subsequent Shostakovich works are scrutinized; the composer's livelihood and personal safety are in danger.

What follows over the next eighteen months is one of the most-famous compositional crises in twentieth-century music. Shostakovich withdraws his Symphony No. 4 (1936) from premiere — the work is too _formalist_ (a Soviet term for _Western-modernist, intellectualist, non-accessible_); he keeps a packed suitcase by his bed expecting arrest; he composes Symphony No. 5 in summer 1937 with the explicit subtitle _A Soviet artist's creative answer to just criticism_. The Fifth Symphony is premiered in Leningrad on 21 November 1937, conducted by Yevgeny Mravinsky (whom we met in Chapter 20 with Tchaikovsky's Pathétique). The premiere is a sensation. The audience reportedly stands and applauds for thirty minutes; many people weep openly. Shostakovich is rehabilitated; _Lady Macbeth_ is banned for decades but the composer's career is saved.

The Symphony No. 5 is one of the most-debated works in twentieth-century music. The question — _did Shostakovich genuinely write a Soviet symphony or was it coded resistance to Stalinism?_ — has produced eighty years of musicological controversy. We will hold the question carefully.

This chapter is about _music under totalitarianism_ (Shostakovich's Symphony No. 5 and the eighty-year debate about it), about _post-war reckoning in choral form_ (Benjamin Britten's _War Requiem_ , 1962), and about a brief primer on **the Second Viennese School** (Schoenberg, Berg, Webern — the founders of atonality and twelve-tone serial composition).

Two anchor works, plus a primer. The chapter is the heaviest in the book because the subject matter is the heaviest.

### 24.1 Before You Listen

#### Hook anecdote — the packed suitcase

For most of 1936–1937, Dmitri Shostakovich kept a packed suitcase by his bed. He had been attacked in _Pravda_ ; his Symphony No. 4 had been withdrawn; his livelihood was uncertain; and the Great Purges had begun (Stalin's mass arrest and execution of Soviet citizens, peaking in 1937–1938). Shostakovich expected, every night, that the NKVD (the Soviet secret police) might come to arrest him. The suitcase was so that _he could leave immediately_. The detail is documented in his wife Nina's recollections, in his son Maxim Shostakovich's interviews, and in multiple Soviet-era memoirs.

The arrest never came. _Why_ it never came is uncertain. Shostakovich's composition of the Fifth Symphony — and its successful 1937 Leningrad premiere — was _part_ of his rehabilitation; the _Pravda_ attack was _never_ publicly retracted but was effectively superseded by the Fifth Symphony's reception. Other Shostakovich biographies emphasize _the role of his patrons_ (Marshal Mikhail Tukhachevsky had been a close friend, though Tukhachevsky was himself arrested and executed in 1937; Shostakovich was reportedly questioned by the NKVD about Tukhachevsky and survived) and _the partial protection of the Composers' Union_ (the Soviet musical-bureaucratic body that managed composers' careers). But the suitcase by the bed was real, and the threat was real.

This detail tells you something important about the Fifth Symphony's _composition context_ : Shostakovich was composing under _political duress that could have led to his death_. The work's subtitle (_A Soviet artist's creative answer to just criticism_) is _not_ something he chose freely. The question of _whether the work is what its subtitle says it is_ — _a sincere Soviet symphony_ — or whether it is _coded resistance_ — has been the central musicological debate about the work for eighty years.

#### What to notice

For **Shostakovich, Symphony No. 5, First Movement** (Moderato, ~16 min):

  1. **The opening.** The strings begin a _jagged, descending_ figure — _low strings_ and _upper strings_ in alternation, with sharp accents. The figure is in _D minor_ ; the harmonic content is _austere, minor-modal_. _This is the opening voice_ — the symphony's serious-tragic opening.

  2. **The first theme group.** Multiple thematic ideas in the early minutes — a _march-like_ second theme, a _waltz-like_ third theme, a _funeral-march_ fourth theme. The first movement is _thematically dense_ — Shostakovich packs several distinct thematic materials into the exposition.

  3. **The piano's role.** A _solo piano_ (and _celesta_) provides distinctive coloring throughout the movement. The piano enters with _sharp, hammered chords_ ; it returns at moments of _crisis_. The use of piano in the orchestra is one of Shostakovich's signature devices.

  4. **The climactic central section.** Around 8:00–11:00 in most recordings, the music reaches a _climactic central section_ — fortissimo, with the _jagged opening figure_ returned in extreme intensity. This is the _crisis section_ of the movement.

  5. **The withdrawal.** After the climax, the music _gradually withdraws_ — the texture thins, dynamics decrease, the music returns toward the austere opening atmosphere. The movement ends _quietly_ — a _transitional ending_ rather than a definitive cadence.

For **Shostakovich, Symphony No. 5, Fourth Movement Finale** (Allegro non troppo, ~10 min):

  1. **The opening fanfare.** The finale begins with a _brilliant brass fanfare_ — fast tempo, fortissimo, in _D minor_ turning quickly to _D major_. The character is _triumphal_. _Or is it?_

  2. **The _forced_ march.** The brass fanfare is followed by a _march_ that some hear as _triumphal_ and others hear as _mechanical, hollow, forced_. The repetition of the rhythmic figure is _insistent_ ; some listeners hear _celebration_ , others hear _coercion_.

  3. **The slow middle section.** Around 4:00, the music _slows substantially_ — strings enter with a _lyrical, slow_ second theme. The tempo _drops_ from the fanfare's _Allegro non troppo_ to a _more thoughtful pace_. This is the _contemplative middle_.

  4. **The build to the final climax.** From about 6:00 onward, the music builds back to a _triumphal_ (or _forced-triumphal_) close. The brass returns; the rhythm accelerates; the dynamics climb to _fortissimo_ ; the symphony ends with _D-major celebratory cadences_.

  5. **The 80-year debate.** The question that has divided Shostakovich scholarship for eighty years: _Is the D-major finale sincere triumph (Shostakovich genuinely affirming Soviet society), or is it hollow triumph (Shostakovich coding his actual feelings under the required affirmative ending), or is it coded resistance (Shostakovich subverting the required ending from inside)?_ The debate is _not_ a question Shostakovich himself could safely answer in writing; it has been argued from _interpretive readings of the music_ and from _subsequent memoirs that may or may not be reliable_.

For **Britten,_War Requiem_ , Op. 66** — Dies Irae section (~10 minutes):

  1. **The structure of the _War Requiem_.** Britten's work _combines_ the Latin Mass text of the Requiem with the _English war poetry of Wilfred Owen_ (a British poet killed in World War I one week before the Armistice in 1918). The Latin and English texts are _alternated and combined_ — the Latin sung by full chorus and soprano soloist, the English sung by tenor and baritone soloists in _chamber-orchestra accompaniment_. The work was commissioned for the consecration of the new Coventry Cathedral in 1962 (the cathedral had been destroyed in German bombing in 1940; the new building was a postwar reconciliation gesture). Britten had designed the soloist cast deliberately to symbolize that reconciliation — soprano **Galina Vishnevskaya** from the USSR, tenor **Peter Pears** from Britain, baritone **Dietrich Fischer-Dieskau** from Germany. At the premiere on 30 May 1962, however, the Soviet authorities refused to allow Vishnevskaya to travel to Coventry, and the British soprano **Heather Harper** stepped in to learn and sing the part at short notice. Britten conducted; the symbolic cast was completed the following year, when Decca brought all three originally-intended soloists into the studio for the now-canonical 1963 recording.

  2. **The _Dies Irae_ section.** The Dies Irae is _the longest section_ of Britten's setting — about 30 minutes total (much longer than what we focus on in this chapter). We focus on a 10-minute section including the opening _trumpet-and-chorus_ fanfare and the _signed Latin text_ setting. **An important distinction** : Britten sets the medieval Latin _Dies irae_ sequence text in full, but he composes his own music for it — he does _not_ directly quote the medieval chant melody. The work's place in the _Dies Irae_ lineage is through the text and the tradition rather than through the chant melody itself.

  3. **The Owen poems.** The English-language poems Britten chose for the _War Requiem_ are _anti-war_ — Owen's poetry was _pacifist in conviction_ , written from the trenches before his own death in November 1918. The Britten setting _uses_ the Latin Requiem text as _the official-religious frame_ and _uses_ the Owen English poetry as _the personal-human counterweight_. The two voices _speak alongside each other_ — sometimes echoing, sometimes contradicting, sometimes simply juxtaposed without comment.

  4. **The signed Latin _Dies Irae_ text** (Thread B!). Britten's setting of the _Dies Irae_ text is _explicit and unmistakable_ — the full Latin sequence text is sung by the chorus, signed openly as the medieval _Dies Irae_. The chant melody itself is not directly quoted (Britten composes his own music for the Latin words), but the work places itself unambiguously inside the _Dies Irae_ lineage: the same text the chant has carried for seven centuries, now set to twentieth-century music against Owen's English war poetry. This is **your fourth encounter with Thread B** (after Berlioz in Chapter 16 — the chant melody directly quoted; Tchaikovsky in Chapter 20 — the Russian Orthodox cousin chant; Mahler in Chapter 21 — allusion-level). Britten's contribution is the _text-setting_ mode of the lineage: the Latin words signed openly, the chant melody not quoted, the tradition continued.

#### One-sentence backgrounds

**Shostakovich, Symphony No. 5 in D minor, Op. 47** — composed April–July 1937 in Leningrad; premiered 21 November 1937 in Leningrad, conducted by Yevgeny Mravinsky (whom we met in Chapter 20); the work's subtitle is _A Soviet artist's creative answer to just criticism_ ; ~45 minutes in four movements (Moderato — Allegretto — Largo — Allegro non troppo). The first movement runs ~16 minutes; the fourth movement runs ~10 minutes.

**Britten,_War Requiem_ , Op. 66** — choral-orchestral work combining the Latin Requiem Mass text with English-language war poetry by Wilfred Owen; composed 1961–1962 in Aldeburgh, England; premiered 30 May 1962 at the consecration of the new Coventry Cathedral, conducted by the composer; ~85 minutes in six sections (Requiem aeternam — Dies Irae — Offertorium — Sanctus — Agnus Dei — Libera me). The Dies Irae section is the longest — ~30 minutes; we focus on a ~10-minute portion of it.

### 24.2 The Listening Window

#### Shostakovich Symphony No. 5, First Movement (Bernstein / NYPO 1959, ~16 minutes)

* **0:00–0:30.** **Opening jagged figure.** Strings begin a descending, jagged figure in D minor — _low strings_ and _upper strings_ alternating with sharp accents. The music is _austere, minor-modal, weighted_. The character is _immediately serious_.

* **0:30–3:00.** **First theme group development.** Multiple thematic ideas emerge — a more _lyrical_ second theme; a _march-like_ third theme; brief moments of _celesta_ ; the opening jagged figure recurs. The music is _thematically dense_.

* **3:00–6:00.** **First major build.** The texture grows fuller; brass enters; dynamics climb toward a first climactic peak. The opening jagged figure returns in intensified form.

* **6:00–8:00.** **Withdrawal and second-theme presentation.** The music withdraws; a _more lyrical_ second-theme statement emerges, with the _piano playing a key role_ (the piano sometimes plays _high register_ with _sparkling_ effect, sometimes _low register_ with _hammered_ effect).

* **8:00–11:00.** **The climactic central section.** Fortissimo. The full orchestra plays the _jagged opening figure_ and other thematic materials at maximum intensity. The brass is at its most prominent. _This is the movement's emotional peak._

* **11:00–14:00.** **Long withdrawal.** Dynamics decrease gradually; the texture thins; the piano returns to _sparkling_ high-register figures.

* **14:00–16:00.** **The quiet ending.** The strings play _very soft_ figures in the upper register; the piano provides distant _celesta-like_ punctuation. The movement ends _quietly_ — _not_ a definitive close but a _transitional ending_ that _prepares the next movement_.

The first movement is _one of the most-balanced_ of Shostakovich's symphonic structures. The _thematic density_ combined with the _clear A-B-A overall shape_ (opening / climactic middle / quiet ending) gives the movement _both intellectual rigor and immediate emotional accessibility_. It is widely considered Shostakovich's most-successful symphonic first movement.

#### Shostakovich Symphony No. 5, Fourth Movement Finale (Bernstein / NYPO 1959, ~10 minutes)

* **0:00–0:30.** **Opening fanfare.** Brilliant brass fanfare — fast, fortissimo, in D minor. The brass plays _triumphal_ gestures with _strong accents_.

* **0:30–3:00.** **Forced march.** The brass fanfare gives way to a _march_ — _strong rhythmic figure_ , _brass and percussion prominent_ , _forte to fortissimo dynamics_. The march has _triumphal character_ but with _mechanical insistence_.

* **3:00–4:00.** **Modulation to D major.** The music modulates from D minor to D major — the _home key for the triumphal close_. The brass continues to lead; the music's character grows _more openly celebratory_.

* **4:00–6:00.** **Slow middle section.** Around 4:00, the music _slows substantially_. The strings enter with a _lyrical, slow_ second theme in _D major_. The tempo drops; the texture becomes more _contemplative_. _This is the movement's brief inward moment_ — the _thinking_ before the final affirmation.

* **6:00–8:00.** **Build back to the triumphal close.** The brass returns; the rhythm accelerates; the dynamics climb. The music drives toward the _final celebratory cadence_.

* **8:00–10:00.** **Final climactic close.** The full orchestra plays _fortissimo D-major_ — the closing 100 bars are _insistent triumphal celebration_. The music ends with _definitive D-major cadences_ — _but at what tempo?_

Mravinsky in his 1937 premiere (and in his subsequent 1956 and 1984 recordings) took the final 100 bars at _slow tempo_ — almost _mechanical-march_ tempo. Some Shostakovich scholars (especially the Volkov-faction — see below) read the slow tempo as _coding the forcedness_ of the triumph. Bernstein in his 1959 recording (and many subsequent Western conductors) took the final bars at _fast tempo_ — _energetically triumphal_. The slow-vs-fast tempo question is _one of the central interpretive choices_ in performing the Fifth. Whether the symphony's ending is _sincere triumph_ or _forced triumph_ depends partly on tempo.

#### Britten _War Requiem_ , Dies Irae portion (Britten / LSO 1963, ~10 minutes)

* **0:00–0:30.** **Opening fanfare.** Brass and percussion play _fanfare-like_ figures — _trumpet calls_ , _military signals_. The opening is _deliberately military_ — the chorus is being prepared for the _Last Trumpet_ imagery.

* **0:30–3:00.** **Chorus enters with _Dies Irae_ text.** Full chorus sings _Dies irae, dies illa_ (Day of wrath, that day). The music is _full-textured, fortissimo, in D minor_. The Latin sequence text is signed openly; Britten composes his own music for it (he does not quote the medieval chant melody directly). Thread B here takes its _text-setting_ form.

* **3:00–5:00.** **Owen poem interjection.** The chorus drops out. _Tenor soloist_ (Peter Pears in the original recording) sings Wilfred Owen's poem _Bugles sang_ in chamber-orchestra accompaniment. The character shifts from _Latin liturgical-monumental_ to _English personal-soldier_. The juxtaposition is _deliberate_ — Britten is asking the listener to hear the two voices simultaneously.

* **5:00–6:30.** **_Dies Irae_ returns with new text.** The chorus returns with _Tuba mirum spargens sonum_ (The trumpet, spreading wondrous sound). Britten's setting of the Latin sequence continues; the orchestral writing is _fuller, more apocalyptic_.

* **6:30–8:00.** **Owen poem:_Be slowly lifted up, thou long black arm_**. _Baritone soloist_ (Dietrich Fischer-Dieskau in the original) sings another Owen poem about long-range artillery in World War I. The chamber-orchestra accompaniment is _darker, more violent_. The English text _contradicts_ the Latin text — the official _Last Judgment_ is being undercut by the personal _World War I cannon_.

* **8:00–10:00.** **The climactic _Dies Irae_ return.** The chorus, soloists, and orchestra come together for a _fortissimo_ statement of _Dies irae_ with full forces. Britten's setting of the Latin text reaches its peak. The music drives to a _full-orchestra climax_ before transitioning to the next section.

The Britten _War Requiem_ is **post-Beethoven 9, post-Brahms-Requiem, post-Mozart-Requiem** — but with the specifically twentieth-century _anti-war_ dimension that _no previous Requiem had_. Britten was a _committed pacifist_ throughout his life (he was a conscientious objector in World War II); the _War Requiem_ uses the Latin Requiem tradition to _make a peace statement_ rather than to _console the dead_.

The work's structure — _Latin Requiem text + Owen English war poetry_ — is _the work's central innovation_. The two voices alternate and combine; the audience hears _the official-religious_ alongside _the personal-soldier_ ; the resulting effect is a _double counterpoint of two historical-aesthetic traditions_ (the centuries-old Catholic Requiem tradition and the contemporary anti-war poetry).

### 24.3 What's Happening in the Music

#### Definition: Soviet Music and Socialist Realism

_Soviet music_ — the music composed under Soviet political control from approximately 1917 to 1991 — was _subject to specific political constraints_. The Soviet aesthetic doctrine of _Socialist Realism_ (adopted formally in 1932 for literature and gradually extended to music) required Soviet art to be _accessible to the proletariat_ , _optimistic about Soviet society_ , _anti-formalist_ (anti-Western-modernist), and _positive in social content_. Composers who deviated from these requirements risked _denunciation, career destruction, exile, imprisonment, or death_.

The Shostakovich Symphony No. 5 was composed _under direct Socialist Realist pressure_ after the 1936 _Pravda_ attack. The work was required to _demonstrate Shostakovich's rehabilitation_ — to show he had _understood the criticism_ and _responded with appropriate Soviet music_. The subtitle (_A Soviet artist's creative answer to just criticism_) was _Shostakovich's compliance with this requirement_. The composer needed to _appear to have learned his lesson_.

Whether he _had_ learned the lesson — whether the symphony genuinely affirms Soviet values or covertly resists them — is the _eighty-year debate_ about the work. The book holds the question carefully and does not adjudicate.

#### Definition: The Volkov Controversy

_Solomon Volkov's _Testimony__ * (1979) is a book published in the West that claimed to be Shostakovich's _secret memoirs_ — dictated by Shostakovich to Volkov in the early 1970s, with the understanding that the contents would be published only after Shostakovich's death. The book paints Shostakovich as _secretly anti-Soviet throughout his life_ , with his official Soviet compositions read as _coded resistance_ to Stalinism. The Symphony No. 5's finale, in the _Testimony_ account, is _not_ sincere triumph but _forced rejoicing_ ; the loud D-major celebrations are _mocking the Soviet demand for celebration_.

The Volkov book has been _contested_ since its 1979 publication. Some musicologists accept it as _authentic Shostakovich_ ; others argue it is _Volkov's invention_ or _Volkov's elaboration_ of partial Shostakovich materials. Documentary investigations have produced _partial confirmation_ and _partial refutation_ — some passages in _Testimony_ match documented Shostakovich speech; some appear to be _composed by Volkov_. The book's status as _primary source_ is _unclear_.

The Volkov controversy has divided Shostakovich scholarship into two camps:

* **The _anti-Soviet Shostakovich_ camp** (which includes some of the leading Shostakovich biographers including Ian MacDonald and Allan Ho) reads the symphonies as _coded resistance_ throughout. The Fifth Symphony's triumphalism is _fake_ , _mocking_ , _anti-Stalinist in disguise_.
* **The _complicated Shostakovich_ camp** (which includes Richard Taruskin and many academic musicologists) reads the symphonies as _not simply anti-Soviet_ — the composer was _navigating_ Soviet pressure with mixed compliance and resistance; the music can be heard _both_ as sincere Soviet symphony _and_ as expressing private feeling, simultaneously.
* **Some argue _Shostakovich was a Soviet patriot_** — the symphonies _do_ affirm Soviet values, and the _Pravda_ attack was a _temporary aberration_ rather than a fundamental break.

The book _does not adjudicate_. The Fifth Symphony is great music; the contextual question is unresolved; the listener can hold the question open while engaging with the music.

#### Definition: The Second Viennese School

The _Second Viennese School_ is the term applied to the composer _Arnold Schoenberg_ (1874–1951) and his two principal students _Alban Berg_ (1885–1935) and _Anton Webern_ (1883–1945). The three composers worked in Vienna in the early twentieth century and developed _atonal music_ (music without a clear tonal center) and then _twelve-tone serialism_ (music organized around the systematic use of all twelve chromatic pitches).

The school's key innovations:

* **Atonality** (Schoenberg's _Second String Quartet_ (1908) — the work that crosses from late-Romantic chromaticism into music with no tonal center; _Verklärte Nacht_ (1899) is still post-Wagnerian chromatic tonality, but Pelleas und Melisande (1903) and the Second Quartet move into atonality).
* **Twelve-tone serialism** (developed by Schoenberg around 1923, codified in his _Five Piano Pieces, Op. 23_ (1923) and _Suite for Piano, Op. 25_ (1923–1924)). The technique organizes all twelve chromatic pitches into a _series_ (a specific ordering of the twelve pitches), with the series used as the work's _thematic-harmonic foundation_. The technique was _the most-influential Western compositional method_ of the mid-twentieth century.
* **Expressionism** (the school's aesthetic orientation toward _intense psychological expression_ through _highly chromatic, dissonant_ music). Schoenberg's _Erwartung_ (1909), Berg's _Wozzeck_ (1925 opera), and Webern's early atonal works are major expressionist works.

The three composers' individual voices were quite different:

* **Schoenberg** : the systematic theorist and the founder. Major works include _Verklärte Nacht_ (1899), _Pelleas und Melisande_ (1903), _Pierrot Lunaire_ (1912), _Five Pieces for Orchestra_ (1909, revised 1922), _Erwartung_ (1909), the _Five Piano Pieces, Op. 23_ (1923), _Moses und Aron_ (unfinished opera, 1932), the _Piano Concerto_ (1942).
* **Berg** : the most-Romantic of the three. _Wozzeck_ (1925 opera), _Lyric Suite_ (1926 string quartet), _Lulu_ (unfinished opera, 1935), _Violin Concerto_ (1935 — his final completed work, dedicated to _the memory of an angel_ — the young Manon Gropius, daughter of Alma Mahler and Walter Gropius).
* **Webern** : the most-concentrated and _aphoristic_ of the three. Webern's works are typically _very short_ (some movements last under one minute); the _Symphony Op. 21_ (1928), the _Piano Variations Op. 27_ (1936), the _Cantatas Op. 29 and Op. 31_ (1939, 1943).

For amateur listeners, the Second Viennese School is one of the more-difficult musical worlds to enter — the music _deliberately rejects_ the tonal expectations the rest of this book has been developing. The technical primer above gives you the framework; the _listening primer_ below gives you brief tastes.

#### Brief listening primer for the Second Viennese School

We will not focus deeply on Schoenberg, Berg, or Webern in this chapter (any one of them would deserve a chapter of their own). The chapter touches each briefly for _literacy_ — so you know what _the Second Viennese School_ refers to and can recognize the idiom when you encounter it elsewhere.

**Schoenberg,_Verklärte Nacht_ Op. 4** (1899, ~30 minutes, string sextet — later orchestrated): The transitional work between _Wagnerian chromatic tonality_ and _atonality_. Listen to the opening five minutes — the sound is _post-Wagnerian_ but the chromaticism is more _intense_ than Wagner's. _This is the door_ into the Second Viennese School.

**Berg,_Wozzeck_ — the Marie lullaby scene** (Act I, scene 3, ~5 minutes): An atonal opera about a working-class soldier's psychological disintegration. The Marie lullaby is the opera's _most-tonally-accessible moment_ — Marie, the working-class woman who is Wozzeck's lover, sings a lullaby to their son. The music is _deeply expressive_ in atonal language. _This is the most-accessible entry point_ into operatic atonality.

**Webern,_Symphony Op. 21_ , second movement** (1928, ~5 minutes): A _twelve-tone serial_ symphonic movement, _extremely compressed_ , with the orchestra reduced to _small chamber forces_. Webern's signature _pointillistic_ texture — _single notes from different instruments_ punctuating the silence. _This is the most-difficult_ listening of the three but the most-revealing of _what twelve-tone serialism sounds like_.

These three brief tastes — _Verklärte Nacht_ opening, _Wozzeck_ Marie lullaby, Webern _Symphony Op. 21_ second movement — give you literacy-level exposure to the Second Viennese School. Each of these composers deserves much more attention than the chapter can give; this is a _primer_ , not a full chapter.

#### Common Misconception

People sometimes assume that the _Pravda_ attack on Shostakovich and the eighty-year Volkov controversy mean that _we cannot enjoy_ the Shostakovich Fifth Symphony as music — that the political-historical baggage _overwhelms_ the music. This is too simple.

The Shostakovich Fifth is _great music regardless of how the political question is resolved_. The first movement's thematic density, the third movement's slow lyrical Largo, the fourth movement's controversial finale — all are _substantial musical achievements_ that reward close listening. A listener can love the Fifth Symphony _while holding the political question open_. A listener can listen to the Bernstein recording _while also_ listening to the Mravinsky recording (which takes the finale slow rather than fast) and noticing the _interpretive difference_. A listener can read the Volkov controversy while listening to the music and recognize the unresolved question.

The music is _enriched_ by knowing the political context — the suitcase by the bed, the _Pravda_ attack, the 1937 premiere as Shostakovich's rehabilitation. The music is _not diminished_ by the politics. The mature listener can hold both — _the music itself_ and _the historical-political dimension_ — without confusing them. The book has been arguing this throughout (with Wagner, with Furtwängler, with Mozart's Requiem, with the Mahler-Alma marriage, with Tchaikovsky's death). Shostakovich is one more instance.

### 24.4 The Stories

#### Shostakovich's life

Dmitri Dmitrievich Shostakovich was born on 25 September 1906 in Saint Petersburg, the second of three children of a chemist and a pianist. The family was middle-class; the household was musical. He studied at the Petrograd Conservatory (renamed Leningrad Conservatory after the Russian Revolution) from age 13 to age 19.

His Symphony No. 1 (1925), composed as his graduation work at age 19, was internationally premiered in 1926 and made Shostakovich a global figure in his early twenties. The 1920s and early 1930s were his _Soviet sensation_ period — he composed prolifically, his works were performed widely in the USSR and Europe, he was _the favorite young composer_ of the Soviet cultural establishment.

The 1936 _Pravda_ attack changed everything (described above). The 1937 Fifth Symphony was his rehabilitation; the 1938 Quintet for Piano and Strings (Op. 57) and the 1939 Symphony No. 6 continued the rehabilitation. The 1941 Symphony No. 7 "Leningrad" (composed during the German siege of Leningrad in autumn 1941) was a major international event — the symphony was _broadcast from besieged Leningrad in 1942_ and was performed by every major Western orchestra during the war; the _Time_ magazine cover for July 1942 showed Shostakovich in firefighter's helmet. The wartime work made Shostakovich an internationally-revered figure.

The 1948 _Zhdanov Decree_ — a second major denunciation by the Soviet cultural establishment, attacking Shostakovich, Prokofiev, and other leading Soviet composers as _formalist_ — produced another period of crisis for Shostakovich. He was forced to _recant_ his compositional style; some of his works were withdrawn from performance; he composed _officially approved music_ (the _Song of the Forests_ in 1949, a setting of Stalinist environmental texts) alongside _private_ works (the Violin Concerto No. 1, the String Quartet No. 5) that were not premiered until after Stalin's death in 1953.

The post-Stalin years (1953 onward) gave Shostakovich more compositional freedom but did not eliminate the political constraints. He continued composing through the late 1950s, 1960s, and early 1970s. The major late works include Symphony No. 10 (1953 — written immediately after Stalin's death, with what some hear as _the composer's personal voice finally emerging_), Symphony No. 13 "Babi Yar" (1962, on Yevtushenko's poem about the Nazi massacre of Kiev Jews in 1941 — a politically sensitive subject in the Soviet 1960s), the late string quartets (Op. 117–138, composed 1960s–1970s), Symphony No. 14 (1969 — eleven songs about death), and Symphony No. 15 (1971 — slow-ending symphony in dialogue with Mahler 9 and Tchaikovsky 6).

He joined the Communist Party in 1960 (an extremely complicated decision — he had refused for decades; the post-1953 thaw and post-1956 Khrushchev period had produced new pressures). He remained a Communist Party member to his death. The party membership has been read by Volkov-faction biographers as _forced compliance under continuing duress_ ; by other biographers as _genuine if reluctant accommodation_.

He died on 9 August 1975 in Moscow, age 68, of lung cancer. He was given an official Soviet state funeral; he was buried at the Novodevichy Cemetery in Moscow, alongside Russia's leading writers and political figures.

#### Britten's life

Benjamin Britten was born on 22 November 1913 in Lowestoft, England, the youngest of four children of a dentist. He showed musical talent early — composing from age 5, studying with Frank Bridge from age 11.

He studied at the Royal College of Music (London) from 1930. In 1934 he wrote the _Sinfonietta_ for orchestra; in 1936 he wrote _Our Hunting Fathers_ for soprano and orchestra (on left-wing political-anti-fascist texts). In 1939 he and his lifelong partner _Peter Pears_ (the tenor for whom Britten composed many of his major vocal works) moved to the United States — partly to avoid the looming European war; partly because Britten was a _pacifist_ and would have refused to serve in the British military.

In 1942 Britten and Pears returned to Britain (Britten registered as a _conscientious objector_ and was assigned to non-combat war work). The years 1942–1945 produced Britten's first major operas — _Peter Grimes_ (1945), his first big international success — and the major chamber works.

The post-war years (1945–1962) were Britten's _operatic-summit_ period. _Peter Grimes_ (1945), _Billy Budd_ (1951, based on Melville), _The Turn of the Screw_ (1954, based on Henry James), _A Midsummer Night's Dream_ (1960, based on Shakespeare), and other operas established Britten as _the most-successful operatic composer of his generation_. He founded the Aldeburgh Festival in 1948 with Pears — an English-village summer festival that became one of the most-important contemporary-music festivals in Europe.

The 1962 _War Requiem_ (this chapter) was Britten's _post-war summation_. The Coventry Cathedral commission was _politically resonant_ (the new cathedral as postwar reconciliation gesture; the multinational soloists symbolizing reconciliation between former enemies); Britten responded with one of the most-substantial twentieth-century choral works. The premiere was a major British cultural event; the Decca recording (with the original premiere soloists) became one of the best-selling classical recordings of the 1960s.

The post-_War Requiem_ years saw Britten continue to compose — three church parables (_Curlew River_ , _The Burning Fiery Furnace_ , _The Prodigal Son_ , 1964–1968), more orchestral works, the operas _Owen Wingrave_ (1971) and _Death in Venice_ (1973, based on Thomas Mann's novella). His health declined in the early 1970s; he died on 4 December 1976 in Aldeburgh, age 63, of heart failure following long illness.

The Britten-Pears partnership is one of the most-documented romantic-creative-collaborative pairings in twentieth-century music. The two lived together from the early 1940s until Britten's death; Pears sang the title roles in most of Britten's major operas; the partnership was _socially complicated_ in mid-century Britain (homosexuality was _illegal_ in England until 1967) and was _publicly discreet_ , _privately central_.

#### Recordings

**Leonard Bernstein / New York Philharmonic, 1959 (Sony Classical / Columbia)** for Shostakovich 5. Bernstein's first recording of the Fifth (he would record it again). _Fast finale tempo_ — Bernstein takes the closing 100 bars at _full speed_ , producing a _triumphal-energetic_ close. The reading is widely loved.

**Yevgeny Mravinsky / Leningrad Philharmonic, 1984 (DG, live)** for Shostakovich 5. Mravinsky was the _premiere conductor of the Fifth_ (he conducted the 1937 Leningrad premiere) and recorded the work multiple times across his career. The 1984 live recording is one of the last. _Slow finale tempo_ — Mravinsky takes the closing 100 bars at _slower-than-typical Western tempo_ , producing a _more mechanical-march_ close. The slow-tempo reading is the _original_ tempo (Mravinsky was conducting from Shostakovich's 1937 markings); the _fast Western tempo_ may be a _later interpretive choice_ not in the score.

**Vasily Petrenko / Royal Liverpool Philharmonic, 2009 (Naxos)** for Shostakovich 5. A contemporary Russian reading with a major British orchestra. Petrenko was one of the leading Shostakovich conductors of the early 21st century; his complete cycle is widely admired.

**Britten / London Symphony Orchestra / Vishnevskaya / Pears / Fischer-Dieskau, 1963 (Decca)** for the _War Requiem_. The classic recording — made by the composer with the original premiere soloists less than a year after the premiere. _The recording captures the work at its inaugural moment_. Decca made the recording in stereo at considerable expense; it was widely distributed and became one of the most-influential classical recordings of the 1960s.

**Richard Hickox / LSO and Chorus, 1991 (Chandos)** for the _War Requiem_. A modern alternative recording, with Heather Harper as soprano. _Clean, structurally clear, dramatically committed_.

#### Cross-piece links

* For more **Shostakovich** , listen to **Symphony No. 7 "Leningrad"** (1941, the wartime symphony, with the famous _invasion theme_ in the first movement), **Symphony No. 10 in E minor** (1953, the post-Stalin symphony), **String Quartet No. 8 in C minor** (1960, the most-personal of his fifteen string quartets, dedicated _To the memory of the victims of fascism and war_), and the **Cello Concerto No. 1 in E♭ major** (1959, composed for Mstislav Rostropovich, the iconic Russian cellist).
* For more **Britten** , listen to **Peter Grimes** (1945 opera, especially the _Four Sea Interludes_), the **Young Person's Guide to the Orchestra** (1946 — the variation-and-fugue on Purcell that introduces every instrument of the orchestra), the **Cello Symphony Op. 68** (1963 — for Rostropovich), and the late opera **Death in Venice** (1973).
* For the **Second Viennese School deepening** , listen to **Schoenberg's _Five Pieces for Orchestra_ Op. 16** (1909), **Berg's _Wozzeck_** (1925 opera, complete), and **Webern's complete works** — Webern's total output runs to about 4 hours; the _Symphony Op. 21_ , the _Concerto Op. 24_ , the _String Quartet Op. 28_ , and the _Cantata Op. 31_ are starting points.
* For **the contemporary anti-war classical tradition** , listen to **John Adams's _On the Transmigration of Souls_** (2002, for the September 11 victims) and to Britten's later **Cantata Misericordium Op. 69** (1963, for the centenary of the International Red Cross).

* _Ask the companion about the Volkov controversy — the claim that the Shostakovich Fifth's finale is coded resistance rather than sincere triumph, what evidence supports each side, and why the question has not been resolved in 45 years since the Volkov publication._
